News.title: Trump says he will declare Strait of Hormuz a US territory after war is over as new aircraft carrier heads to blockade
News.content:
TRUMP has said he will make the Strait of Hormuz US territory after the Iran war is over, as a new warship heads for the global chokepoint.

During a speech at a Long Island police academy, the US President confidently declared that the gateway to the Gulf would one day be “a territory of the United States”.



About a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies pass through the narrow channel, making it one of the most critical transit pathway on the globe.

During the speech Friday the president said: “After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon, I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.



“Essentially, that’s what it is.

“We have the blockade.



“No ships get through unless we want them to.”

Prior to the US launch of strikes on Iran earlier this year, the Strait of Hormuz was a crucial maritime passageway for oil tankers.



But since the start of the war passage through the strait has been difficult and has, at times, completely closed – causing sever global shocks due to skyrocketing oil prices.

Control of the flow of traffic through the strait has been a burning issue in peace negotiations between the warring states.

The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and is governed by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

No single country owns it, as parts overlap the territorial waters of both nations.

Trump’s speech comes as the US Navy deployed another aircraft carrier to waters off Iran after a scandal erupted over the conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.



While it was first thought that the USS Theodore Roosevelt would make its way to the Middle East, the Washington is said to have been been deployed to the area, according to an anonymous US official.

The strait has been the site of renewed fighting in recent months.

Despite a memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June to bring a stop to military operations in the war, fighting resumed by the end of the month.

Iran has continued to target commercial vessels in the strait, claiming that part of the strait falls within its territorial waters and therefore remains under its control.

Meanwhile the US has set up a naval blockade in the strait, where the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln launches airstrikes.

News.title: Shocking moment yobs leap on cars & smash windscreens in random early hours wrecking spree on ‘Wild West’ estate
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment two yobs smashed up parked cars in an early morning wrecking spree on a “Wild West” estate.

The shameless pair were caught on camera damaging a Renault Clio and a Nissan Duke, in footage released by cops.



Video footage shows the two yobs approaching two vehicles on a motorbike, before one jumps on a car bonnet.

The thug then boots the windscreen on the “Wild West-like” estate in Worcester.



The hooded lout then darts to a neighbouring motor which appears to be a Nissan Juke, stamping on the glass again.

He visibly cracking the windscreen glass with his feet in the unnecessary act of vandalism.



The thug then sprints back to the waiting motorbike before the pair make their escape at 4.28am on July 27.

Furious locals later found their car wing mirrors kicked off and shoe prints stamped across bonnets and roofs.



Disgruntled residents said that they are now “fearful” for their property after the chaotic scenes.

One neighbour, who asked to remain anonymous, said their once peaceful area had turned into the “Wild West” in recent years.

The homeowner said: “You never know what new chaos is going to greet you at the front door each day.

“There’s a lot that could be done with the abandoned plots of land around here.

“Instead it’s just filled with trash, vandalised abandoned cars and brainless kids doing doughnuts in rented cars.”



The resident added: “I’m aware that it’s probably just kids but I’ve been told they are targeting cars belonging to residents.

“I’m just fearful for my own property now.”

A spokesperson for West Mercia Police confirmed that enquiries are on-going into the incident.

The spokesperson added: “We received a call around 8am on July 27 with a report of two vehicles being damaged on Williamson Road in Worcester.

“Enquiries are on-going.”

News.title: ‘Aggressive’ dolphins spotted at UK seaside beauty spot as holidaymakers warned ‘do not approach’
News.content:
FLIPPING HELL ‘Aggressive’ dolphins spotted at UK seaside beauty spot as holidaymakers warned ‘do not approach’

HOLIDAYMAKERS have been warned to stay away from dolphins after a new mum and her calf were surrounded by tourists at a popular seaside beauty spot.

Officials said visitors got too close to the animals at New Quay harbour in Cardigan Bay, west Wales, risking serious injury.



The area is home to one of Britain’s biggest populations of bottlenose dolphins, which regularly visit the harbour and nearby coastline.

Now the Ceredigion Harbour Authority has issued an alert to paddleboarders, kayakers, swimmers and other water users, urging them to keep their distance.



Experts warned that female dolphins protecting young calves can become aggressive if they feel threatened.

Melanie Heath, Cardigan Bay marine protected area officer, said: “We are incredibly fortunate to have dolphins regularly visiting and living in Ceredigion and seeing them is often a highlight for those enjoying our coastline.

“While we understand the excitement that comes with such encounters, this is a dangerous situation.

“Dolphins are big powerful animals, up to four metres long, and apex predators.

“A female with a calf is particularly vulnerable to disturbance and may become aggressive to protect her calf.

“There have been incidents around the UK of bottlenose dolphins attacking humans who are in too close proximity by ramming, tail thrashing or trying to hold them under the water.



“To keep both people and the dolphins safe, we need everyone to give them space and keep at least 100 metres, the length of a football pitch, away.”

Dolphins are protected under wildlife legislation, and it is an offence to deliberately disturb them.

She added: “Mother dolphins with young calves can be particularly vulnerable to disturbance.

“We are asking paddleboarders, kayakers and swimmers not to approach, follow or attempt to interact with dolphins.

“Move away if you are in the water, and do not enter the water from the beach to get a closer view.”



The warning comes after reports that visitors had crowded around the mother and calf in the harbour,.

It prompted fears both people and the animals could be put at risk.

News.title: Horror doorbell cam footage shows moment family’s home was engulfed by Stourbridge inferno that destroyed 19 houses
News.content:
THIS is the horrifying moment a family’s ring doorbell captured their home being engulfed by an inferno that ripped through Stourbridge.

A total of 19 homes were completely destroyed and 18 others damaged as families forced to evacuate as the fire spread across Stourbridge, West Midlands, on Thursday afternoon.



Now, footage captured by one heartbroken family has revealed the extent of the devastation.

Richard and Rose-Anne Vinten only moved in five months ago but their home is one of dozens destroyed or damaged by the wildfire.



Shocking video released by the couple’s showed their garden catching alight with just a few flames.

But moments later an inferno was in full force as their house was engulfed by the blaze.

The raging fire continued to consume all in its path as it decimated the surrounding area and other houses.

As the horrifying video came to an end, thick black smoke had completely obscured the camera.



Speaking to ITV Rose-Anne added: “It was really scary to be honest, it felt like I was in a movie”.

“I was really scared but I knew at the same time I needed to be brave for my kids, because my daughter was really worried.

“When I went over to next door and saw them just standing there at the window, looking and they could see that their house was on fire, so I had to just hold it all in.”

West Midlands Fire Service chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said the fire spread over more than 500 acres in Stourbridge.

He confirmed 19 properties were gutted, with drone footage showing homes completely destroyed and covered in ash.



Horrifying aerial footage shows the blaze ripping through a 40-acre residential area, destroying homes and gardens.

A rescue centre has been set up for those forced to flee their homes.

Local resident Jane Baxter said she could see the flames from her “bedroom window” and described the “horrendous” choking smell in the air.



She and neighbours were given a few minutes to gather their belongings before fleeing, with the blaze just 200 yards away.

Stourbridge councillor Andrew Tromans said: “The apocalyptic scenes in Norton and across Stourbridge are sadly just a taste of what is to come if we don’t act.

“It is my view, and it has been for a while, that Dudley councillors must have an emergency meeting about [how] we protect our borough from the impacts of climate change.”

Cops are investigating the cause of the Stourbridge inferno, with reports of it starting in a nearby grassland before spreading to homes.

A total of 11 major fire incidents were reported in the past 24 hours, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council chairman.



The surge in the number of blazes saw millions of Brits receive an emergency alert on their phones warning against the high risk of wildfires on Friday evening.

The government issued the alert warning people “not to light anything that could spark a fire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks” with the country in the middle of another heatwave.

The blaring alert pinged the phones of millions across the nation around 7pm on Friday.



The alert has gone through even if a phone is set to silent, with the sound and vibration lasting about 10 seconds.

Accompanied by a siren sound, it warned that “even a small flame can rapidly develop into a major wildfire placing lives, homes, businesses and emergency responders at risk”.

The alert added: “Recipients will also be urged to report any fire immediately by calling 999.”

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the request “came directly from Fire and Rescue Services”.

He urged the public to help “keep everyone safe and prevent more fires from starting”.

News.title: Over 1,200 tourists and locals evacuated from holiday hotspot as huge wildfire inferno spreads quickly killing one
News.content:
HELL-LIKE infernos have torn across Croatia’s coastline killing one and forcing thousands to urgently evacuate.

Spreading at “lightning speed,” the catastrophic blazes were captured in harrowing footage that defies belief, marking what is thought to be the most severe fire in the country’s history.



Around 1,200 terrified holidaymakers and locals were evacuated – forced to stay the night in emergency shelters.

Some desperate individuals escaped into the sea from boats near the coastline to escape the fire.



The inferno broke out near the coastal village of Lokva Rogoznica on Thursday evening.

It quickly spread to the nearby tourist town of Omis and eventually reached villages near the popular Brit holiday spot Split.

The destructive firestorm burnt through “everything in their path”, according to Croatia‘s fire chief Slavko Tucakovic who described it as “one of the worst” blazes in the country’s history.

Officials confirmed flames, exacerbated by strong winds, engulfed 1,000 hectares of land in just four hours.



One person was confirmed dead after firefighters discovered a body at an area ravaged by the blaze.

Ten people are fighting for their lives as a total of 14 victims were hospitalised and 40 injured.

Over 300 fire personal fought the flames with the blaze so intense at points, crews were forced to retreat.



Footage shared online shows thick smoke and huge flames tearing through surrounding landscape, turning the sky orange, as dumbfounded residents and tourists looked on.

Roads were gridlocked with motorists attempting to flee while bright orange flames licked in the near distance.

Praising the work of the hero firefighters who toiled throughout the night and morning, Croatia’s Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said what they achieved was “truly a miracle”.

Later on Friday Plenkovic visited the incinerated epicentre near Omis.

The flammable pine forests lining the Croatian hillside compounded the already complex firefighting response.



The Commander of Omis Volunteer Fire Department, Viseslav Pesic told Reuters the blaze was so intense that people had abandoned vehicles “directly in the fire zone”, making it difficult for emergency crews to pass through.

Extensive damage was inflicted on homes, cars and the landscape.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It comes as devastating wildfires struck the Halkidiki peninsula, Greece, on Thursday.

Hundreds of people were evacuated from beaches as a “wall of flames” threatened two tourists resorts.

News.title: Huge 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes Indonesia quickly followed by second 6.2 shock as tsunami warning issued
News.content:
A HUGE 7.7-magnitude earthquake has rocked Indonesia’s coast, with a tsunami warning issued as powerful tremors rippled through the region.

Footage shared online shows buildings reduced to crumbling shells, with walls and roofs collapsing into heaps of concrete and twisted wreckage.



The videos show terrified locals scrambling to safety as debris comes hurtling down.

It’s epicentre was 68km north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province.



Other clips capture structures violently buckling and giving way, leaving behind little more than piles of rubble.

In one terrifying scene, a building can be seen violently shaking as furniture is thrown from balconies.

A bridge was also filmed swaying from side to side, as terrified locals watched the unstable structure shudder.

The quake was initially measured at 6.9 magnitude before being dramatically upgraded to 7.7 by the EMSC, marking a far more powerful jolt than first feared.

The seismic shock struck at a depth of 35km at 5.58am local time.

A second 6.3-magnitude earthquake hit the same region just 15 minutes later at 6.13am local time, according to the EMSC.



The agency has issued an early tsunami warning for East Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi, West Nusa Tenggara, and Southeast Sulawesi.

Fears have mounted over the possibility of a tsunami after one local captured the moment the sea receded along the Indonesian coastline.



Residents along affected coastlines were advised to move to higher ground as officials are closely monitoring coastal tide gauges for any changes.

In April, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck in the Molucca Sea off Indonesia’s Ternate island killing at least one person.

A 70-year-old woman in North Sulawesi died after being crushed by building debris.

Another person broke their leg after jumping off a building, Indonesia’s national news agency Antara reported.



The monster quake marks the 6th global earthquake of magnitude 7.0 or higher within the last two months.

Just hours earlier, Mount Ibu erupted in a spectacular blast, unleashing an enormous ash plume that soared 5km into the sky above Halmahera.

Indonesia is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone nations, with its 17,000-plus islands sitting along the volatile Pacific “Ring of Fire” – a vast horseshoe of active volcanoes and powerful fault lines responsible for frequent seismic activity.

News.title: Spies catch Russian hitman who ‘planned to kill popular rapper helping launch drone strikes on Moscow’
News.content:
SHADOW WAR Spies catch Russian hitman who ‘planned to kill popular rapper helping launch drone strikes on Moscow’

SPIES have caught a Russian hitman who allegedly planned to kill a popular rapper helping launch drone strikes on Moscow.

The suspected assassin was allegedly dispatched by Russian intelligence to “execute” Ukrainian-American rapper Slevin Dadyan, 34, in a chilling bid to silence the Kremlin’s alleged enemy.



Polish security services swooped on the 29-year-old Russian national in Warsaw after allegedly foiling the sinister plot.

He was detained last Friday in Mokotow, a residential district just south of central Warsaw, by the capital’s counterterrorism and homicide police.



Polish authorities said the suspect was allegedly acting on orders from a Russian intelligence agency and was plotting to kill the US and Ukrainian citizen.

It is unclear which attacks the drones were being used for, but Ukraine has been striking Russia daily with the deadly aerial weapons.



In one huge recent blitz, at least 13 people died when Ukrainian drones blasted around 20 Wildberries houses last month.

Ukraine has intensified its attacks on Wildberries facilities this month, launching strikes on 11 hubs that inflicted major damage on seven.

The strikes on the regime’s biggest online marketplace are part of Volodymyr Zelensky‘s cunning plan to cripple the logistics operation that supplies Russia‘s military with drone parts and other equipment.

Dadyan, formerly known as Albert Vasilyev, performs under the alias Kyivstoner and has been accused by Russia’s Federal Security Service of masterminding the “logistics of delivering drones to the Moscow region”.



The FSB claims the deadly drones were destined for attacks on “strategic facilities” in Moscow and its sprawling surroundings.

Polish media reported the alleged weapons pipeline ran from Slovakia through Poland and Belarus before reaching the Moscow region.

Moscow has since branded Dadyan an extremist and terrorist, adding the rapper to its notorious blacklist.

The Kremlin also accuses him of working with Ukrainian security services – claims the musician flatly denies.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the country’s ABW domestic intelligence service had smashed the alleged hit plot at the last minute.



“We must assume that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient [to it] for various reasons, in various places around the world,” he said.

Tusk refused to expose further details, saying the explosive investigation remains live.

Polish authorities are also believed to have received assistance from their US counterparts.



Dadyan first rocketed to fame through a string of viral comedy videos before becoming one of the founders of Ukrainian band Hryby.

He later stormed into a solo career as Kyivstoner, while also appearing in films.

Before Putin unleashed his full-scale invasion in 2022, Dadyan spent years in Moscow and worked with Russian rap star Vasily Vakulenko, known as Basta.

His activities in Russia during the annexation of Crimea and the war in Donbas had already drawn fierce criticism in Ukrainian media.

But when Putin launched his widespread conflict in February 2022, Dadyan fled Kyiv with his young son and wife for the US.



He remained there for two years before saying publicly from 2024 that he was living with his family in Slovakia.

The rapper has continued making music while also pursuing e-sports and competitive gaming.

In an interview last September, Dadyan took aim at President Zelensky while making clear he condemned Moscow’s aggression and supported Ukrainians fighting Russia.



The alleged hit plot comes as Poland battles an intensifying wave of Russian espionage, sabotage and so-called “greyzone” warfare.

Polish security officials say the country is now facing daily hostile incidents, with cyberattacks having rocketed since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The sinister campaign has already included the murder of Russian satirical artist Semyon Skrepetsky in Poland, sabotage of a crucial railway route linking Warsaw with the east and a Russian cruise missile crashing in the Lublin region.

Skrepetsky, a fierce critic of Putin, was gunned down on June 15 in Biała Podlaska in the Lublin Voivodeship.

His attacker allegedly walked up and fired twice before stepping closer and unleashing three more shots at point-blank range as the stricken artist lay on the ground.



Now the thwarted plot against Dadyan has thrust Poland into the crosshairs of an increasingly brazen Kremlin espionage war.

News.title: Andy Burnham cannot afford to ignore huge public anger over release of PC Harper’s killers any longer
News.content:
PM’s deaf ears

MORE than one million people have now signed the petition demanding the remorseless killers of PC Andrew Harper stay locked up.

Andy Burnham cannot afford to ignore such a massive swell of public outrage.



The still new Prime Minister says he is “increasingly confident” he can find a fix to stop them being freed under Labour’s catastrophic early release scheme.

That isn’t good enough.



For as long as thugs Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers have hope of getting out, PC Harper’s family will still suffer.

This has become a huge first test of Burnham’s leadership and he is fluffing it.



So far, he has presided over a shambles that has sown anguish and confusion.

There are only a few short weeks for the PM and his officials to get their act together and free up jail places before the mass release of hardened criminals.

Prison experts are already warning of a wave of rape and murder to come.

If Burnham continues to get this wrong, he will pay a heavy political price.



Bungle? You bet

DOES anyone in Labour understand the real reasons behind the decline of our High Streets?

Andy Burnham went on a tour of the country this week promising to listen to voters’ concerns.

Bizarrely, he then decided betting shops were the root of all evil and has set about cutting the already dwindling number of them.

Even in his own constituency there is widespread bafflement at his attack on bookies and the bizarre comparison with vape shops.

As one punter in Ashton in Makerfield said of the Government yesterday: “They don’t know what they are doing. No one forces anyone to have a bet.”



Burnham claims to be a champion of sport and the working classes.

But if he is capable of misjudging the mood in his own back yard, what chance have the rest of us got?

Zero sense

THE Green lobby has been out in force claiming the heatwave-fuelled wildfires in Stourbridge and the East Sussex train derailment prove we must spend £400billion on Net Zero.

Few argue with the need for Britain to adapt to changes in the climate.

But it’s insane to chuck so much taxpayers’ cash at renewable schemes that don’t work.



Solar panels often don’t operate in extreme heat and wind farms don’t work when it doesn’t blow. Electricity from both cannot be stored.

Until these systems become more reliable, we will need the oil and gas currently sitting untouched under the North Sea.

That’s not climate change denial. It’s basic common sense.

News.title: Jason Arday, ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row, found dead
News.content:
Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row, has been found dead.

Emergency services said a man was found "unresponsive" at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

Arday's family said in a statement that they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

Earlier on Friday, police officers were called to an address in Battersea by the London Ambulance Service.

In a statement, the Metropolitan Police said: "At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious."

Cambridge University vice-chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said: "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news."

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" to hear about the death and she urged people to "remember there are real people with loved ones involved".

Arday, 41, had denied any plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and last week said the recent controversy about his work had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

"We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the Times newspaper, external earlier this month.

News.title: Fires prompt national alert as 19 homes destroyed
News.content:
Fires across England and Wales have prompted a national government alert warning people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire.

The warning on Friday evening came as it was revealed 19 homes were destroyed and a further 18 damaged in a huge fire in Stourbridge, West Midlands, that spread rapidly through grass and woodland on Thursday before damaging homes.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told members of the public to take the warning "seriously", adding it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

West Midlands Fire Service chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said the Stourbridge blaze was one of the most significant incidents the service had ever dealt with.

It was one of several fires being dealt with across England and Wales on Friday.

In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed

In Hampshire, firefighters spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, Hampshire, which broke out on Sunday.

Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath, off Gurney Road in the city.

Elsewhere in the West Midlands fires caused extensive damage in Warstock and Kings Norton, Birmingham on Thursday. A 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life .

In Stoke-on-Trent on Thursday four homes in Sandyford were destroyed, with other properties damaged. Two people were arrested on suspicion of arson. Six firefighters were taken to hospital due to smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion.

In Willenhall, West Midlands, at least three homes and several gardens were destroyed in fires on Stonehouse Avenue and Harry Perks Street.

Investigators said they were working with other emergency services to establish how the Stourbridge fire started, with police saying they were keeping an open mind.

Some of the worst-affected areas have been cordoned off and many residents who were evacuated, including the Bishop of Dudley, the Right Reverand Martin Gorick, have not been able to return home.

News.title: Temporary ban on sale of disposable BBQs over wildfire risk
News.content:
"We have a fire and rescue service across the country that isn't properly set up to deal with these incidents," Burnham said.

"We don't have the capability in the way that we should have to fight these fires.

"There's thousands of firefighters out there today doing back-breaking work, in full kit, in the most difficult conditions", he added.

He said the UK must face up to the "changing climate" and transition to "more clean energy".

His comments came ahead of the appointment of Baroness Blake of Leeds as fire minister.

Friends of the Earth urged the prime minister to tackle the "root cause" of the "climate emergency" that is fuelling this summer's extreme weather events.

"Without urgent action to curb the carbon emissions driving this crisis, future heatwaves, droughts and wildfires will only get worse and the ability for future generations to adapt will disappear" the environmental group warned.

Burnham was speaking during a visit to Stourbridge to see the impact of a devastating blaze.

As the UK experienced its hottest day of the year on Thursday, residents fled their homes when fires spread through dry grass and tore through houses.

West Midlands Ambulance Service said it treated 54 casualties at eight different fires across the region. Nineteen people were taken to hospital for treatment.

In 2025, fire and rescue services in England and Wales broke a new record when they responded to nearly 1,000 wildfire incidents, with the NFCC warning at the time that climate change is increasing their risk and severity.

The conditions the UK is experiencing so far this summer also mirror the warnings given by climate scientists that human-induced climate change would lead to more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as potential summer droughts.

In England, the Rugby Football Union has delayed the start of the community rugby season because of concerns about player welfare and pitch conditions because of the drought conditions.

News.title: Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?
News.content:
But now, even this is being squeezed too. Recent rules say women have to ask men to take their products to market, and only men can sit at their stalls to show their wares at trade fairs. The Taliban gives various reasons for this, including claiming that women aren't wearing proper hijab or head covering.

"The world has to talk to the Taliban in a different way because it's just not working," says Najia. "The lives of Afghan women have to change because we're losing hope."

Five years after this ultra-conservative Islamist movement took charge, women are banned from much of the public sphere and girls are prohibited from going to school over the age of 12. Many inside and outside Afghanistan are asking the same pressing question: what's the best way to engage the Taliban to try to achieve meaningful change?

The issue is deeply divisive. There are fissures between many groups, with a huge array of conflicting issues at stake. These include women's rights, unpredictable Taliban edicts, international sanctions and aid cuts during a spiralling humanitarian crisis. The international response is split between Western countries often focused on human rights and others more interested in investment opportunities. And the West itself is divided on the best response.

Many now accept that whatever they're doing, it's not working.

News.title: Derailed Essex to London train leads to travel chaos
News.content:
Martin Frobisher, of Network Rail, said the summer's hot weather had "presented exceptional challenges to the railway".

In an interview with the BBC Transport Correspondent Katy Austin, Frobisher also confirmed speed restrictions were not in place in either Wickford or Lewes.

On the possible impact of the hot weather, he said "yes, that's one of the things that we're looking at.

"We've got our investigations underway. We've got technical engineers on site, our best experts who are on site with the Rail Accident Investigation Branch.

"They're looking very thoroughly at what's happened. And based on that, we will act on what we learn."

However, he added it was "too early to speculate on the full findings".

The investigation would specifically assess "whether or not this was weather-related", said Mark Francois, the Conservative MP for Rayleigh and Wickford.

The Department for Transport stressed Britain's railways were "among the safest in the world" as it reacted to the incident.

It said derailments were "incredibly rare" events.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train.

"Following assessment, all patients were discharged at the scene.

"We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment.

"There were no casualties among those on board."

A spokesperson for BTP also confirmed there were no reported injuries.

News.title: Hodgkinson beaten to European gold by rival Werro
News.content:
Keely Hodgkinson was forced to settle for European silver as Switzerland's Audrey Werro denied the Briton a third consecutive title in a thrilling women's 800m final in Birmingham.

The most eagerly anticipated event of the championships culminated in the expected three-way battle for supremacy between Hodgkinson, Swiss 22-year-old Werro and Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol in front of a captivated sellout crowd of 23,000 inside Alexander Stadium.

Seeking to reassert her dominance in the event, Olympic champion Hodgkinson was roared on in pursuit of Werro by her home support but was unable to overhaul her new rival in the closing stages.

Having this season become the fastest athlete since the world record was set 43 years ago, Werro finished strong to land her first senior international title in a championship record one minute 54.81 seconds to her rivals' 1:55.01.

"Mixed emotions," Hodgkinson told the BBC.

"I think with that level of competition, any medal is a really good achievement and another one to add to my collection, so I can never be disappointed with that. But I'm defending champion, so I wanted to do that.

"I knew it was going to come down to the wire but I really thought I was going to win today.

"It wasn't meant to be. I didn't do anything wrong - it was just one of those things."

News.title: Chris Mason: Where does this unorthodox by-election victory leave Nigel Farage?
News.content:
It is a question prompting at least some debate within the party.

"When he goes down this angry route he doesn't help himself," the prominent Reform activist Tim Montgomerie told Radio 4's The World At One.

Montgomerie, the founder of the ConservativeHome website, defected to Reform two years ago. He praised Farage's political ability but added: "It's very frustrating how he's behaved today. He needs to get a grip of this problem."

Montgomerie argued Farage and Reform were at their best when they were more positive rather than "inward looking" and focused on "grievances."

The "grievances," as Montgomerie puts it, are real and legitimate, say Farage's friends.

In the short term at least and from a point of weakness I have previously written about, the by-election allowed Farage to get on the front foot and to frame an argument, as he saw it, as the people versus those out to get him.

Rubbish, say his critics, the rules apply to all MPs and the undeclared Â£5m gift from the billionaire businessman Christopher Harborne, in the months before Farage became an MP, should have been registered, they insist.

Talking to GB News in the early hours of this morning, before the result, Farage repeated a concession, of sorts, about this: "If I made one sin, it's that I haven't filled in a piece of paper.

"I've broken no law, I've broken no tax law, I've taken no public money. I don't even own a motor home. Maybe I haven't filled in a piece of paper. I'm confident I'm right - we'll see where we go."

He has long maintained he sought legal advice about whether he needed to declare the money and had been told he didn't.

The wider question is where Nigel Farage and Reform find themselves in the big picture politically and whether their current approach is a wise one.

There is early evidence of something of a Burnham bounce for Labour, which has disrupted Reform's long standing lead in the opinion polls.

And the Conservatives appear more chipper and competitive than a year ago too.

Then there is the rise of Restore Britain, run by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

Let's be clear: none of the political parties are wildly popular at the moment, but Reform's support has shrivelled a bit and their rivals are more upbeat.

The landscape for the new political season at Westminster is taking shape, ahead of MPs returning to the Commons in a few weeks.

Labour with a spring in its step, for now at least. Reform punchy but feeling under the cosh and plenty of the others scrapping for attention too.

It will be a fascinating few months ahead.

News.title: Britain's Finlay Tarling dies in Volta a Portugal accident
News.content:
British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died aged 19 after an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

In a statement provided to local media, Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said there had been "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" and that an investigation was under way.

The Welshman was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe.

In a statement, NSN said: "We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

"Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president Antonio Jose Seguro added that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park, added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time."

News.title: Prisoners charged over attack on Sara Sharif's father
News.content:
Two prisoners have been charged with the attempted murder of fellow inmate Urfan Sharif who was jailed for killing his daughter Sara Sharif.

Steven Sansom, 47, and Adam Watson, 39, have also been charged with other offences relating to the incident in Belmarsh Prison on 1 January 2025, the Crown Prosecution Service said.

The men will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court for a first hearing on 26 August.

Sharif, 43, and Sara's stepmother Beinash Batool were sentenced to life imprisonment after being convicted at the Old Bailey for murdering 10-year-old Sara at their home in Woking, Surrey.

Sharif reportedly suffered cuts to his face during the attack, and received medical treatment at the prison.

Daren Streeter, deputy chief crown prosecutor at CPS London, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the Metropolitan Police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and pursue criminal proceedings."

Sara was hooded, burned and beaten during a "campaign of torture" that lasted two years before her body was found at the family home in August 2023.

During the trial, Justice Cavanagh told the court "the degree of cruelty involved is almost inconceivable".

Urfan Sharif was sentenced to a minimum of 40 years in prison for murder, while his wife Beinash Batool, 30, received a minimum of 33 years.

Sara's uncle, Faisal Malik, 29, was sentenced to 16 years' imprisonment for causing or allowing her death.

The three fled to Islamabad, Pakistan, with Sara's five siblings, the day before her body was found, prompting an international manhunt.

They hid out there for four weeks before returning to the UK, where they were arrested.

News.title: Two dead after light aircraft crash
News.content:
Two people have died following a light aircraft crash in north Wales.

The aircraft was found in a remote location close to Trawsfynydd, Gwynedd, with the two people on board pronounced dead at the scene, North Wales Police said.

The force received reports shortly after 12:00 BST that a light aircraft travelling from an airfield in England had not arrived at Caernarfon Airport as scheduled.

Multi-agency air and ground searches were carried out until the aircraft was found.

A team of investigators have since been deployed by the Air Accidents Investigations Branch (AAIB).

News.title: Stephen Bear jailed over sex offender breaches
News.content:
Reality TV contestant Stephen Bear taunted police by "bragging" he was on a beach in Brazil while he breached his requirements as a sex offender, a court has heard.

He was not on the run during the trip last year, but under the rules of his registration requirements he was ordered to tell authorities about foreign travel.

Bear, 36, admitted five counts of failing to comply with the register notification requirements at Thames Magistrates' Court and was sentenced to 24 weeks in prison.

He is already in prison having been jailed on Thursday after admitting breaching a restraining order that banned him from posting online about his ex-partner Georgia Harrison.

News.title: Weekend cancellations after East Sussex train derailment
News.content:
Rail services on a busy line in the South East are being cancelled this weekend after a train carrying 150 people derailed in East Sussex.

Two passengers suffered serious injuries and 18 others were also hurt when three carriages of the train came off the tracks near Lewes on Thursday. Police have since said none of the casualties had life-threatening injuries.

Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) inspectors are at the scene gathering evidence, examining infrastructure and reviewing CCTV, signalling and train data.

The derailment was followed by another incident in Essex on Friday, when a Greater Anglia train came off the tracks near Wickford.

Train operator Southern Rail said trains between London Victoria and Eastbourne will be cancelled this weekend as the line between Haywards Heath and Lewes has been closed indefinitely in both directions.

Southern says Cooksbridge and Plumpton will also not be served all weekend, with rail replacement buses operating.

Eastbourne is expected to get a bumper number of visitors this weekend when the seaside town hosts its popular Airbourne air show.

The rail company has advised people to travel to Eastbourne along the coast via Brighton.

It has also urged commuters planning to travel on Monday to check for updates on its website, external on Sunday evening.

News.title: UK diplomats no longer get hardship bonus for being posted to Buenos Aires
News.content:
British diplomats in six locations around the world, including Buenos Aires and Santiago in South America, will no longer get hardship payments for working in dangerous cities.

Bonuses and respite breaks are granted to those working in cities considered risky, like Beirut in Lebanon, or with high crime, such as Pretoria in South Africa, or high air pollution in cities including New Delhi and Beijing.

The UK government has removed Santiago, in Chile, Panama City in Panama, Pyongyang in North Korea, Bamako in Mali, and Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in addition to the two south American cities, according to the latest list published last week, external.

The 144 locations still on the list include many trouble spots but also popular holiday destinations such as Bali and Rio De Janeiro, prompting criticism from the Conservatives.

Tory chairmanÂ­ Kevin HollinÂ­rake said civil servants receiving extra pay for working in such areas is unfair on the taxpayer.

The Foreign Office has given civil servants extra payments for working in areas where there is a high level of danger, or high risks to health, for the past 30 years.

They are meant to compensate staff and families for the additional costs and challenges of living overseas in difficult locations and are reviewed regularly.

Factors and risks covered by the allowance include security measures, climate, natural disaster, isolation and other impacts on quality of life.

Amounts are not routinely published but in 2009, the last time a breakdown was released, the highest payments for civil servants and their spouses were for postings to Karachi, Pakistan, which was worth an extra Â£26,647, or Â£14,804 in Abuja, the capital of Nigeria.

The hardship payment for being posted as part of a couple to Buenos Aires was Â£1,517 and Santiago was Â£777, according to the 2009 Diplomatic Services Allowances, external.

Answering a parliamentary question from Tory peer Lord Moylan, external, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield said assessments of hardship take into account factors that mean members of staff are required to take additional breaks for the benefit of their physical or mental health.

He added: "These arrangements are not new, and indeed have applied consistently under successive governments for a number of decades."

Bangkok, Cape Town, and Kuala Lumpur are still among the cities that qualify for hardship payments, alongside Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Muscat.

Hollinrake said it was unfair that taxpayers were "footing the bill" for these destinations and pledged to cut the size of the civil service if Conservatives were returned to power.

"Whilst businesses and families are paying higher taxes to fund this government's policies, civil servants are being sent on taxpayer-funded jollies to places like Bali, Cape Town and the Maldives," he said.

"This kind of nonsense has no place in government."

But the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office defended the scheme, with a spokesperson saying: "British diplomats serve their country around the globe, including in some of the toughest and most challenging physical and political environments in the world.

"We have a duty of care to ensure our staff are properly supported, and compensation and other provisions reflect the circumstances of the posting, as it would be in any private sector job."

News.title: Woman cleared of owning XL bully which fatally bit man
News.content:
A woman has been cleared of owning an XL bully dog that bit her partner's father, causing him to bleed to death.

Chanel Fong, 33, was accused of owning the dog, Cookie, which was dangerously out of control and of an alternative charge of being the person in charge of the animal at the time of the attack.

She was found not guilty of both by the jury at Caernarfon Crown Court.

Her partner's father, Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, died from severe blood loss after being bitten on the leg.

The attack took place before XL Bullies were added to the banned dog list.

The court heard Keven Jones had been in poor health and had been taking methadone and blood thinning medication, and had been staying at Fong's Wrexham home in May 2022.

Fong said the dog belonged to her partner Joshua Jones, who was not present when his father was bitten, although the prosecution claimed she was Cookie's joint owner.

The court was told there had been a number of dogs at the home on Holt Road in Wrexham, including two XL Bullies, called Fire and Rogue.

Rogue was Cookie's mother and in season at the time, so had to be kept separate from other dogs.

At about 11:30 BST on 23 May, Jones told Fong he would get Cookie and another dog in from the garden, but he was then heard shouting at Cookie to "get off" him.

The court heard Fong also called into the garden for Cookie to get down, which is when Jones came towards her "wobbly".

He pointed to his leg, which was pumping blood, and he said to Fong, "he's got me there".

Fong called the emergency services and attempted first aid, including applying pressure to the wound, but Jones could not be saved.

A post-mortem examination said he had died from extreme blood loss caused by dog bites.

Cookie was later humanely euthanised.

News.title: Sign of life as bright orange 'fire fungus' grows at park ravaged by wildfire
News.content:
A fungus that grows in places damaged by fire has been found at the site of a major wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park.

Forestry and Land Scotland (FLS) said the bright orange, pyrophilous (fire-loving) fungus could be the first sign of nature's recovery at Glenmore near Aviemore.

A wildfire started in the area on 15 July and the incident, which has burned through thousands of acres of woodland and moor, continues to be monitored for hotspots.

FLS said the fungus was among the "first colonisers" of burned ground and played a role in breaking down carbon and preventing soil erosion.

News.title: Mother jailed for killing baby by burning her with a hairdryer
News.content:
A mother who killed her baby daughter by burning her with a hairdryer has been jailed for six years.

Courtney Gartshore, 28, used the appliance to subject three-month-old Dahlia-Rose to "significant and sustained heat" on her head and body.

Emergency services were called to the scene at a property in Peterhead, Aberdeenshire, in September 2023, but the child had died.

Gartshore was convicted of culpable homicide - the closest equivalent to manslaughter in Scots Law - following a trial at the High Court in Aberdeen in July.

Warning: This article contains details readers may find upsetting

Sentencing Gartshore at the High Court in Edinburgh, judge Simon Collins KC told her, external she had inflicted "severe and disfiguring" burns on her daughter.

He said: "Given Dahlia-Rose's very young age, and the horrifying way that she died, this is a uniquely disturbing and distressing case.

"But it is tragic as well as terrible. And that is because the evidence suggested that the accused loved Dahlia-Rose, yet will have to live the rest of her life with the knowledge that she was responsible for her death."

The stars of Apple TV+’s newest hit series, Widow’s Bay, have revealed their hopes for the show’s highly anticipated second season.

The word-of-mouth comedy thriller, which has been nominated for 19 Emmys this year, stars Matthew Rhys as the mayor of a fictional New England seaport town, who seeks to boost tourism despite knowing the island may be cursed.

Throughout the show’s debut season, Rhys’s Tom Loftis experiences supernatural occurrences, suggesting that the town is indeed haunted. Still, he tries to keep the eeriness at bay in an attempt to market the cash-strapped town as the next Martha’s Vineyard. By the end of the season, however, Loftis acknowledges that there’s something truly wrong with the island.

While the show was renewed in June, the creator-showrunner Katie Dippold remains tight-lipped about her plans for the next installment.

But the show’s stars, including Rhys, Dale Dickey and Katie O’Flynn, have freely divulged their preferred theories for Widow’s Bay’s future.

open image in gallery ‘Widow’s Bay’ earned 19 Emmy nominations ( Apple TV )

open image in gallery Matthew Rhys achieved a rare feat, earning Lead Acting Emmys for both ‘Widow’s Bay’ and ‘The Beast in Me’ ( Apple TV )

“It’s the ultimate setup, I think, for a Season 2,” Rhys told Deadline. “Massive cliffhanger. I’m just talking personally now. A father who now knows the folklore is true. Therefore, if he suddenly leaves the island, his son will die. He realizes he has the Scooby-Doo mission. It’s like, OK, how do we figure this out? What breaks the curse?”

Dale Dickey, who plays Loftis’s cigarette-smoking secretary Rosemary, recalled a recent conversation with co-star Jeff Hiller, who portrays Dale, the town hall clerk.

“I was talking to Jeff Hiller,” she said. “I would love to do a boat scene where Rosemary and Dale are out searching for the sea hag to get some answers. I thought that would be fun. And then we tip over and there’s only one life jacket. Who’s going to live?”

British actor Kate O’Flynn, who stars as Loftis’s trusty executive assistant Patricia, added: “Next season, I don’t know, but I would love to play a British ancestor of Patricia or something… I like the idea of wigging up and doing a bit of period drama. Why not?”

open image in gallery Jeff Hiller and Kate O'Flynn star in 'Widow's Bay' as part of the municipal team ( Apple TV )

Widow’s Bay trails behind HBO Max’s smash-hit comedy Hacks in the comedy categories for the 2026 Emmys.

The former collected 19 nominations, including Outstanding Comedy Series and acting nods for Rhys, O’Flynn, Dickey, Stephen Root, Betty Gilpin and Hamish Linklater. The latter landed 24 nominations.

Rhys achieved a rare feat, earning two Lead Actor Emmy nominations for Widow’s Bay and for Netflix’s limited drama series The Beast in Me.

The Welsh star recently admitted that money is the driving force behind his role selection. “Like what pays most wins. Very simple. Three children and a mortgage, I’ll get after it. I have no shame. I’ll whore myself to the best of them,” he humorously told Variety.

“In fairness, Widow’s Bay is a script I’d never seen the like of,” Rhys added in a more serious tone. “I was desperate to do that.”

Widow’s Bay season one is available to stream on Apple TV+.

Five people were killed and a suspect is dead Friday after a series of killings that took place at two homes and a wooded area in Michigan, according to law enforcement.

Michigan State Police were responding to reports of a shooting at a home in Missaukee County, about 169 miles (272 kilometers) northwest of Detroit, when they found three people dead and another wounded, police said in a statement. The person injured was taken to the hospital.

Police said the suspect, Chad Hickman, 39, fled before law enforcement got to the home. As police searched for him, they found a fourth person dead at another home, according to officials.

Law enforcement found Hickman's vehicle in a wooded area near Whitlock Lake, which led them to his body as well as another individual who was also dead, according to police.

Police originally said they were investigating a shooting but have not released information on how each person died, nor whether they had any relation to one another.

“This situation is heartbreaking for the community and challenging for the investigators involved,” Lt. Ashley Miller said in a statement. “We remain committed to conducting a thorough investigation and will provide updates as new information becomes available.”

Police area investigating the shooting and have asked the public to avoid the area.

The names and ages of the people killed are not being released until their families have been notified, according to police.

Former child actor Justin Cooper has revealed that his mother had just one request for the late comedy great Don Rickles on the set of 1998’s Dennis the Menace Strikes Again: Don’t swear.

Rickles, who was known as the “master of the insult”, died in 2017 at the age of 90.

He played Mr Wilson in the 1998 comedy, opposite Cooper as the titular menace. Cooper, who is also known for his childhood role in the 1997 Jim Carrey film Liar Liar, later left acting and now works in sports broadcasting.

Cooper, now 37, was just 9 years old when he played Dennis. He told the Not So Little Rascals podcast that his mother had been proactive about “shielding” him from both creepy fans and uncomfortable situations on set.

“There’s a lot of acting parents that you hear of back in the day that were just like, ‘Yeah go do whatever they tell you to do,’ ” said Cooper. “My mom was not like that, like, almost to a fault.”

open image in gallery As well as ‘Dennis the Menace Strikes Again’, Justin Cooper also starred in the blockbuster Jim Carrey comedy 'Liar Liar' ( Universal )

He went on: “I remember a story that just blew my mind. So Don Rickles played Mr. Wilson in Dennis the Menace Strikes Again! And you know, he’s known for being a foul-mouthed comic. And she went up to him and was like, ‘I don’t want you to use any language like that in front of my kid.’ I was like, ‘Mom, whoa!’”

Rickles was so well-known for his quick-fire insults that he was sarcastically nicknamed “Mr. Warmth”. As an actor, he won acclaim for his performance in Martin Scorsese’s Casino and for voicing Mr Potato Head in the Toy Story films.

He first came to America’s attention after insulting Frank Sinatra, telling the singer midway through a performance in a Hollywood club: "Make yourself at home, Frank. Hit somebody”.

Rickles’ reputation for mocking celebrities grew thanks to his appearances on The Dean Martin Celebrity Roasts series that ran between the 1970s and 1980s. Targets that appeared on the show included Sinatra, Ronald Reagan, Bob Hope, Lucille Ball, Kirk Douglas, Sammy Davis Jr. and Mr. T.

Along with celebrities, the most common targets for Rickles were those less intelligent audience members, whom he often called “hockey pucks”.

When initially performing stand-up, Rickles found his impromptu insults won more applause than scripted material, so he decided to work them into the shows.

After Rickles died, Scorsese paid tribute by saying: “Don Rickles was a giant, a legend… and I can hear his voice now, skewering me for being so lofty…”

Keely Hodgkinson offered a blunt assessment of her feelings after graciously conceding European 800m gold to Swiss rival Audrey Werro and settling for silver on home soil.

After days of controversy over empty seats, Birmingham finally delivered a capacity crowd, no doubt drawn to the Alexander Stadium to watch the Olympic champion and the three other fastest women in Europe clash in the most hotly-anticipated race of the championships – if not the season.

Werro, the favourite before she fell in the semi-final and was controversially advanced, overtook Hodgkinson on the back straight in the first lap and never relinquished her lead after 200m, winning in a championship-record one minute and 54.81 seconds, and bronze went to the Netherlands’ Femke Broeders-Bol.

open image in gallery Keely Hodgkinson had to settle for silver in Birmingham (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

“I don’t want it to be easy,” said Hodgkinson, who experienced her own knee-scraping freak fall in training before the Prefontaine Classic.

“We’re all going to win some, lose some. S*** happens. Audrey fell over yesterday, she did amazing to bounce back. I know what that took out of me a few weeks ago. So yeah, incredible to her. And, yeah, life goes on. I’ll go back and train, and just hope I get it next time.”

Hodgkinson, who set a new indoor 800m world record in March, had insisted before this race that Birmingham gold would mean almost as much as her Olympic title at Paris two years ago.

She said: “Yeah, that last 50m, I really thought I had it. But she’s a strong athlete. Sometimes you want it so much, and sometimes in terms of real parts it might just not be enough.”

open image in gallery Audrey Werro celebrates her gold medal (Martin Rickett/PA) ( PA Wire )

Werro, who like Hodgkinson is targeting the 43-year-old women’s 800m world record, has enjoyed a spectacular season, flawless outdoors before the Birmingham semi-final.

That included her shock victory over Hodgkinson in Stockholm – despite a national record from the Briton – to move third on the women’s 800m all-time list, then lowered her personal best to 1:53.80 a few weeks later.

Two-time world 400m hurdles champion Broeders-Bol entered Birmingham with just four professional outdoor 800m races under her belt, having debuted at the Ostrava Golden Spike in June and was a dark horse.

Hodgkinson added: “It doesn’t sting because I was beaten by a great athlete. I think I put together a pretty good race. I don’t think I did anything wrong.

open image in gallery Hodgkinson was gracious in defeat (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

“The thing about the 800m is you have a million different ways it could go in your head. Nobody really knew, so you have to think on your feet, but I think I covered every move well. I just didn’t have enough.”

Earlier, Zharnel Hughes had to settle for silver in the men’s 200m final behind Germany’s Owen Ansah.

Ansah clinched gold with a time of 19.95, while Hughes followed him home in 20.16s and the bronze medal was shared by Fausto Desalu and Timothe Mumenthaler.

Ansah is a controversial winner as he faces possible sanctions by the National Anti Doping Agency of Germany for alleged whereabouts failures, but the German has denied any wrongdoing.

A Maryland state tax court has struck down the state’s first-in-the-nation tax on digital advertising and ordered state officials to repay the tax money already collected from big tech firms.

The Maryland Tax Court said the tax violates the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act as well as the First Amendment and the commerce and due process clauses of the U.S. Constitution.

The legal fight has been watched by other states that are considering taxes for online ads. Maryland estimated the tax, approved in 2021, could raise about $250 million a year to help pay for a sweeping K-12 education measure.

In Friday's decision, the tax court ordered the state to repay the tax money already collected by Apple, Google and Peacock TV.

The law taxed revenue that large companies make on digital s shown in Maryland. Companies making more than $100 million in global annual gross revenues were taxed at a 2.5% rate. The rate increased for companies with larger revenues, topping out at a 10% rate for companies making $15 billion or more in global gross annual revenues.

Supporters of the law contended that Maryland needed to overhaul its tax methods in response to significant changes in how businesses advertise. But attorneys representing Big Tech companies including Meta and Amazon challenged the law in multiple legal venues, arguing in part that they were unfairly targeted.

Last year, 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled part of the law violated the Constitution because it blocked Big Tech companies from telling customers about the tax. That, Judge Julius Richardson said, violated the right to free speech.

Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson and House Speaker Joseline Pena-Melnyk, both Democrats, issued a statement saying they “respectfully disagree” with the tax court ruling and expect the legal process to continue.

They said the tax was enacted to keep the state's tax system in pace with a changing economy.

“We remain committed to ensuring that Maryland’s tax system is fair, sustainable, and reflects today’s economy,” they said. “We will continue working with the Attorney General and Comptroller as this matter proceeds through the courts.”

The tax court said Congress — not the state legislature — is tasked with regulating interstate commerce, and that the tax law was inappropriately based on global revenue rather than revenue from in-state advertising.

The federal Internet Tax Freedom Act bars the taxation of e-commerce if similar services are not taxed. At least for now, the tax court found, there isn't much of a difference between digital advertising and print or billboard ads, which means the bar on taxation applies.

Thirty lions and tigers that were kept alive — barely — for years in cramped concrete cages at a shuttered Argentine zoo began entering jumbo-size transport crates Friday as they embarked on ambitious journeys to wildlife sanctuaries halfway across the world in South Africa and the United States.

The cats are being rescued from the former Luján Zoo, about 70 kilometers (43 miles) northwest of Argentina's capital of Buenos Aires, after years of uncertainty over their fate. Four Paws, the international animal-welfare organization overseeing the transfer, described it as one of the largest relocations of captive big cats in the world.

“We are putting everything into making this go as smoothly as possible so we can celebrate that 30 lives have improved because of this effort,” said Luciana D’Abramo, program director for Four Paws.

Once loaded into their crates and placed aboard cargo and passenger jets, nine tigers and six lions will be flown to Lionsrock, a Four Paws sanctuary in South Africa that houses more than 80 big cats across natural enclosures sprawling 60 hectares (148 acres). The remaining eight tigers and seven lions will travel to The Wild Animal Sanctuary in Colorado, a vast refuge on the grasslands northeast of Denver where rescued lions, tigers and other animals roam expansive habitats.

But getting there is no easy feat: The big cats bound for Colorado will fly through Chile, while the others will travel to Johannesburg via Frankfurt or Amsterdam before a four-hour drive to Lionsrock.

The Four Paws handlers trained many of the lions and tigers to enter the crates voluntarily. But some of the big cats required sedation, including two tigers that veterinarians hoisted in canvas slings Friday and carried by hand to their transport crates.

Argentine authorities shut down the Lujan Zoo — famous for letting visitors handle and pose for pictures with tigers and lions — over safety and animal welfare concerns in 2020. D’Abramo said about 200 big cats were living there when it closed. Only 112 remained when Four Paws first arrived in 2023 seeking a solution.

By the time the organization was allowed to take over the site two years later, that number had fallen to 62. Some of the captive animals can barely walk because of obesity, muscle loss or poor nutrition. Others suffer from dental and kidney disease, complications from declawing and injuries that never healed properly.

“That alone shows the level of overcrowding and the conditions in which these animals have endured,” D’Abramo said.

The organization retrained longtime zoo employees in modern animal-welfare practices and began improving the cats’ diets and medical care. This transfer leaves more than 20 lions and tigers at Luján while Four Paws searches for their long-term homes.
