News.title: Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn
News.content:
Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Mowbray: It feels like a defeat

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Iran war threatens to cripple growth, Treasury warns Burnham | Officials predict economic expansion of just 0.3pc in 2027 if Strait of Hormuz stays blocked

2) Britain facing £54bn bill for North Sea shutdown | Costs soar amid shortage of specialised ships needed to clear up abandoned oil rigs

3) Ban on zero-hours contracts to cost companies up to £3bn | Businesses face huge bill to offer workers guaranteed hours under Employment Rights Act

4) Nvidia’s AI push has echoes of Enron, says Big Short investor | Michael Burry claims chip giant is engaging in ‘circular’ financing

5) Shadow bank founder battles to stave off bankruptcy threat | Paresh Raja launches legal claim to prevent administrators from chasing him for repayment

What happened overnight

Asian shares were mostly higher, powered by gains for AI-related stocks including computer chips as regional markets tracked a rally on Wall Street.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 advanced 1.6pc to 68,601.21. In South Korea, the Kospi jumped 4pc, climbing to 6,844.65, as shares in Samsung Electronics surged 5.4pcc. Computer chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 7.1pc.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 3,967.28, while the Shanghai Composite index added 0.5pc to 3,967.65.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4pc to 9,155.80.

Data from the US on Wednesday showed consumer prices had risen in line with analysts’ expectations in July.

Wall Street stocks were boosted on Wednesday by gains made by tech companies CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer, both of which closed up by more than 19pc.

The Nasdaq Composite ended the session up 0.5pc, with the S&P 500 up nearly 0.3pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the session marginally down.

Oil prices were little changed as investors weighed the deadlock in talks between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was broadly flat at nearly $89 a barrel.

News.title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
News.content:
H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife.

Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1, a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020.

Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species.

While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth.

An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction.

Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes.

Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments.

Sports.title: Former Arsenal star Francis Coquelin, 35, rushed to hospital after sickening head clash as ‘Red Cross intervene’
Sports.content:
FORMER Arsenal star Francis Coquelin has been rushed to hospital after a horrific head clash while playing for French Ligue 2 side, Laval.

The brutal scene even saw the French Red Cross get involved, according to reports.



Laval midfielder Coquelin and Nantes man Wilitty Younoussa violently collided heads early on in the second game of the league campaign.

It was a heartbreaking moment for the ex-Arsenal man, as his first start since rejoining his boyhood club was cut very short.



Volunteer medics from the French Red Cross were called onto the field of play before the Frenchman was rushed off to hospital.

Following the incident, French reporter Cyprien Legeay wrote: “Major concern in Laval after Francis Coquelin and Wilitty Younoussa violently collided with their heads.



“The players quickly made big gestures to get the Red Cross to intervene quickly.”

Later reports suggest he’s getting a scan, with bleeding and a fracture suspected.

The 35-year-old’s Laval career has been brought to a gutting halt if reports turn out to be true.

He played for the Northern French team between 2005-2008 as a youngster before earning a move to Premier League giants Arsenal.



While he never made a senior appearance for the club, they played a huge part in his development.

And today’s injury won’t have done him any favours in attempting to repay them.

The clash with Nantes ended in a 2-1 win for Laval after a 95th minute winner.

However, according to reports coming out of France, a storm knocked out the broadcast towards the end of the clash.

This reportedly forced broadcasters to film with phones at the end of a dramatic night in the North West.



The victory takes them up to tenth in Ligue 2 after losing their season opener to Rodez.

Sports.title: England star, 32, was offered a place at Harvard University before taking up footie career
Sports.content:
PATRICK BAMFORD would choose a freezing, rain-lashed night at Burnley or Stoke over the ivory towers of Harvard every single day of the week.

The Sheffield United striker has zero regrets about snubbing America’s most famous university to take up a career in football.



For him the brutal, bruising war of the Championship beats a fancy economics degree.

And Bamford, 32, has a clear promotion message for Blades fans ahead of the gruelling new campaign.



He said: “We’re going to try everything we can to go up.

“And the fans should just know that’s what all the players are aiming for and what we’re hopefully heading towards.”



Forget the high-society lecture halls and quiet libraries. The forward has famous brains as well as footballing brawn.

He famously turned down the chance to study at Ivy League giants Harvard back in the day.

But when the winter grind kicks in, he never wishes he was sitting in a warm Massachusetts classroom instead.

Asked if studying in America ever sounds more appealing during three-game weeks, Bamford was brutally honest.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

He said: “No, I think that as bad as it sounds, that was always my back-up plan.

“It might sound silly not to want to go to one of the world’s top universities — but I always wanted to be a footballer from as young as I can remember.”

It takes a serious work ethic to make it to the very top. And Bamford had to strike a strict deal with his parents to chase his sporting dream.

He revealed: “I always had a promise with my mum and dad that they’d support me in football as long as I always got my A-levels. And I got good results.



“And yes, that was the deal. And it was something I had to stick to until I was 18. But football was really always the dream.”

And now, that dream is all about getting back to the promised land of the Premier League.

The gruelling 46-game slog of the Championship is notoriously one of the hardest in world football.

It takes much more than just silky skills and expensive squads to get over the line.

Bamford, who joined the Blades in November, knows exactly what it takes to escape the second-tier rat race.



He explained: “Normally it’s the teams that have the mentality to turn a loss into a draw or draw into a win.

“And even when it’s not pretty, achieve a good result.”

That grit is forged deep inside the dressing-room walls. Tactics are great, but team spirit and raw passion are what truly win titles.

Bamford said: “You need a few vocal leaders in the dressing room to keep everyone on song.

“And you must keep everyone pushing in the same direction.”



On the pitch, the mission for any frontman is simple: score goals.

And the star has a very straightforward philosophy when it comes to hitting the back of the net.

It is not about over complicating things or waiting for the perfect tactical blueprint.

Bamford said: “I think that you need to find yourself in between the posts — goal side of the penalty spot.



“Try and finish the attack in the middle of the goal.

“Because you’d be amazed just by being in there, you seem to be in the right place all the time.”

It is a clever knack that separates the good strikers from the great ones.

He added: “Sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t. But you’d be amazed how many easy goals you get from just being in the right place.

“I think that’s something you kind of learn as you gain experience.”



Modern football relies heavily on technology and complex data.

Managers and analysts spend hours breaking down every single movement on the pitch.

But the savvy forward likes to keep things sharp and focused.

Former Middlesbrough and Leeds star Bamford explained: “I’d look at the other team before and see where the chances are coming from. I’m going to look for isolation during the game.

“I’m analysing chances — just seeing what I could do better. What I think I did wrong or what decision I made that was wrong.”



Yet the one-cap England man, who played against Andorra in 2021, knows you cannot ever let the bad days linger in your mind.

He added: “There are also some games where I just seem to forget about it all. It’s not always going to go your way.”

Away from the pitch, finding a proper balance is completely vital.

The mental pressure of the game can easily weigh players down.

Bamford admits it is almost impossible to fully switch off from the sport.



He said: “I think it’s important to have other aspects to your life.

“Other things that take your mind off football. But it is very hard to not have your mind on football all the time.”

The summer break offers only a tiny window of peace.

He added: “You only really truly have a little bit of time away from thinking football for the first two weeks or so of the off season.

Sports.title: McIlroy toils as Scheffler produces stunning 61 at St Jude Championship
Sports.content:
World No 1 Scottie Scheffler produced a stunning second-round 61 at the FedEx St Jude Championship as Rory McIlroy toiled again.

Scheffler charged in 54 feet of putts to birdie six of his first seven holes, and then closed with three consecutive birdies to total a nine-under 61 and three-shot lead at the turn of the PGA Tour's playoff opener.

It was a striking turnaround for a player who admitted his patience was tested during the opening round in Memphis with 33 putts and too many missed opportunities.

"Yesterday [Thursday] was a day in which I felt like I played better than my score, but also early in the round I was out of the fairway a lot," Scheffler said.

"It could have been a day in which my score could have definitely been worse, and it definitely could have been a lot better. But today was a day in which I felt I got a lot out of the round."

McIlroy, who endured an opening day to forget sitting on four over, failed to turn things around on the second day either as a poor finish saw him bogey the 17th and 18th holes to remain on four over, some 15 shots behind Scheffler.

How do the FedExCup Playoffs work?

All season long, players have earned points based on how they have performed in PGA Tour events, with extra points available for the signature events and majors.

Only the top 70 in the standings have reached the FedEx St Jude Championship (August 13-16), with just the top 50 then progressing to the BMW Championship (August 20-23) and then only the top 30 making it to the finale, The Tour Championship (August 27-30).

Winners of the first two play-off events earn 750 points apiece - the same as The Players and the majors - before the points reset to zero ahead of the Tour Championship.

In the closing event, all players begin at even par, with the starting-strokes model based on FedExCup placings at that point axed in 2025.

The winner of the Tour Championship becomes FedExCup champion for 2026, earning $10m (£7.4m) and a five-year PGA Tour exemption.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Simeon Gholam explains all you need to know on how the play-offs have changed this season in the Championship

The most significant alteration to domestic football in decades has happened over the summer, with the Championship play-offs expanding from a top-six spot to a top-eight position this season, presenting clubs with more opportunity for promotion.

What has (and hasn't) changed?

1st and 2nd are automatically promoted as normal.

3rd and 4th still qualify for the semi-finals.

5th vs 8th and 6th vs 7th in one-off eliminator ties at the home of the side who finishes higher up the league.

The winners of the eliminator ties progress to the semi-finals, to face 3rd and 4th in two-legged ties with the second leg at the home of the side that finishes higher up the league.

One other key thing to note is that, whatever happens, 3rd will face the lowest-ranked team remaining in the semi-finals. So if 8th beats 5th, and 6th beats 7th in the eliminators, 3rd will face 8th and 4th will face 6th. There is no pre-set path for the semi-finals before the eliminators.

Middlesbrough go big to try and get over the line

It was some campaign for Middlesbrough last season. They spent more days in the top two than any other club, but managed to finish fifth.

They were then the victim of the Spygate saga, lost to Southampton in the play-off semi-finals, were reinstated to the final, then lost at Wembley to a stoppage-time Oli McBurnie goal for Hull City.

But any potential hangover looks like it has already been left behind with some of their work in the transfer window.

Owner Steve Gibson has taken his chequebook out and spent serious money to strengthen. Striker Will Lankshear has already made his mark with the winning goal against Wrexham in the Carabao Cup. He scored 11 goals for a struggling Oxford side last season and arrives from Spurs.

Sebastian Berhalter comes in, having last been seen playing for the USA at the World Cup, while goalkeeper Radek Vitek from Manchester United is also an eye-catching addition. He impressed on loan at Bristol City last season.

Kim Hellberg and some Boro fans may be wondering where this backing was in January when they were crying out for reinforcements, but it has certainly led to a swell of excitement at the Riverside about what's possible this season.

Can Southampton escape Spygate scandal?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking exclusively to Sky Sports' Mark McAdam before the FA charge, Southampton boss Tonda Eckert revealed the challenges he has faced after the Spygate scandal that resulted in their expulsion from the Championship play-offs

It was the story that dominated the landscape of last season. A shockwave went around the footballing world when Southampton were expelled from the play-offs after their role in the Spygate scandal.

But the club were quick to back Tonda Eckert, and although an FA charge still hangs over the boss, they have tried to move on and heal the wounds caused by the damage.

Fears of a player exodus have been quelled, with only midfielder Shea Charles departing so far, and the club has brought in goalkeeper Daniel Peretz and striker Cyle Larin permanently, after both starred on loan in the second half of last season.

They will have to overcome a four-point deduction. But they came from a long way back last season with a remarkable run in the second half of the campaign, and they certainly have the quality to challenge.

Managerial changes in the Championship

There are also a few other managerial changes to make a note of. Tony Mowbray is back at Blackburn Rovers four years after he left the club, while Watford have brought in Alessio Dionisi.

Elsewhere, Michael Skubala left Lincoln City after leading them to promotion to join Bristol City. While his exit opened the door for the Imps to make the unique move of appointing joint-managers in the role. Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw take the reins at Sincil Bank.

League One

Will Leicester turn things around?

Image: Leicester City manager Russell Martin

For just the second time in their history, and just 10 years after they won the Premier League title, Leicester City have found themselves in League One.

Russell Martin has taken the helm, as they look to end a miserable run of back-to-back relegations. He also has work to do in winning over some doubters, after miserable ends to his spells at Southampton and Rangers in his last two roles.

The addition of experience has been the aim of the summer, with the likes of Liam Cullen, Conor Chaplin and Wes Burns already joining.

A new dawn for Wednesday and who else could compete for promotion?

The Chansiri era is finally over at Sheffield Wednesday, and there has been a swirl of optimism around the club under new owner David Storch, despite relegation.

Henrik Pedersen, who led the Owls through the grim 2025/26 season, has been given the opportunity to see if he can get more out of a squad that is actually built to compete.

Louie Barry is an eye-catching addition. Injuries have blighted his progress but he has shown what a star he can be at this level for Stockport County, while Barry Bannan is back home after his stint at Millwall.

Luton are quite fancied under Jack Wilshere after a positive run in the second half of last season.

As are Plymouth Argyle, who have been exceptional so far in 2026, just missing out on the play-offs.

Managerial changes in League One

Image: Aaron Ramsey has taken his first permanent managerial role at Oxford United

There has been a particularly notable appointment at Oxford United, with Aaron Ramsey taking his first permanent managerial role to replace Matt Bloomfield, who surprisingly departed in the summer.

It has not been an easy start for Ramsey, however, as he has already had to deal with a transfer embargo which has left him unable to make any additions at the relegated club.

Elsewhere, Daniel Stendel has returned to Barnsley, Martin Drury has taken charge at Huddersfield Town and Jimmy McNulty left Rochdale to join Stockport following the departure of Dave Challinor.

Bromley's first season in the third tier!

Bromley were promoted to the EFL for the first time in their history in 2024, and it took just two seasons for them to seal promotion from League Two.

The Ravens won the title last season, and will now compete in the third tier of English football for the first time. It has only been 11 years since they were promoted to the National League for the first time.

They have been installed as the favourites for relegation, but Andy Woodman's side have defied the critics before and will be keen to do so again. Don't rule out anything at Hayes Lane.

All change at York and Rochdale

Image: Scott Lindsey has been appointed at York City

After 10 years away, York City are back in the EFL!

But it has not been all smooth sailing since. A couple of weeks before the start of the season, manager Stuart Maynard - who led them to promotion with more than 100 points - departed the club.

His replacement Scott Lindsey has not proven popular so far. In his first game in charge York exited the Carabao Cup at the preliminary phase, with fans booing and calling for the return of Maynard.

Not quite the return the Minstermen would have wanted to League Two.

The side they edged to automatic promotion in the National League, Rochdale, have also lost their manager after fighting their way through the play-offs.

McNulty moved on to Stockport, and they have dipped into non-League to appoint their new manager, with Ian Watson joining from National League North side South Shields.

Will Salford City finally get over the line?

Image: Macaulay Langstaff is one of the summer arrivals at Salford City

It is seven years now since Salford City were promoted to League Two, and still they have not managed to get over the line.

Last season was the closest they have come, losing in the play-off final to Notts County. Manager Karl Robinson has since departed, with Peter Cklamovski taking his place, having most recently been in charge of the Malaysia national side.

They have gone big in the transfer market, too. Macaulay Langstaff and Luke Molyneux have already arrived. Could this be the year the club owned by Gary Neville and David Beckham finally reach League One?

Managerial changes in League Two

Elsewhere, there are a lot of new managers to keep an eye on. Chris Hogg has come in at Northampton Town, while another relegated club in Rotherham United have appointed Alex Bruce.

Darrell Clarke takes charge at Tranmere Rovers, Lee Grant is at Walsall and Hayden Mullins will lead Newport County this season.

Sports.title: Jimenez salvages dramatic point for Wolves on Molineux return
Sports.content:
Raul Jimenez scored a stoppage-time equaliser from the penalty spot on his return to Molineux to salvage a 2-2 draw for Wolves against Blackburn.

Wolves took the lead through Marshall Munetsi when Fer Lopez threaded the ball through for him to finish neatly beyond Balazs Hoth. But Blackburn scored a deserved equaliser when Sean McLoughlin nodded in from Ryoya Morishita's right-wing cross.

And Rovers stunned most of the 30,984 inside Molineux when Andri Gudjohnsen converted from close range early in the second half. Wolves turned to returning hero Jimenez off the bench but there was very little sign of them finding an equaliser.

That changed when Jackson Tchatchoua's left-wing cross struck the hand of the otherwise excellent Ryan Alebiosu just inside the box and the referee awarded a penalty. Jimenez held his nerve to snatch a point for Cesar Peixoto's Wolves side.

It was barely deserved. Tony Mowbray's Blackburn, unfancied going into the campaign before a ball was kicked, could not hold on for the victory but did exceed expectations. Wolves will need to improve significantly if they are to come close to satisfying theirs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Marshall Munetsi slotted home Wolves' opening goal against Blackburn

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sean McLoughlin's first goal in English football levelled the game for Blackburn

Key moments at Molineux

18 - GOAL! Munetsi opens the scoring for Wolves

28 - GOAL! McLoughlin nods Blackburn level

49 - GOAL! Gudjohnsen slots Blackburn ahead

60 - SUB! Cometh the hour? Jimenez is introduced

90+3 - GOAL! Jimenez converts a penalty to equalise

Jimenez: We need to learn from this

Image: Jimenez scores Wolves' late equaliser from the penalty spot

Wolves hero Raul Jimenez speaking to Sky Sports:

"It's amazing to be back, scoring in the first game of the season. It's not the result we were looking for in our first home game of the new season, so we need to learn from this. All the games are going to be difficult here, no matter who we play against.

"We need to keep going, it's just the start. I'm going to keep working and going forward to keep improving with the team, to hopefully earn many points and score a lot of goals."

On giving out free 'Si Senor' scarves to the Wolves supporters in the Sir Jack Hayward Stand:

"It's nice to give them back some love that they were showing me for the past eight years, even when I wasn't here at the club. I felt the big love they had for me, so it's the least I could do."

Peixoto: We played with heart not head

Wolves boss Cesar Peixoto speaking to Sky Sports:

"It's not the result we wanted, we wanted to win. We were better in the first half, we created a lot of situations but didn't score. In the second half we suffered a bit more, we conceded the goal.

"After that we played more with heart than with our heads or brain. We lost organisation and it was more difficult after that.

"But the effort of the players was good. We showed big heart to fight until the end. We want to be a team who never gives up, but we have to improve and stay organised."

Relegation hangover for Wolves?

Speaking to Peixoto in the press conference afterwards, it was a chance to ask him why Wolves lost their organisation. It is hardly a new phenomenon at Molineux but it would have been new to the Portuguese coach who has seen a controlled team in pre-season.

"The stadium is amazing, a lot of supporters, a good crowd that supports until the end. But it's normal when things are not the right way, the way the team wants, the players want, and the past comes and they play more with the heart than with the brain."

The past comes. That is the fear for Wolves. It was a packed house but that brings expectation and the players struggled to cope with that once they fell behind. On paper, the problems came before - conceding twice - and they did find that late equaliser.

In reality, the most worrying period came when behind. "We didn't wait for the right triggers to go like we do normally in the last games and because of that if you go press high, the team doesn't stay compact in the right moments. We had more difficulties."

Panicky players and a panicky crowd on night one of this Championship slog does not bode particularly well. Wolves will make changes to the personnel in the coming weeks and the hope is that this will help. But if past frustrations linger it could be a real issue.

Mowbray: It looks outside the box to me

Blackburn Rovers boss Tony Mowbray speaking to Sky Sports:

"Having watched the still pictures it looks outside the box to me.

"If it hits him on the hand and it's away from his body I suppose in modern-day football [it's a penalty] I suppose. But it still looks outside the box to me."

Blackburn boss answers the doubters

Mowbray revealed afterwards that he had been listening to the radio on the journey down to Wolverhampton and heard a number of pundits tipping his Blackburn team for relegation. They saw a team that narrowly escaped the drop and might have weakened.

Speaking to Mowbray in the press conference, it was a chance to ask him how that talk made him feel. "We invested in a young boy from Stockport County [Jayden Fevrier] and a free transfer [Sam Morsy] and they probably think, 'oh they're going down now'," he said.

"I have asked the dressing room and the collective spirit of the dressing room to stand up and say what we thought. And I think we showed today there's enough quality there to give teams problems, even better teams in the league." This was an encouraging start.

Castleford Tigers ended a disastrous run in Super League with a late 18-14 win at Hull FC on Friday.

Castleford - whose head coach Ryan Carr remains absent for personal reasons - opened the scoring after 10 minutes when Renouf Atoni took a short ball at speed and Tom Weaver added the conversion

Sports.title: Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as Werro wins 800m gold
Sports.content:
Britain's Keely Hodgkinson was denied a hat-trick of European 800m golds

Keely Hodgkinson came up just short of a coveted European 800m title hat-trick after Swiss favourite Audrey Werro won their hotly-anticipated showdown in Birmingham as the British Olympic champion settled for silver.

Hodgkinson started quicker but was overtaken by Werro on the back straight and the latter was never overtaken after the first 200m.

Double-defending champion Hodgkinson was just behind as they rounded the final bend, but Werro would not be caught and crossed the finish in a championship record 1:54.81.

Werro, Hodgkinson and Femke Broeders-Bol finished first, second and third in the highly-anticipated 800m final

Twitter Due to your consent preferences, you’re not able to view this Privacy Options

Hodgkinson claimed silver in 1:55.01 and the Netherlands' Femke-Broeders Bol took bronze in a national record 1:55.54.

After losing her title, Hodgkinson said: "Mixed emotions. With that level of competition, any medal is an achievement.

"I thought I was going to win. I didn't do anything wrong, just one of those things.

"I've had a pretty good day today, just didn't go the way that I wanted.

"There were so many different ways that could have played out and we'd figure it out after the first 100m. Audrey wanted to take it on and with that wind I was happy to let her. We're all really great athletes so I knew it was going to be close. I'm looking forward to the next match-up.

"I've said all year it's really motivating to be in such a competitive event. I love it, it brings out the best in me. Championship racing, that's what it's all about, you don't know how it's going to go and some people can have a good day or a bad day. I had a pretty good day today but it just didn't go how I wanted it to."

The world record remains the longest-standing record in athletics set in 1983 by Jarmila Kratochvilova's with a time of 1:53.28 seconds.

While the world record wasn't troubled, Werro's time of 1:54.81 did break the championship record set by Olga Mineyeva in 1982.

Hodgkinson's silver medal is Britain's 10th medal in five days on home soil. Earlier on Friday, Zharnel Hughes claimed silver in the men's 200m.

Sports.title: Arteta says he will sign new Arsenal contract in 'organic way'
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has revealed he will sign a new Arsenal contract and there is no need for fans to be worried about his future.

Arteta has entered the final year of his contract with the Premier League champions - despite co-chairman Josh Kroenke saying in May that a new deal was an "upmost priority" of the club.

But Arteta says he and the club will come together to "resolve" a contract extension in "an organic way" - because he is happy at the club, and his bosses appear happy with him.

"They [the fans] don't have to worry about any of that because I want to be here, I'm extremely happy and I feel very grateful to work with the people I work with," said Arteta about his contract talks.

"When we have the possibility, we will resolve that. That's it.

"Everybody feels comfortable that the timing of the contract is not going to be an issue because my will certainly is to be here and I'm very happy here. My feeling from the club is the same one. That's why everyone is doing things in a very organic way."

Does Arteta have enough attacking firepower this season?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arteta says the transfer window still offers an opportunity to evolve and does not rule out players joining or leaving the club

Arteta also addressed questions about whether his team have enough firepower this season to reclaim the Premier League title - and win the other competitions as well.

Despite winning the Premier League and reaching the Champions League final, Arteta's Arsenal were accused of not being too attacking last term - although there was praise for their defensive solidity.

Arsenal have added Bruno Guimaraes and Christos Tzolis to their midfield and attack this season - having sold Leandro Trossard to Besiktas.

Apart from that, the Gunners have mostly the same midfielders and forwards that ended last season - despite showing an interest in Vinicius Junior, Julian Alvarez and Bradley Barcola in the attacking areas.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' James Savundra takes a closer look at the numbers of Arsenal target Victor Osimhen

Asked if he has enough attacking quality up front at the moment, Arteta replied: "If they are fit, yes.

"But when you look last year at the amount of days, games, months that we missed a lot of our important players and players with a lot of goal threat, the manner that we sustained to have the season that we had, I think is remarkable.

"It talks about the team playing and conducting, and I think it's something that the team deserves credit for.

"We're going to prefer to elevate our level, for sure, expecting that the rest will do the same, because that's traditionally what happened in the league in the last few years. And that's what we have planned this season, and we want to evolve it.

"I have to prepare a team that is capable of winning in whatever the context is: because we're not good enough on the day, because the opponent is so good, because the differences in games. That's my job, that's how I will prepare the team."

Sports.title: Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsed
Sports.content:
Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped.

In a letter to the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, the influential European Football Clubs (EFC) group warned that its cooperation with future tournaments would hinge on Infantino backing down. It said the threat would hold unless a joint venture between EFC and Fifa – a framework for which has already been agreed – is completed before television rights can be sold for the 2028 Women’s Club World Cup.

The letter, dated 31 July and signed by the EFC chief executive, Charlie Marshall, said Infantino’s actions could constitute a “substantial breach” of the bodies’ existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) and suggested this could be grounds for its termination. It floated the idea that EFC and its clubs may push back against the international match calendar and its player release rules, which are crucial to ensuring national team tournaments can function. Infantino shelved the privately backed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE) in the early hours of 1 August after widespread condemnation.

Fundamental to EFC’s complaints was the impression FFE would bring all broadcasting, commercial and sponsorship rights under its own umbrella. The letter asked Fifa to confirm this and said it would take decisive action if these elements were not included in the long-proposed joint venture, whose creation is enshrined in the MoU and intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions. It witheringly wrote that the tie-in had, “unlike the FFE proposal, made no meaningful progress over the past year”. EFC already has a similar joint venture with Uefa, named UC3, which was launched in 2025.

A potentially incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”

In theory the threat still holds although Fifa, in a response to EFC’s letter since Infantino climbed down, is understood to have promised a swift meeting to keep the joint venture on track. EFC’s position followed concerns raised by a vast number of clubs around Europe, who were angered by the lack of consultation around the design of FFE. One major European club expressed concerns in its own letter saying it would support EFC in any “firmer collective action” if necessary and called for “more rigorous and transparent governance processes”.

Any European withdrawal from Club World Cups would in practice mean those tournaments could not run. EFC and Fifa operated last year’s Club World Cup, the first to take place with 32 teams, using a short-term prototype for any future joint venture. No hosts have yet been announced for the new-look Women’s Club World Cup or the next edition of the men’s tournament in 2029.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea won the Club World Cup in July 2025 by beating Paris Saint-Germain in the final. Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty Images

EFC’s letter also raised the continuing delay, first reported in February, in distributing £185m of solidarity money to clubs that did not participate in the Club World Cup. Transparency over the event’s financial performance was also requested.

“We ask that you urgently share the final surplus revenue generated by the 2025 Fifa WC, together with a full profit and loss statement, so that all revenues, expenses and costs can be properly assessed in line with our partnership in this competition,” it said. “The absence of information on this matter, as with the lack of a solution on CWC solidarity for over a year, is also of serious concern and disappointment to EFC and our member clubs.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is understood there is increasing optimism that this issue is on the verge of resolution, although a notional average £50,000 windfall for every global top-flight club, if the pot was divided equally, pales in comparison with the £84m reward long since banked by last year’s winners, Chelsea.

Referring to clubs releasing players for international duty, EFC continued: “Our memorandum of understanding, set to expire on 30 December 2030, includes EFC’s and its member clubs’ acceptance of the international match calendar and the release rules. Both are directly relevant for Fifa’s non-European member associations and to any value FFE may have.” It said Fifa’s apparent commercial vision for FFE constituted a “serious breach of trust” and warned the MoU could be jeopardised.

The letter demonstrates the extraordinary level of leverage EFC, which is chaired by the Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, can claim over Fifa and its increasing influence on football’s future. The organisation, set up in 2008 as a lobby group for clubs around the continent, now has well over 800 members although only a minority hold full voting rights. Some stakeholders elsewhere in football’s ecosystem have expressed fears about the level of power it has assumed. A separate representative body, the Union of European Clubs, was created in 2023 to represent smaller sides but is not recognised by Uefa.

One potential consequence of EFC’s discussions with Fifa could, in the medium term, be its expansion into a group representing clubs around the world. More immediately, last month’s letter demanded that Fifa deliver on a previous promise to fully integrate Al-Khelaifi into the Fifa council, which is purportedly its main decision-making body.

Sports.title: Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos
Sports.content:
Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.

Elaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.

Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.

FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.

It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.

View image in fullscreen The sale will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Gordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.

“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”

With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Speaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”

Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.

Sports.title: Raúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against Blackburn
Sports.content:
Raúl Jiménez marked his return to Wolves with the stoppage-time equaliser that saved them from an embarrassing start to their return to the Championship. The Mexico striker, who scored against England during the World Cup, came off the bench to convert a penalty given for handball by Ryan Alebiosu that would have had VAR questioning whether the defender was in the area when Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross struck his arm.

One minor consolation from Wolves’ relegation is that the video assistant referee is no longer their problem. Jiménez, who had bought scarves for all supporters in the South Bank in gratitude for their welcome home, tucked away his first goal in this second spell for the club he graced during their recent heyday before leaving for Fulham.

“He’s an important striker,” César Peixoto, Wolves’ new head coach said. “He lives for scoring and making goals. Raúl is a key player for us. He helped the team inside and outside the pitch but we have to go slowly with him because he is 35 years old and comes back from the World Cup. We want him to stay good and scoring for us is good for him and for the team.”

Goals from Sean McLoughlin and Andri Gudjohnsen allowed Blackburn to provide Wolves with a reality check after Marshall Munetsi had scored early. Confidence is a fragile commodity and, after their decision to replace Rob Edwards with a manager with no experience of English football, the Wolves board know that their supporters’ patience is thin. Leading Gil Vicente to sixth place in the Portuguese first division does not make Peixoto a guaranteed winner.

Conceding the equaliser, through Jiménez’s first goal for Wolves in 1,311 days, denied unfancied Blackburn a deserved victory after Wolves lost their shape. Tony Mowbray, their head coach, felt the penalty decision was harsh. “I’ve just been shown an angle by my analyst where he [Alebiosu] is outside the box; another angle I’m told shows he’s just inside the box. I just felt like more and more decisions were starting to sway their way,” the former West Brom manager said. “It’s harsh to take because I don’t think they deserved that second goal.”

Molineux was awash with fading golden sunlight and rising optimism at kick-off. A summer that started with such a surprising managerial departure was promising to end with renewed faith in the team’s direction of travel, until Peixoto’s admired high press came unstuck as his team started to “play with their hearts more than their heads”.

View image in fullscreen Marshall Munetsi (right) celebrates scoring Woves’ first goal with Fer López. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

The Blackburn defence had split generously to allow Munetsi a clean run through on to Fer López’s sumptuous pass. The left-footed finish from the Zimbabwean, himself coming back to Molineux after a loan at Paris FC, strengthened the feelgood factor.

Peixoto’s tactics do currently lead to gaps on transition. Blackburn, who have not done so much in the transfer market to suggest they should aim higher than last season’s 20th place, got behind Wolves on several occasions. It was no great surprise when, from Ryoya Morishita’s superb right-wing cross, McLoughlin headed beyond Dan Bentley to equalise.

Some of Wolves’ best business this summer has been bringing players back to Molineux. While Jiménez started the night on the bench, after a late start to pre-season following his impressive World Cup for Mexico, López was the classiest player on view. Back from a loan at Celta Vigo, he has been invited to make the No 10 position his own, and the Spaniard nearly regained Wolves the lead only to curl his shot wide.

View image in fullscreen Blackburn’s Andri Gudjohnsen gives his side a 2-1 lead early in the second half. Photograph: Simon Davies/ProSports/Shutterstock

Blackburn continued to benefit from Wolves’ soft centre however. Oladapo Afolayan’s shot needed tipping over by Bentley before the right winger again got space down Wolves’ left – where David Møller Wolfe, in for the injured Hugo Bueno, showed he is still not match fit after his World Cup endeavours with Norway – to cross for Gudjohnsen to turn in Rovers’ second goal. “The team lost some organisation and played with their heart rather than their head and brains,” Peixoto said. “It’s a lesson for us in the future, we need to stay with mental stability for the 90 minutes.”

By the hour mark, the South Bank were swirling their Jiménez scarves above their heads and chanting “Si Señor” in honour of the veteran striker who was such an esteemed figure at Molineux for five of the club’s best years in modern times. Before his horrific head injury, he was the pivotal attacking player as Nuno Espírito Santo’s team reached the later stages of the FA Cup and Europa League. The scene was set for the Mexican. Could he deliver? Si, señor.

Sports.title: ‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situation
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has said he is relaxed about his Arsenal contract expiring at the end of the new season and believes his side will need to be better than last year to defend their title successfully.

The Premier League champions will face Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff on Sunday and are heavy favourites to win back-to-back league titles for the first time since the 1930s. The departure of Pep Guardiola from their traditional rivals City means Arteta is now the Premier League’s longest-serving manager, with the Spaniard having joined in December 2019.

He signed a three-year contract extension in September 2024 after Arsenal finished as runners-up to City and had been expected to agree a new deal over the summer that would make him one of the highest-paid managers in the world. Arteta acknowledged on Friday that his priorities have been elsewhere this summer as he attempts to strengthen his squad before the new season but reassured supporters that he is fully committed to the club.

“They don’t have to worry about any of that, because I want to be here. I am extremely happy. I feel very grateful to work with the people that I work with and when we have the possibility, we will resolve that. And that’s it,” he said.

Asked if he expects talks over a new contract to continue after the transfer window, Arteta added: “There is always another priority, I think. And that’s the way we have been treating it, I think because everybody feels comfortable that the time on the contract is not going to be an issue. I think because my will, certainly, is to be here and I am very happy here. My feeling from the club is the same one. That is why everyone is doing things in a really organic way.”

Arsenal have opened negotiations with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber, while they are still in the market for another attacker if they can offload Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus. After missing out on Vinícius Júnior when the Brazil forward opted to sign a new deal with Real Madrid, Arteta defended Arsenal’s strategy this summer and is hoping that they can still add to their squad.

“I am really happy with the squad, the players that I have and I am really happy with the ambition of the club. There is zero question about that. We have shown that in the manner we have tried to act,” he said.

“But I think we need to do it our own way. We have super strengths and we have other areas we need to be very conscious [of] because we don’t have the elements or the structure that other clubs have. We need to do it our way. We are always on it that way and we will do what we believe is the right thing to do. To have the best possibility to compete in every competition that’s for sure.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta added: “We’re going to prepare to elevate our level, expecting that the rest will do the same. That’s traditionally what happened in the league in the last few years, and that’s the way we have planned the season, and the way we want to evolve the team.”

Sports.title: Chelsea expect Enzo Fernández to stay after Manchester City opt not to meet deadline
Sports.content:
Manchester City did not make a £120m bid for Enzo Fernández before Chelsea’s 5pm deadline on Friday but Enzo Maresca still expects a busy end to the transfer window, as the club seek incomings and outgoings. Chelsea, meanwhile, now expect the Argentina midfielder to stay at Stamford Bridge.

Maresca takes charge of City for the first time in a major match on Sunday against Arsenal in Cardiff in the Community Shield but is a long way from finalising the squad he will have for the season. Fernández, who played under Maresca at Chelsea, remains a target for City, who could still test the water despite missing the deadline.

“For sure there are things we need to do, how many I don’t know, can be one, can be two, depends also if players want to leave, so we can see,” Maresca said on Friday, having suggested City would not agree to Chelsea’s demands. “It’s 48 hours for the final, my first final in this club, I would like to win my first trophy, so my focus isn’t on players that can leave or players that can arrive, my focus is on the game.”

City have rejected two bids from Barcelona for Rodri but anticipate a third, and are expected to sell Tijjani Reijnders in the coming days. They are also in the market for reinforcements as they aim to challenge on four fronts. City are close to signing the 18-year-old Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille but are willing to bring in others.

Rodri, who has a year remaining on his contract, returned to the club on Friday after his holiday which followed a triumphant World Cup, but Maresca would not be drawn on the midfielder’s immediate future with a third Barcelona offer expected.

“The transfer window is open, we can buy players, we can sell players, anything can happen. I just saw Rodri now in the building, I gave him a big hug, he looks good, so we’ll see what happens.”

Reijnders is set to join the Saudi Pro League side Al-Qadsiah after the two clubs agreed a £51m fee for the Dutchman, who moved to City last summer from Milan but wants more regular playing time.

“They all work every day, they all do sessions every day and at the end of the week they all want to play a game,” Maresca said. “When they don’t play they struggle to understand or they struggle to see the reason why, and I can understand that after one season some of them would like to play a little bit more. It’s a normal situation.”
