Sports.title: British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies following tragic accident in Portugal
Sports.content:
British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies following tragic accident in Portugal

Finlay Tarling, the 19-year-old younger brother of Ineos Grenadiers rider Josh, was competing for the NSN Development Team at the Volta a Portugal when the incident occurred

View 2 Images Finlay Tarling has sadly died (Image: Huw Fairclough/Getty Images)

British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died aged 19 following a tragic accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal. Tarling, the younger brother of Ineos Grenadiers rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on both the road and track.

‌



The Welsh teenager was competing for the NSN Development Team on Friday and the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe. No details regarding the nature of the incident have been released.

‌



NSN announced his death in a statement which read: "We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

‌



Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend. Rest in peace, Fin."

View 2 Images Finlay Tarling pictured with his parents in 2025 (Image: Huw Fairclough/Getty Images)

‌



The Portuguese Cycling Federation also issued a statement which confirmed the race had been neutralised and that the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of 'respect and mourning'.

It said: "The organisation of the 87th Volta a Portugal em Bicicleta Jogos Santa Casa deeply regrets to announce the passing of British cyclist Finlay Tarling, from the NSN Development Team, following a serious accident that occurred during the 8th stage of the race.

"At this moment of profound dismay, the organization of the Volta a Portugal and the Portuguese Cycling Federation express their most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his teammates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones.

‌



"In light of this tragic event, the race will be neutralised until reaching Fafe and, as a sign of respect and mourning, the podium ceremony scheduled for today will not take place. The organisation will provide all additional information as soon as conditions allow it to do so."

Stephen Park CBE, Performance Director for the Great Britain Cycling Team, paid tribute by saying: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

‌



"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man. Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time."

In the comments of NSN's Facebook post, fans from around the world offered their condolences to Tarling's family, loved ones and his team. "This is terrible, shocking news," one wrote. "My deepest condolences to Fin's family, the team, and the whole cycling family."

"Such sad news," another added. "Deepest condolences to Finlay's family and the wider cycling community."

Article continues below

"Deepest condolences to the family, friends and teammates as this is heartbreaking," a third posted. "May you rest in peace."

Sports.title: Championship 1-24 predictions: Every club's finishing place this season decided
Sports.content:
The most unpredictable, chaotic league in the world is officially back tonight, with Wolves and Blackburn kicking us off at Molineux.

Between now and May, 24 teams will battle it out over 46 gameweeks for a chance to land a golden ticket to the Premier League. Two will succeed with another joining them following an extended play-off campaign (don't forget it's now the top eight!). Three other teams will also exit the Championship, albeit through the trapdoor.

We all know from experience how gruelling and unpredictable the Championship is. So it's only logical that, for the second year running, I take a stab at calling where every team will finish.

Check out our 1-24 predictions below ahead of the big kick-off...

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

24 - Bolton Wanderers

I'm backing two of the promoted teams to stay up this year, or at the very least make a good fist of doing so. I'm less optimistic on Bolton, largely because in Amario Cozier-Duberry and Mason Burstow, they will have to make do without two of their most influential attackers from last season. It also feels like a lack of business has been done, particularly in those forward areas.

Ryan Hardie was signed on loan earlier this week and has double figure pedigree at this level but goals may still be hard to come by with loanees Cozier-Duberry and Burstow (their top scorer last term with 12 league goals) not returning. Sam Dalby was next best in the scoring charts with 10 goals but is an unknown quantity at this level. It feels like more firepower is essential before the transfer deadline. David Watson, Ben Davies, Akin Famewo, Luca Stephenson, Kyliane Dong and Gaizka Larrazabal have all come through the door but none really jump out at you. If any team needs a big final few weeks in the window, it's Bolton.

‌



23 - Charlton Athletic

Charlton got over the line last year after a bit of a slog to give themselves an opportunity to kick on under Nathan Jones. The issue is that they will have to try and do so in a division which feels significantly stronger this time around - and I'm not totally sold on the business they've done being enough to keep their heads above water.

Jones has spoken about Charlton wanting to evolve but it's hard to see where the goals are coming from for them to do so. The Addicks were the third lowest scorers in the division last year; other than Charlie Kelman (7) and Sonny Carey (8) no other Charlton player registered more than three goals in the league. Millenic Alli and Karlan Grant have been brought in to add to Charlton's wide attacking options but the former has a dearth of Championship experience and Grant last hit double figures in the league back in the 2021-22 campaign. Their midfield options don't inspire confidence either; it's one thing questioning whether the strikers can get more goals but the service into them also needs to be better. I'm not seeing that correlation right now.

Charlton will be solid and diligent but I don't think that will be enough. It feels like Jones recognises that with his desire for Charlton to be less limited this year. Have they done the business to do so? It doesn't feel like it.

‌



22 - Lincoln City

View 7 Images Lincoln City went 29 games unbeaten to romp League One last season (Image: PA)

Momentum can be a force of nature in football and it half feels like Lincoln have forgotten how to lose games after going 29 unbeaten to absolutely romp their way to the League One title. But even for one of the most sensible and well-run clubs in the pyramid, take away your manager and star player from that formula and it's a pretty devastating one-two.

The reason I have them in the final relegation spot is that I fancy them to at least give a good fist of upsetting the odds again. However, Jack Moylan was their talisman and his loss is significant, maybe more so than Michael Skubala. On the incoming front, it feels like Tanto Olaofe has the tools to make a nuisance of himself at this level even if he may not be prolific. Mason Melia, the promising young Tottenham striker, is a wildcard in attack after signing on loan. There's not been loads of business done but Lincoln do still have the nucleus of the team that absolutely demolished League One last season.

‌



The step up will be significant and they will undoubtedly become reacquainted with the feeling that comes after losing games. But Lincoln can hold their own and will bloody some noses.

21 - Blackburn Rovers

Blackburn have arguably had the weakest transfer window of any side in the division, adding just Moussa Baradji, Jayden Fevrier and Sam Morsy to a squad that flirted with relegation for most of last season. Already, we're in alarm bell territory.

Tony Mowbray returning to Ewood Park has probably been Blackburn's most significant capture of the summer but the squad he will start the season with is threadbare. Rovers will play on the front foot more under Mowbray and have players who can outscore teams; that will be what sets them apart from others down the bottom. The fact they have attacking players who you would genuinely back to deliver over the course of a season, like Ryoya Morishita, Andri Gudjohnsen and Yuki Ohashi, is encouraging. But they lack depth in other areas and that will prove problematic as the season goes in.

‌



20 - Portsmouth

After two consecutive survival battles, it feels like Portsmouth are trying to kick on this summer by opening up the purse strings, operating at a different level in the transfer market compared to what we have seen previously. Big striker Marko Milovanovic and the all-action midfielder Rocco Shein after intriguing pick ups and the onus will be on the former to hit the ground running to ease some of the goal-scoring burden on Adrian Segecic, who is a right player. A fit and firing Josh Murphy will also go some way to helping on the goal front; plagued by injuries last year, he racked up 22 goal contributions in 45 league games during the 2024-25 campaign.

I think Portsmouth will be okay but I don't see them having the depth to climb the table significantly compared to last year. A lot will hinge on how their new signings adapt. We've seen lots of clubs, Millwall most recently, enjoy success from overseas signings and effective player trading. This year could be Portsmouth's first step in emulating that model, which would serve them well.

19 - Stoke City

‌



It almost feels like Stoke are stuck in some weird sort of Narnia whereby they do business I like each summer but don't tend to go anywhere. Therefore I just can't bring myself to back them for any sort of decent finish.

It's now been nine years since Stoke dropped out of the Premier League and they still haven't recorded a top-half finish in the Championship. Ethan Galbraith quickly established himself as one of the Championship's best playmakers at Swansea after making the step up from Leyton Orient last summer and landing him for big money felt like a real statement of intent at the time. But beyond that I'm not sold on any of their other incoming business. Viktor Johanssen and Million Manhoef are quality and Mark Robins should, theoretically, be the perfect manager to finally get Stoke out of their 14th-18th malaise. Maybe this will be the year. But it'll be a braver man than me who backs it.

18 - Preston North End

A Championship without Preston North End just doesn't feel right. I did initially have fears that could change, but late transfer business has convinced me to nudge them up this list.

‌



Ambition wise, PNE smashed their transfer record to retain the services of star man Alfie Devine after his stellar loan last year earlier this summer. But beyond that, it all felt a bit underwhelming for a while. Delano Burgzorg managed just three Championship goals last season and five the year before, while Jusef Erabi, also joining in attack, is an unknown quantity at this level. Captain Ben Whiteman chucking the towel in a fortnight before the season starts following interest from Wrexham is hardly a resounding vote of confidence for where PNE were at, either.

But they have replaced him swiftly with Leo Leroy from Basel, who looks a good signing. And it was confirmed on Friday that a deal for Stan Mills to join the club in January has been agreed due to Oxford United's current transfer embargo. More could follow before the window shuts. So although the vibes at Deepdale haven't been great throughout the summer, I don't see them in a relegation fight.

17 - Cardiff City

View 7 Images Cardiff City are back in the Championship after winning promotion last season (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA)

‌



Cardiff look by far the best equipped of the promoted sides to cope with life in the Championship and I debated placing the Bluebirds a fair bit higher on the list here. I always think this pool of teams, the ones who won't be troubled by relegation but are perhaps unlikely to mount a realistic play-off push, are the hardest ones to place.

Brian Barry-Murphy's total football should translate well to a higher level and in Yousef Salech they boast a striker whose game will suit the league. Moylan is another player I fancy to replicate his stunning League One form in the Championship, while signing Nathan Trott permanently is huge after his excellent loan last season. Maybe Cardiff can maintain their momentum from last season and push for a higher finish than this. There has also been talk of significant further spending in the transfer market, which could skew these predictions. One thing I am certain of is they won't be looking anxiously over their shoulder.

16 - Watford

Individually, Watford have some proper talent in their squad. But they are another team that you just wouldn't feel comfortable backing to achieve something based on a lots of factors. One big one is the manager: Alessio Dionisi starts the season, but will he end it? Who knows. Probably not even Watford.

‌



Giorgi Chakvetadze and Nestory Irankunda (who is finalising a move to Sporting Lisbon as I finish these predictions) are big losses. Imran Louza would be another with intense speculation over his future. That would be three big losses and probably kill off any outside chance of a play-off push. That being said, who really knows what any season holds for Watford. The only thing I'll stick my neck out and say is that, like Cardiff above, they won't be looking over their shoulder at any point.

15 - Birmingham City

Birmingham will have grand ambitions this season and will be all the better for last year's campaign, where they consolidated themselves in steady if not spectacular fashion. The problem I think they'll find is that there are just too many teams who are better than them currently for them to really kick on this year.

Maybe that sounds harsh. Or lazy. Or both! But I just don't see the significant upturn in points they will require to break into the top eight, although they do have the scope to do something completely bonkers in the final weeks of the transfer window to make me look foolish.

‌



14 - Derby County

Derby came close to the play-offs under John Eustace last year and the nucleus of that squad is still intact. But I think they will be one of the teams who find themselves finishing lower this term simply due to the strength of others.

The unexpected collapse of a takeover by the Saudi Arabian boxing kingpin Turki Alalshikh is likely to have an impact on the club's incoming transfer activity, though they have managed to secure the permanent signings of popular loanees Sammy Szmodics and Bobby Clark. Derby are a strong, powerful team who nobody will fancy playing. And on their day, they are a match for any team in the division. Across the course of a season is another matter, though I wouldn't be too shocked if any of the teams placed between 10 and 14 here end up in slightly different spots.

13 - Bristol City

‌



It felt like Bristol City needed a big summer after falling away bigtime last year and, on paper, they've delivered. They've spent the best part of £9million on League One's two top strikers in Dom Ballard and Lorent Tolaj. Plus they've brought in the highly-rated Sam Tickle as their new No 1 keeper, the industrious Sam Greenwood to further strengthen in the attacking areas and Championship stalwart Jed Wallace. On paper, not bad, right?

Does all that equate to a play-off finish under the guidance of new head coach, Michael Skubala? Maybe. I still reckon Bristol City fall just short, mainly due to the strength of the division. There are just too many good teams ahead of them and, let's not forget, they are effectively ripping things up and starting again with Skubala at the helm. A top eight finish at the first time of asking is probably a stretch, but a good season here should set them up nicely for next year.

12 - West Brom

View 7 Images James Morrison will lead West Brom permanently after keeping them up last season (Image: Adam Fradgley/West Bromwich Albion FC)

‌



James Morrison is one of the big unknown quantities ahead of the new season. His arrival as caretaker boss was the catalyst for West Brom retaining their Championship status after a truly chastening campaign He rightly landed the job on a full-time basis off the back of that, but can he now oversee a promotion challenge?

The Baggies went back to basics under Morrison in a bid to accumulate the points necessary to stay afloat and it remains to be seen if they will stick with the same approach given the former midfielder has now effectively been given a blank canvas to work with. Squad-wise, West Brom have good players and better depth than some others. Does that translate into a top eight finish? I'm unsure, so I'll hedge my bets.

11 - Swansea City

Swansea start the season with perhaps the best striker in the division in Zan Vipotnik. But will they end the window with last season's Championship top scorer still in tow with Hull City circling? That remains to be seen and plays a factor here.

‌



Keeping Vipotnik would be a major transfer win and they've done smart business too: Elijah Just looked a right player at the World Cup and will bolster their attack and if they can keep Ross Stewart fit after snapping the striker up from Sunderland, then it could be the signing of the summer. Unfortunately, it's at the other end Swansea look less convincing. The news on the eve of the new season that Cameron Burgess has suffered an ACL injury isn't particularly helpful for Vitor Matos.

10 - Wrexham

Wrexham came agonisingly close to landing a play-off spot last season and will be in the mix to go one better this season. But again, the quality of the other teams pushing for those top eight positions could just nudge Phil Parkinson's team aside.

After hitting their stride in the second half of last term, Wrexham have opted for continuity and strengthened smartly rather than opting for full-scale surgery. Danny Imray is an excellent pick-up at right-back and will enhance their attacking threat from that area. Anthony Patterson will come in as first-choice keeper and is an upgrade on last season. Josh Windass will lead from the front again after bagging an impressive 17 goals last season with only Vipotnik, Ollie McBurnie and Haji Wright netting more. Kieffer Moore and Sam Smith will provide support but I reckon a marquee addition in attack is needed for them to gatecrash the top eight this time.

‌



9 - QPR

View 7 Images QPR could be dark horses for a top eight finish (Image: MI News/NurPhoto)

In terms of transfer window wins, QPR are right up there. Looking at their business, there is a lot to like: Pierce Charles on loan feels shrewd, albeit the youngster dropped a clanger in the cup game with Millwall. Picking up Dennis Cirkin on a free transfer is just tremendous business and Tariq Lamptey could still be a game-changer if he can rediscover his fitness and hit top form again. Glenn Kamara also adds some steel in midfield.

The bonus QPR have despite their form absolutely falling off a cliff at the end of last season (and largely why I'm choosing to ignore that) is that they already have an adequate attacking arsenal to compliment their new signings. Richard Kone and Rumarn Burrell should both be in the goals after acclimatising to Championship level last term and are backed up by the likes of Karomoko Dembele, Kwame Poku and Koki Saito. And Illias Chair. What does that all up to? My prediction is QPR will be a good watch and dark horses for a top eight finish.

‌



8 - Sheffield United

Sheffield United were an absolute calamity last season and probably ruined many an ante-post bet. They were steady if unspectacular following Chris Wilder's return and feel safer to back this time around, albeit with the caveat that troubling the top two feels beyond them.

The incoming business so far doesn't feel like much to crow about, while the sale of Andre Brooks to Norwich was a painful one. But the team that finished the season is far superior than their final league standing of 13th. This time around, Wilder and Co won't be playing catch up after the sort of nightmare start even a depressed supercomputer would struggle to realistically muster up. They've lost Gustavo Hamer, but the squad still boasts plenty of firepower and players who have experience of doing the business at this level. Defensively they have some of the division's top performers in their respective positions in keeper Michael Cooper, Japhet Tanganga and Femi Seriki. That's a nice mix and I reckon they return to the pack challenging for promotion.

7 - Burnley

‌



Of all the relegated sides, Burnley feel like the hardest to predict. They are not the only club to head into the season with a manager who is untested on these shores but it feels like Nicky Hayen has a bigger job on his hands than Cesar Peixoto. If they retain the services of Zian Flemming, then Burnley could finish higher. They absolutely haemorrhaged goals last season - almost two a game - but I like the loan signing of Max Alleyne from Manchester City.

Cards on the table time: I really don't know what to expect from Burnley and they were by far the hardest to place on this list. My gut and head says they will not be the force they usually are in this division after dropping down. I had a couple of absolute shockers last year and Burnley could very well be the shout I try to avoid looking at for the next 12 months.

6 - Millwall

Millwall enjoyed their best campaign in a generation last time out as they defied all the odds to finish third, missing out on automatic promotion on the final day. Emulating that feat will take some doing, even though the nucleus of the squad that won more games than any other team in the division bar champions Coventry City largely remains.

‌



Talisman Femi Azeez is likely to depart and losing his ability to conjure up something from nothing in the final third will hurt a team who were the lowest scorers in the top eight. On paper, Millwall's incoming business looks positive and you can tell from their recent track record in the transfer market that they generally know what they're doing on that front. They also boast one of the division's top managers in Alex Neil, who underlined his credentials with last year's showing. The squad does feel imbalanced, though, with just two out and out senior wingers in Azeez and Kyrell Lisbie. And with Azeez likely to depart and Tristan Crama recently undergoing ankle surgery, Millwall will be without the dynamic right hand pairing that was so influential last term.

The Lions may not finish as high as last year, but another play-off finish feels within reach and would represent another strong season.

5 - Southampton

View 7 Images Tonda Eckert remains in charge of Southampton but he could face a ban over 'Spygate' (Image: Matt Watson/Southampton FC via Getty Images)

‌



Southampton were absolutely motoring at the end of last season and probably have the squad to finish better than the fifth place I've got them down for. But the uncertainty over Tonda Eckert plays a big role in that; if the German is handed a ban for the Spygate scandal that marred last year's play-offs, then that could skew Southampton's season massively. The shadow of that possibility even hanging over them might even do the trick.

Regardless of who is at the helm, Southampton won't be on minus points for long and will be among the teams slugging it out for promotion. It's hard to pinpoint a weakness in the squad: Daniel Peretz is back permanently and we already know his quality, while Cyle Larin, Lewis Dobbin and Divin Mubama give the Saints even more firepower. The squad is just a joke all around, really. Leo Scienza and Tom Fellows on either flank...forget the spying, are we sure that's allowed? Really, it's a poor season for Southampton if they are in the play-off eliminators. If the Eckert situation had been resolved and there was clarity on that front, I've have them well clear of them.

4 - Norwich City

Under Philippe Clement, Norwich feel like proper promotion contenders. The former Rangers boss inherited a team in turmoil with Norwich second from bottom after failing to win a staggering seven straight home games in the Championship. He would oversee 17 wins from 31 games, which is promotion form.

‌



I feel like a broken record banging on about strikers and firepower, but goals win prizes and Norwich have some seriously heavy artillery up top. Jovon Mokoma is the business and should be a decent shout for top scorer, while Mo Toure has adapted to the Championship seamlessly. Norwich are less convincing at the other end and will ship goals. But for every goal they concede they could go and score three. I can see them troubling the top, top dogs but having to settle for a play-off spot, eventually. Again, think they will be a really good watch for any neutrals who find themselves flicking through Sky Sports + via the red button on midweeks.

3 - West Ham

I know, I know: West Ham was the banker. This was the no-brainer, the one that couldn't fail etc etc. If we're speaking about absolute jokes of a squad then West Ham are bang up there in terms of invidual players (Jarrod Bowen in the Champ? Come on). And yet I think that's also part of the reason why a top two finish could elude them. They have the tools to succeed but does it all work together?

Nuno Espirito Santo has been there, done that, got that t-shirt when it comes to promotion from the Championship, so he's not walking into the unknown. But the landscape has changed drastically since then. West Ham in the Championship now feels far more significant than it did when they were last in here more than a decade ago and the dynamics have shifted; if they attempt to continue with the same pragmatic style Nuno has typically deployed throughout his career, then I don't see them doing enough to crack the top two. And that's before we even touch on the weight of expectation that will be on them and their manager. With respect, Wolves in the Championship at the time was a big job. But this feels like another level for him and a group of players who went down last year.

‌



I don't mean to go into full-on cliche mode, but how will this star-studded squad cope with being the scalp of the division? Can they, in fact, do it on a cold Tuesday night away at Stoke? Maybe I'm wrong and West Ham will absolutely romp it. But coming off the back of a bruising relegation and with off-field drama still prevalent in the background, I'm not sure it'll be as straightforward as some are expecting.

2 - Middlesbrough

You've got to give it to Boro - they have had the sort of transfer window that wouldn't look out of place in Football Manager (the good ones, not 2026). They've scooped major windfalls from sell-on clauses, banked a tidy sum from the sale of their talisman Hayden Hackney (bittersweet but necessary as his deal was up next year) and they've used it to level up in the two positions that cost them automatic promotion last year in goalkeeper and striker.

Radek Vitek is a huge upgrade on Sol Brynn and will be one of the division's top keepers, while Will Lankshear should absolutely feast if he is served up the same number of quality chances that Boro's forward's spurned last season. Just the impact from those two alone will serve Boro incredibly well. We know the squad is strong, even though the loss of Hackney is a huge blow.

‌



Backing Boro to finish second ahead of some of the other quality teams in this league might feel bold, but the team and manager Kim Hellberg are impressive. And while others, like the teams coming down, may have to find their feet back at the level, Middlesbrough should get motoring far quicker.

1 - Wolves

View 7 Images Wolves are likely to be in the frame for an instant return to the Premier League (Image: David Rogers)

Wolves needed a huge revamp after one of the worst Premier League seasons in history…that hasn’t happened. Wolves needed to shift the deadwood and high earners out of the club…that hasn’t happened either. So why - I hear you ask - are we tipping Cesar Peixoto’s side to finish at the top of the Championship pile?

‌



Simply put, Wolves have an embarrassment of riches for the second tier. In midfield, they have a Brazilian international in Andre, the exciting Fer Lopez and potentially Jordan James. Signing Kieran Trippier was an impressive coup, bringing Raul Jimenez back to Molineux was potentially even more eye-catching. Adam Armstrong, who was on course to be the league’s top scorer before moving to Molineux in the 2025/26 campaign, may have to settle for a place on the bench this time around.

Pre-season has shown Wolves will play on the front foot and press high, a method which has worked for previous title winners. They will need to start well to ease the toxicity and could still do with a new keeper and centre back, but Wolves will fancy their chances of lifting the trophy next May.

Sports.title: Bradley Barcola to Liverpool transfer twist as decision made over £145m PSG demand
Sports.content:
Bradley Barcola to Liverpool transfer twist as decision made over £145m PSG demand

Bradley Barcola has been Liverpool's priority transfer target for the summer window but a bold decision looks to have been made on the Paris Saint-Germain star

View 2 Images Liverpool have made a big decision in their transfer pursuit of Bradley Barcola (Image: (Photo by Maciej Rogowski/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images))

Liverpool have chosen to pause transfer negotiations for Bradley Barcola with Paris Saint-Germain still demanding £145million. The Reds have been strongly linked to Barcola over the last few weeks as they look to strengthen in attack after Yan Diomande opted to join Real Madrid over both them and PSG.

‌



Luis Enrique's side are currently in the process of finalising two incomings with Mika Godts joining from Ajax and Ferran Torres on his way to the European champions from Barcelona.

‌



Maghnes Akliouche has already joined from AS Monaco, which suggests Barcola, who did not play in their UEFA Super Cup final win over Aston Villa, could be free to leave.

‌



L'Equipe have claimed that Liverpool are yet to find a breakthrough in talks and will thus wait until the final days of the window before restarting their attempts to sign him.

Steven Gerrard lands new job as career takes a twist before Premier League season READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

PSG are currently holding firm on their sizeable financial demands despite his unwillingness to sign a new contract. The Frenchman is reportedly open to an Anfield switch but Liverpool are not currently bending to their demands, seemingly in the hope their asking price decreases.

‌



With roughly £150m to be spent on attackers, it is fair to assume that the Parisians may need to sell and will accept a fee lower below their current demands, but it is certainly a big risk to take.

Having parted ways with Mohamed Salah, Liverpool need to sign a new elite-level forward particularly with Tottenham showing a keen interest in Cody Gakpo.

Diomande was an option before Real paid £120million to sign from RB Leipzig. Barcola and his club teammate Ibrahim Mbaye have subsequently emerged as options. The latter was also an unused substitute against Unai Emery's side.

‌



View 2 Images Ibrahim Mbaye has also been linked with Liverpool

Liverpool have not been too active in the window thus far with Victor Munoz and Ronald Araujo the only signings made this summer.

The latter is the second new defender into Anfield, however, with an agreement reached to sign Jeremy Jacquet from Rennes back in February.

Article continues below

Departures and rumours surrounding Liverpool players have been more prominent with Curtis Jones still a target of Inter Milan and Gakpo potentially set to join Spurs.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina

Final: Wales/Bosnia and Herzegovina vs Italy/Northern Ireland - Tuesday, 7.45pm kick-off
