World.title: Migrant charity SOS Méditerranée says 11 bodies spotted in sea off Libya's coast
World.content:
A plane operated by non-governmental organisations assisting migrants in the Mediterranean spotted 11 decomposing bodies in the sea off the coast of Libya on Friday.

 

The SOS Méditerranée NGO called it a "harrowing scene" in a statement, saying "some of the bodies still had clothes on, others were kept afloat by tire inner tubes".

It said the bodies were "in an advanced state of decomposition."

"This sighting is a stark reminder of the human consequences of Europe's deadly policies of indifference and deterrence-at-all-costs," the organisation said in a statement.

The Italian coast guard said it had been notified and had informed Libyan authorities since the bodies were in Libya's search and rescue zone.

It said the bodies were around 57 nautical miles (105 kilometres) from the Libyan coastal city of Zuwarah.

The monitoring plane was operated by SOS Méditerranée and the Humanitarian Pilots Initiative.

Every year, tens of thousands of migrants attempt to cross the sea from north Africa to southern member states of the European Union.

The International Organisation for Migration said this week that the number of known migrant deaths in the central Mediterranean has increased drastically, even as migrant numbers fall because of harsher European policies.

It said 821 people died or went missing in the first four months of 2026, a 111% increase from 2025. More than half of the deaths were caused by severe weather in January.

Over the same period, migrant arrivals on that route fell by 46% to 8,577.

The EU border agency Frontex said the total number of irregular border crossings into the European Union fell by 26% in 2025 from the previous year to almost 178,000.

World.title: EU pushes back as US revives trade pressure on bloc and accuses Brussels of enabling China to evade tariffs
World.content:
The EU pushed back at renewed trade pressure from the United States on Friday, as Washington said the bloc was enabling Chinese evasion of US tariffs and stepped up calls for it to roll back flagship green rules on businesses.

 

Washington's ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, called on the bloc to "align" the provisions of two landmark new laws on environmental and human rights supply chain standards with the EU-US trade deal struck last year.

"Now it's time for the EU to deliver," Puzder posted on X, along with a US government document detailing a long list of "concerns" with the rules.

"The United States will take any actions necessary to address unreasonable burdens on US commerce absent a solution that addresses these concerns," the document warned.

Responding to Puzder's message, European Commission spokesperson Arianna Podesta said the EU continued to "exchange on both tariff and non-tariff issues" with the United States, calling the process "constructive."

But she added: "We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation."

The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) requires large companies to fix the "adverse human rights and environmental impacts" of their supply chains worldwide, while the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) requires them to provide information on their climate impact and emissions and steps to limit them.

"The directives' extraterritorial reach and costly and onerous supply chain due diligence obligations will adversely impact the ability of US businesses to compete on a level playing field in the EU market," read the US document.

The EU has already dialled back the scope of both laws under pressure from businesses both inside and outside the bloc, delaying implementation and sparing smaller firms, but the US document said that did not go far enough.

Puzder's comments came a day after he hit out at the bloc's carbon border tax, CBAM, which he charged was "a tariff in substance, no matter the 'climate policy' label."

Separately, the EU was among dozens of trading partners flagged in a White House report on Thursday as risks regarding "illegal transshipment" from China, where goods are sent through third countries to avoid paying sweeping levies imposed by President Donald Trump.

US President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the Trump Turnberry golf course in Scotland, 27 July, 2025 AP Photo

The report, which also targeted Mexico, Canada and Japan, vowed to tap artificial intelligence to help detect illegal practices in future.

"The EU shares the US objective of tackling customs fraud," the commission spokesperson said in response to the accusations.

Podesta said Brussels was "engaging" with Washington to better understand the report's "potential implications for the EU," while noting that the document found the EU transshipment risk to be "embedded within broad legitimate trade flows."

World.title: Russia admits new petrol shortages amid ongoing long-range Ukrainian strikes
World.content:
Russian authorities acknowledged on Friday that some regions face new petrol shortages, as Ukraine steps up attacks on the country's oil refineries.

 

Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy sites with drones and missiles for months, hoping to hit a vital source of revenue for the Russian army.

Russia has shut down one major refinery at Orsk, around 1,300 kilometres from the front line, for six months after it was attacked this week.

"The situation remains tense in several regions of the country regarding fuel supplies to service stations," the government said in a social media post.

Oil companies are "taking the necessary measures to increase deliveries to the most vulnerable regions," according to the statement.

It said a government meeting had been held on the shortages and the Deputy Prime Minister responsible for energy, Alexander Novak, has ordered that fuel prices be monitored.

Companies and car drivers have suffered repeat shortages in recent months because of the conflict.

Vehicles line up at a Rosneft gas station in Moscow, 29 June, 2026 AP Photo

Nearly every Russian region has at some point had to limit fuel sales or impose other kinds of rationing, such as banning the filling of jerry cans.

The Krasnodar region on the Black Sea, known for its tourist beaches, has been one of the worst hit.

"The situation regarding petrol supplies at service stations has become complicated," regional governor Venyamin Kondratyev said.

Oil companies "have again started imposing restrictions on the amount of fuel supplied and reduced service station opening hours," he added.

"This is causing concern among the region's residents and visitors," the governor added, stating that he had asked the authorities to send more fuel.

The governor of the Orenburg region, where the Orsk refinery is located, said on Thursday it had been shut down and repairs would take months.

Russian President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

Rare admission

Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged for the first time in June that his country was facing a “certain deficit” of fuel.

Speaking at a meeting with officials that focused on the fuel situation, Putin admitted that the country was “going through a difficult period,” but insisted that Moscow would “honour all its social obligations.”

Shortly after, he told state TV that the country's arms industries will quickly ramp up production of air defence systems to fend off Ukrainian attacks.

Claiming the issues that arise are not critical, Putin also said that Russia will import more fuel and speed up repair works at oil facilities to end the “temporary deficit.”

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has referred to strikes on Russian energy sites deep inside Russia as “long-range sanctions.”

World.title: Luigi Mangione admits shooting healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York court
World.content:
Luigi Mangione admitted on Friday to gunning down UnitedHealthCare chief executive Brian Thompson, as he appeared in US federal court to change his plea to guilty.

 

"On the morning of December 4, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione told a federal judge.

Mangione also pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges, admitting matter-of-factly that he trailed the executive to an investor conference in 2024 and gunned him down in the street.

Mangione, 28, said he even used a ruse to glean information about the event, contacting the health insurance company ahead of time under the guise of being an investor at a multibillion-dollar firm.

Mangione is set for sentencing 18 December. When US District Judge Margaret M. Garnett asked whether he understood that he could spend the rest of his life in prison, Mangione answered neutrally: “Yes.”

Mangione entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death.

Luigi Mangione appears for a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan Criminal Court in New York, 11 August, 2026 AP Photo

Mangione's lawyers are now seeking to have his separate New York state murder case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.

“Mr. Mangione has accepted full responsibility for the death of Brian Thompson,” defence lawyer Karen Friedman said outside the court, arguing that her client shouldn't face two prosecutions over a “single tragic event.”

Surveillance video of the ambush showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson, 50, from behind.

Police say “delay, deny, depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims.

That detail and revelations that Mangione's private writings lambasted health insurers as greedy, according to authorities, made the case a fulcrum for debate about the industry and made Mangione a celebrity for some of its critics.

Stickers are displayed on a pole in front of Manhattan federal court on the day of a hearing for Luigi Mangione, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

Mangione told the court on Friday that he pursued Thompson “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”

Mangione was never a UnitedHealthcare customer, according to police and the company.

A University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, he was arrested five days after the shooting, when he was spotted at a McDonald’s in Pennsylvania.

Thompson led one of the United States' largest health insurers, but he wasn’t well known outside the industry.

Trained as an accountant, he had worked at parent company UnitedHealth Group Inc. for 20 years and became CEO of its insurance arm, UnitedHealthcare, in 2021. He and his wife have two sons, who were in high school when their father was killed.

Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence for Mangione. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed him to a potential death penalty.

Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition.”

Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first.

The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.

In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.

Members of the media wait in line outside of Manhattan Federal Court on the day of a hearing for Luigi Mangione, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defence, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.

They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and a notebook in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.

In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defence in the state case but reversed course a day later.

The defence, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.

World.title: Italian police recover stolen Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse artworks worth millions
World.content:
Paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth over $10.4 million (€8.9 million) which were stolen from an Italian museum in March have been recovered, Italian police said on Friday.

 

The paintings were taken by thieves from the villa of the Magnani-Rocca Foundation, near Parma in northern Italy, in a heist that lasted under three minutes.

Parma chief of police Andrea Pagliaro said the investigation centred around a gang of nine Moldovan suspects.

Five are accused of carrying out the theft, he said.

Video footage released by police showed two thieves wearing headlamps and with their faces covered entering the villa by breaking through a window.

They headed straight into a room where the three paintings hung and took them off the wall, before heading back to the window and passing them through to an accomplice waiting outside.

Italian newspapers carry the news of the heist of three paintings from a museum near Parma, 30 March, 2026 AP Photo

They made off with "Fish" by Auguste Renoir, "Still Life with Cherries" by Paul Cézanne and "Odalisque on the Terrace" by Henri Matisse.

The Renoir is worth €3 million, the Cézanne €6 million and the Matisse around €20,000, police said.

The paintings were recovered at the house of one of the suspects, police chief Pagliaro told the AFP news agency.

The Magnani-Rocca Foundation, 20 kilometres from Parma, houses the collection of art historian Luigi Magnani, which also includes works by Durer, Rubens, Van Dyck, Goya and Monet.

The theft is the latest in a series of robberies targeting European museums.

Last October, thieves broke into the Louvre in Paris in broad daylight, escaping in less than eight minutes with jewellery worth €88 million.

World.title: US backs Japanese sovereignty over disputed islands after Putin visit
World.content:
The United States has backed Japan's sovereignty over four islands controlled by Russia after Vladimir Putin became the first Russian president in 15 years to visit the disputed territory, prompting Tokyo to summon Moscow's ambassador and describe the trip as "absolutely unacceptable."

 

"The United States remains unwavering in its support of its most important ally and in its recognition of Japanese sovereignty over the Northern Territories," the US ambassador to Tokyo George Glass said on X.

"At a time when the US-Japan alliance is dedicated to cultivating prosperity across the Indo-Pacific, we strongly oppose any action that undermines its peace and stability," Glass added.

Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by the four southernmost islands in a volcanic chain off the coast of Hokkaido seized by the Soviet Union following an invasion in August 1945, in the final days of World War II.

Moscow broke its formal neutrality with Japan just days before the invasion.

The Japanese government maintains that the four islands and groups of islets that make up the Northern Territories — Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and Habomai — are part of its territory that the Soviets illegally occupied and Russia has continued to occupy since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.

The dispute has kept the two countries from signing a peace treaty that would formally end their hostilities. They terminated the state of war in 1956.

Moscow has reinforced its military presence on the islands as recently as December 2021, when it deployed Bastion coastal defence missile systems on an uninhabited volcanic island in the middle of the chain.

FILE: Bastion missile launchers move to their positions on the disputed island chain near Japan, 21 December 2021 AP Photo

The island hosted a Japanese army base prior to the Soviet occupation. A Soviet base there was shut down amid funding shortages in the wake of the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Moscow previously deployed Bal and Bastion missile systems on two of the four southernmost islands in 2016.

In the following years, Moscow further beefed up its arsenal on the islands by sending top-of-the-line air defence missile systems, setting up an air base on Etorofu Island, and deploying fighter jets.

The sparsely inhabited islands are strategically significant to the Kremlin as they sit at the entrance to the Sea of Okhotsk and give Russia's Pacific Fleet access to the open Pacific without passing through Japanese-controlled waters.

Putin's visit was the first by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.

'Absolutely unacceptable'

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters "the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law."

Putin's visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," she added.

Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country “strongly protests” Putin's visit to the largest of the islands, Etorofu.

“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu Island, are Japan’s inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law,” Motegi said in a statement.

He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he "promptly report the message back to Moscow,” the minister told reporters afterwards.

FILE: Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks during a news conference at the prime minister's office in Tokyo, 18 February 2026 AP Photo

Russia's embassy in Japan said the ambassador reiterated Moscow's claim that the islands are part of Russia and that Putin's trip there was not "a matter for discussion with foreign states".

The Kremlin boasted about the visit by posting a video of Putin on one of the four main islands. Russian state-run media said he had visited a fish-processing plant and showed him trying local caviar.

Takaichi said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.

Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

It also placed export controls on technology with military applications and provided financial support to Ukraine. Russia responded by designating Japan an "unfriendly state".

Tokyo is now considering strengthening those sanctions as part of its countermeasures in response to Putin's trip.

“We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term,” she said.

“We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this.”

World.title: The rise of 'conscious' festivals, where music, spirituality and nature meet
World.content:
The Medicine Festival brings together more than 10,000 people in the United Kingdom for four days of music, ceremony, spirituality and environmental activism.

 

The festival in Berkshire reflects a growing interest in alternative ways of connecting with oneself, others and nature.

The sixth edition of the festival features a full programme of events, including concerts, yoga classes, ways of exploring movement and spiritual awareness and traditional ceremonies.

Main stage at Medicine Festival. Berkshire, United Kingdom. Ana Torres

Many Europeans have crossed the border to attend. Ayla, from the Netherlands has come to the festival for the first time.

“What I like about Medicine is the sharing of wisdoms. I hope I get out of here inspired, rested and motivated as well," she told Euronews.

In Europe and around the world, there is a growing interest in "conscious festivals" such as Medicine, which encourage people to explore their inner self, reconnect with nature and create a sense of community.

“We see ourselves as part of nature," explains Joshua Dugdale, Co-Founder of the Festival.

Jamming session at Medicine Festival. Berkshire, United Kingdom. Ana Torres

“We promote the medicine of dance, the medicine of music, the medicine of community, but also seeing people who have maybe a different world view and engaging with that, learning new skills, understanding new ways of seeing the world, we would call it a sacred festival”.

To date, the Medicine Festival has donated over one hundred thousand euros to support the environment and indigenous communities.

World.title: UK must 'face up to changing climate,' PM says on visit to fire-hit Stourbridge
World.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Friday that Britain must face up to the changing climate and accelerate its move to clean energy as he visited a town where a wildfire gutted homes.

 

In Stourbridge near the UK's second largest city of Birmingham, smoke rose from smouldering ruins of several roofless houses as firefighters sprayed water on the wreckage Friday.

The West Midlands Fire Service said 19 houses were completely destroyed and 18 others damaged in the town.

Meeting firefighters after viewing the scene, Burnham sounded shocked as he said the "combustible situation" was related to climate change and showed the need for a more rapid transition to clean energy.

"I've never seen scenes like this in Britain, where you just see a whole house gutted, smouldering," he said.

The burnt out remains of houses in the Quarry Park Road area following a huge blaze in Stourbridge, 14 August, 2026 Peter Byrne/PA Wire

"We have to face up to the changing climate...there's no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy," he stressed.

Britain has set a target to consume zero-carbon electricity by 2030 and is aiming to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 to combat climate change.

Describing Britain as "a tinderbox" with 37 blazes around the country on Friday, the prime minister warned against lighting fires outdoors, as the government introduced a ban on selling disposable barbecue equipment.

Residents of Stourbridge were evacuated and people treated for smoke inhalation after the fire spread on Thursday, the UK's hottest day of the year so far.

One firefighter was hospitalised and five others suffered minor injuries, the fire service said Friday, as crews were still extinguishing "hotspots" in open grassland, along a railway and in gardens.

As dry conditions sparked multiple wildfires, six other firefighters farther north in Staffordshire, were taken to hospital suffering from smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion, the fire service said.

The ambulance service in the West Midlands region, including Stourbridge and Staffordshire, said that on Thursday it had treated 68 people with symptoms such as smoke inhalation, 25 of whom were hospitalised.

The West Midlands, alongside nearly three-quarters of England, is in drought after weeks of high temperatures and scant rainfall, increasing the risk of fires.

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the West Midlands Fire Service incident command unit during a visit to Stourbridge, 14 August, 2026 AP Photo

'Extensive devastation'

Emergency services said some of the blazes around Stourbridge were set deliberately in grasslands before spreading.

"This has been one of the most significant incidents that West Midlands Fire Service has ever attended," chief fire officer Simon Tuhill told a press conference late on Thursday.

He blamed the rapid spread on "tinder dry" conditions and said the "devastation is extensive."

So far this summer, firefighters have mainly battled wildfires in rural areas and moorland across the country.

Burnham promised to convene a summit with fire services, acknowledging the government had not supplied enough resources to deal with wildfires.

And he revealed plans to commission firefighting planes, of the types used to douse flames in Europe and the United States.

"It's been a particularly difficult, busy period for the fire and rescue service, where we've been under significant pressure," the head of the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), Phil Garrigan, told BBC Radio 4.

"Firefighters have been on the front line of climate change for a number of years. They're doing their absolute best to protect communities and properties," he said.

World.title: Donald Trump to declare Hormuz US territory 'soon'
World.content:
Donald Trump said the strait would become part of the US after Iran is defeated. He also told Americans to accept higher gas prices, which have soared since Iran closed Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks.

President Donald Trump said Friday that he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.

"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump said at a rally at a police academy in Garden City, New York state. "It's true," he added.

It was not clear whether his remarks were serious or whether they signal a new policy shift for Washington in its war against Tehran, which is more than five months old.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi dismissed Trump's remarks, saying the country would "not be intimidated" and that the strategic waterway would remain under its control and authority.

What is the situation in the Strait of Hormuz?

The US and Israel launched the war against Iran on February 28. At the time, senior White House officials, including Trump, said the aim was to end Iran's nuclear program and spark a popular uprising to force regime change in the Islamic Republic, among other goals.

Iran's response has been to target US allies across the Middle East with drone and missile strikes, as well as to impose a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments passed before the war.

The US responded to Iran's closure of the strait with its own naval blockade of Iranian ships and ports. The two countries have been locked in a stalemate over the vital waterway for months, causing energy prices to soar.

Rising oil and gas costs and the economic fallout from the war are likely to be leading issues in the midterm elections in November.

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What else did Trump say during the rally in Garden City?

During the rally, the US president also urged Americans to accept that they would have to "pay a tiny little bit more" for their gasoline as a worthy price for preventing "a very evil country" from getting a nuclear weapon.

"What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a ​great job," Trump told the crowd, adding that "no ships get through (the US blockade of Hormuz) unless we want them to."

On Friday, Trump also dismissed concerns over the living conditions aboard a US aircraft carrier that was deployed to the Middle East amid the war with Iran.

Relatives of service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln told US military media outlets that personnel are struggling with difficult living conditions and deteriorating mental health. There have also been reports of suicide attempts.

Trump denied that the deployment of the aircraft carrier , which has been at sea for nine months, had lasted too long, instead insisting that the aircraft carrier's deployment was "not nearly enough."

He also confirmed that the ship would be replaced by another "very similar" vessel.

World.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to let White House ballroom construction continue
World.content:
Justice Department lawyers echoed the US president's claim that the $400 million White House ballroom ​project is a security necessity.

The Trump administration on Friday asked the US Supreme Court to allow construction to continue on the president's $400 million White House ballroom.

It comes a week after an appeals court ruled Donald Trump's ballroom project, planned for the site of the White House's East Wing after it was demolished, lacked congressional approval and ordered above-ground construction to stop.

"This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security," Trump's Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in a petition to the Supreme Court.

Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for a response by plaintiffs challenging the ballroom project.

Trump assassination attempts and flight from Turkey mentioned

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation first brought the case after the East Wing was torn down and work began on a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom.

In a 2-1 ruling on August 7, the DC Circuit upheld a lower-court judge's order directing the administration to halt above-ground construction.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the appeals court panel wrote.

To justify the need for a secure ballroom, Justice Department lawyers pointed to the July 8 missile threat against Air Force One when Trump was flown out of Turkey aboard a secret flight and other recent assassination attempts.

The filing also claims the project is on time and under budget, funded by about $400 million in private donations. Democrats, however, say Trump's tax law is helping pay for the ballroom, while lawmakers in Congress have not approved a request by the administration for additional funding.

The ballroom is part of a broader set of projects planned by Trump for Washington D.C., including upgrades to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool as well as the construction of a large arch Image: Nathan Howard/REUTERS

Responding to the petition, the trust accused the White House of trying to "outrun the courts" by accelerating construction. It cited plans to install 1 million pounds (453,592.37 kilograms) of rebarand pour 3,000 cubic yards (81,000 cubic feet, 2,293.66 cubic meters) of concrete over the next week.

"The Administration's transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review, and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here," the plaintiffs said.

The National Trust has urged the Supreme Court to reject the administration's appeal.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism scandal found dead
World.content:
Jason Arday, the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge, was found unresponsive at an address in London. Arday had recently resigned in the midst of a plagiarism row.

Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor who resigned amid allegations of plagiarism, was found dead on Friday.

Without naming him directly, the Metropolitan Police said he was found "unresponsive" in Battersea, south London, and pronounced dead at the scene.

"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," a spokesperson said. "His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers."

Arday, a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, one of the world's top universities, resigned just over a week ago amid mounting allegations that he plagiarized parts of his PhD thesis and overstated his personal achievements.

He had denied wrongdoing, saying in a resignation letter last week that he did not accept "the narratives that have surrounded me."

Questions mounted over thesis and fundraising claims

British newspapers and commentators have seized on the allegations, arguing that he gained an unfair advantage through diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.

Scrutiny of Arday's credentials intensified last month after criticism from former Cambridge researcher Nathan Cofnas.

The Times of London later reported similarities between passages in Arday's 2015 PhD thesis and an earlier paper by another researcher.

Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated and cleared by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

But last week, Cambridge launched an investigation following "new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."

British media also questioned Arday's claims of having raised £5.5 million (€6.4 million, $7.4 million) for charity through endurance challenges. Arday told The Guardian the funds were raised collectively over two decades.

Supporters reject claims, cite racial bias

Supporters, including over two dozen academics and politicians, characterized the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to discredit Arday and other Black people in influential positions.

In his resignation letter, Arday said that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

His family issued a statement denouncing the "campaign of sustained abuse" Arday had faced since he took the role at Cambridge University more than three years ago.

"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," Arday's family said.

"We won't comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long," the statement added.

Cambridge's Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said, "We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."

Edited by: Rob Turner and Karl Sexton

World.title: Vast German wildfire forces evacuation in Eifel forest
World.content:
08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 RECAP — Massive wildfire hits Hürtgenwald area, nearby village to stay empty overnight

As evening drew in on Friday, the fire was still far from under control, with authorities expecting to continue their efforts throughout the weekend Image: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance

In case you're just joining us, here's the lowdown on developments in Germany's far west near the Belgian border this Friday.

A large forest fire in the Hürtgenwald forest, not far east of Aachen, forced authorities to clear a nearby village early in the morning.

Various emergency services and the military have rushed to the area to try to contain almost certainly the largest such blaze in the history of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, thought to cover an area of at least 200 hectares.

Authorities said on Friday that around 400 personnel were in service simultaneously across various agencies.

The village of Gey, home to around 2,000 people, will remain evacuated overnight. Five people, four of them rescue workers, have suffered injuries amid the response to the fire.

The state premier has cut short his vacation and expects to arrive on site on Saturday afternoon.

Emergency services anticipate that efforts to contain the fire will last all weekend, and perhaps longer. Hot summer weather and a dry forest floor are not helping the response.

Weather forecasts do point to falling temperatures over the weekend, and even a roughly 50% chance of light rain in the area on Saturday.

Police are investigating the cause and have appealed to the public for information, particularly photos or videos from the area taken around the time the fire began.

World.title: In Germany record heat meets climate action fatigue
World.content:
For the German government climate action does not seem to be a priority — despite record temperatures, heat-related deaths and drought. Why don't more people take to the streets in protest?

When Lars Werner of the "Last Generation" glued himself to the road four years ago to protest for greater climate action, Germany had not yet seen 12,500 heat-related deaths (Germany's number for 2026 so far), or record temperatures across western Europe, and fully loaded ships were still navigating the Rhine without difficulty.

"Of course, I could say 'I told you so,' because it was foreseeable and comes as no surprise whatsoever," Werner tells DW.

"The fact is, even back then, I was constantly explaining in my presentations that the Rhine would eventually run dry during hot summers and that this would have an incredible impact on the economy."

Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Something very strange is happening in Germany in the summer of 2026: While entire villages are being evacuated due to forest fires, farmers are losing around their harvest to drought, and hospital patients and the elderly in nursing homes face an acute threat to their lives in buildings with no air conditioning, the federal government remains astonishingly quiet.

Despite the crisis, it has still not convened a "heat summit."

"It is utterly irrational for the federal government to resort to tinkering with regulations — such as lifting the Sunday ban on truck traffic — in the hope of somehow scraping by without implementing a comprehensive climate protection policy for the long or even short term," Werner argues.

Fridays for Future Germany: not the same group from a few years ago

The government no longer has to worry about "Last Generation" protesters calling out its inaction by setting up road blockades. The climate activists halted their protests two years ago, worn down by hostility, fines and prison sentences. Now, the task of fiercely criticizing political decision-makers on climate policy falls primarily to the Fridays for Future Germany (FFF) movement.

"The federal government is doing virtually nothing when it comes to effective climate policy. Instead, various 'pseudo-solutions' are being promoted — such as dredging the Rhine to make it deeper or lifting the Sunday driving ban for trucks," FFF spokesperson Linda Kastrup told DW. She deplores what she sees as short-term fixes for the symptoms of the climate crisis, and notes that effectively nothing sustainable is being done.

Activist Lars Werner used to glue himself to the street in Munich in protest against CO2 emissions Image: Benjamin Rückert

Only a few hundred protesters turned out for a demonstration outside the Chancellery in Berlin a week ago. It was a far cry from the protests in 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to demand climate action.

A recent study by the Bertelsmann Foundation found that 80% of people in Germany are worried about climate change, and more than 50% want to see more government spending on climate protection. But that doesn't mean they take to the streets.

Kastrup is not surprised.

"When Chancellor Friedrich Merz completely dismisses and ignores climate policy — when we see tens of thousands of heat-related deaths in Germany alone yet not a single word is said about it — it inevitably leaves people with the impression in their private lives that climate protection doesn't matter. Naturally, that makes it very difficult to motivate people to take to the streets," she says.

In addition, there has been a rise in hateful speech directed at climate activists on social media.

"Two days ago, I posted a reel and within a very short time, there were 2,000 hateful comments on it," says Kastrup.

Focus shifted to Ukraine, Gaza

Sebastian Haunss, a researcher in political science at the University of Bremen, says it is surprising that the scorching summer of 2026 has not led to climate protests. He finds it remarkable that on the one hand, more and more people in Germany are installing solar power systems, but on the other, they take vacations on environmentally damaging cruise ships.

He sees several reasons for this development.

"A strong counter-position has emerged," he says. "Specifically, political actors like the AfD [the far-right populist Alternative for Germany Party, Eds.] are pursuing an agenda that opposes climate protection regulations. Such actors — whether at the international or national level — did not exist just a few years ago."

Also, Haunss points out that large organizations like Fridays for Future have been replaced by a vast number of local groups, who operate largely out of the public eye. However, a pivotal event could bring people back onto the streets in large numbers at any moment, he says.

"Then there is the competition for attention; the COVID pandemic and the war in Ukraine pushed the climate issue out of the spotlight, and current economic concerns also play a major role," says Haunss, adding that many of those who took to the streets against climate change a few years ago are now focusing on different topics: "In some cases, their issues have shifted, and other topics — such as the war in Gaza and solidarity with Palestine — have moved to the forefront:"

A divided government

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) now wants to amend the constitution, the Basic Law, to make heat protection a joint responsibility of the federal government, the states, and the municipalities. However, the larger coalition partner, the center-right bloc of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), is skeptical and cites "legal concerns."

"Within the coalition, I do indeed see us — the SPD — as the bulwark for energy transition to renewables," Nina Scheer, energy policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group, tells DW. "All my colleagues in our parliamentary group would like to achieve more in terms of climate protection. But we also have to accept setbacks regarding climate measures in order to maintain unity within the coalition."

For instance, she says, she voted in favor of making air travel cheaper and expanding regional airports, although she personally finds it wrong.

Scheer has long advocated for a faster expansion of renewable energy, and does not see eye to eye with Economics Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU), who favors gas over wind and solar power for energy supply.

"Reiche goes around pushing the narrative that while we do want climate protection and remain committed to the goals, renewables are simply too expensive. And to that, one has to say: 'No, that is simply not true,'" says Scheer.

Under the Paris Agreement and the national Climate Action Act , Germany has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2045. However, recent statements by some politicians raise doubts as to whether the federal government is pursuing this goal with great determination.

"We cannot halt climate change from Germany alone," said Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently.

SPD politician Scheer considers this a disastrous statement.

"Fundamentally, it is a rejection of greater climate action, even though we ought to be stepping up our efforts," she says.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges in Brian Thompson death
World.content:
The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty in a Manhattan federal court to stalking charges tied to the death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

"I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died," he told the court.

Prosecutors said Mangione traveled to New York City and fatally shot Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel on December 4, 2024, as he walked to UnitedHealth Group's annual investor conference.

The judge has accepted his guilty plea and said sentencing would take place in December. Mangione faces a possible sentence ‌of life without parole on the two counts of stalking.

Thompson led one of the United States' largest health insurers Image: UnitedHealth Group/AFP

Mangione's lawyer seeks dismissal of state murder charges

Mangione had previously pleaded not guilty to federal murder, weapons and stalking charges. Earlier this year, the judge dismissed the murder and weapons counts on legal technicalities, leaving only the stalking charges and eliminating the possibility of the death penalty.

Mangione still seperately faces murder, weapons and forgery charges in New York state court.

Outside federal court, Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, told reporters that "state charges must be dismissed under New York's double jeopardy protections."

Under double jeopardy protections, defendants are protected from being prosecuted for the same crime twice.

How Mangione explained his guilty plea to the court

Mangione told the federal court he pursued Thompson "after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system."

Thompson was chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, one of the largest health insurers in the United States.

He was walking into a Midtown Manhattan hotel for the annual investor day when he was shot three times in the back.

Mangione said he then used a 3D printer to make part of the gun used in the shooting.

Mangione supporters attebded his every court appearance Image: Jordan Tovin/REUTERS

The killing underscored widespread frustration with the US healthcare system, and some supporters portrayed Mangione as a hero.

Conservatives, including President Donald Trump, however, have called for a tough punishment.

Jamie McDonald, the Manhattan US attorney, told reporters that his office would seek a sentence of life imprisonment.

"There can be no celebrity in assassination," he said.

Thompson's wife, Paulette, repeatedly wiped tears from her eyes as Mangione pleaded guilty in court Image: David Dee Delgado/REUTERS

Outside the courthouse, a man shouted "America loves Luigi" at relatives of Thompson as they left court Friday in a convoy of black SUVs.

Thompson's family said in a statement that the plea marked an "important step toward justice."

"We look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family said.

World.content:
08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Extreme athlete arrives in Cologne after swimming from Frankfurt

Pohl did not swim continuously for four days — she swapped with other swimmers every two hours and had a break every night Image: Christoph Hardt/Panama Pictures/IMAGO

Nathalie Pohl has completed her four-day swin down the Main and Rhine rivers from Frankfurt to Cologne.

The 31-year-old extreme swimmer started the aquatic journey of more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) on Tuesday morning, arriving on the banks of the Rhine in Cologne on Friday afternoon.

Her aim was to raise awareness on the importance of safe swimming among children, and to fund swimming projects. Her team says they managed to raise around €616,000 ($713,000) in total.

"Every child has the right to feel secure in the water," she said upon arrival. At the same time she was keen to point out that her challenge shouldn't be taken as a "false signal."

"Especially in the Rhine, far too many people still drown," she said. "It's not bathing water."

World.title: France: Top watchdog blocks social media ban for children
World.content:
Denying access to platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and YouTube for under-15s would infringe upon freedom of expression, the Constitutional Council has said.

France's highest constitutional authority on Friday struck down the ban on social media for children under 15.

The Constitutional Council ruled that the flagship policy of President Emmanuel Macron's second term infringed on freedom of expression.

"By prohibiting minors under the age of 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them," it said in its decision.

The Council is a review body that ensures laws comply with the Constitution.

Macron still wants social media ban for children

French lawmakers last month approved legislation that barred children under 15 from opening social media accounts from September 1. Beyond that, platforms would have until the start of 2027 to close children's existing accounts.

The law would also have banned the use of mobile phones in high schools and required social media platforms to introduce age-verification measures in accordance with France's privacy regulator.

France: First EU country to ban social media use under 15 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Council, however, found lawmakers had failed to set out clear rules on how people should prove their age and what limits should apply, meaning there were not enough legal safeguards in place.

Macron has instructed Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to revise the bill to address the Constitutional Council's concerns, the Elysee Palace said. It added the president wanted the reform in place before France's 2027 presidential election.

Social media bans for teens and children also considered elsewhere

Australia became the first country in the world to ban social media for under-16s in 2025. France was the first in Europe.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last month pledged to pursue an EU-wide social media ban for children following a recommendation by an expert group to restrict access for under-13s.

"Our children need time in the real world. Time to play, time to build friendships, time to make mistakes. Time to shape their own identity, their own personality, before an algorithm shapes them instead," von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels.

"This is not about whether children can access social media. It is about whether and when social media can access our children," she said.

A number of other countries have announced plans to consider similar bans, including Brazil, the UK, Canada, Norway and Denmark.
