World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: Skinks facing extinction find new hope away from predatory snakes
World.content:
A critically endangered skink almost wiped out by predatory snakes on Christmas Island has been given a new chance of survival after being relocated to a remote island off Western Australia.

More than 500 blue-tailed skinks were released on Horsburgh Island in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, about 2,900 kilometres north-west of Perth, in July, and researchers are hopeful their numbers could increase into the hundreds of thousands.

The species was hunted to the brink of extinction due to predators introduced to Christmas Island, mainly the South-east Asian wolf snake.

Blue-tailed skinks caught the plane over to Horsburgh Island. (Supplied: Parks Australia)

Christmas Island National Park threatened species manager Brendan Tiernan said the snake had devastated lizard populations.

"By 2009 there was only one population left on the most remote pocket of Christmas Island, and extinction was imminent," Mr Tiernan said.

"We realised that we're about to lose these species and it was time to get out there and secure them into captivity before they fell off the edge of the cliff."

The skinks are about 10 to 12 centimetres long. (Supplied: Parks Australia)

Parks Australia's threatened species program coordinator Shayla Stefanetti said despite being only 10 to 12 centimetres long, the absence of the tiny skink had been noticed by island residents.

"Locals used to see them everywhere; they were very well described with their bright blue tails," she said.

Lizards travel by air

When Parks Australia began tracking the lizards, they captured only 66.

Those blue-tailed skinks provided the foundation for a successful breeding and conservation program on Christmas Island, and their numbers swelled to around 400.

The breeding program enabled staff to translocate the lizards to the neighbouring islands of Pulu Blan and Pulu Blan Madar in the Cocos (Keeling) archipelago in 2019 and 2020, where predators were absent.

More than 500 blue-tailed skinks were released on Horsburgh Island. (Supplied: Parks Australia)

The lizards were transported by air and sea in special containers.

"Those two islands were very successful and reached capacity of around 5,000 animals each," Ms Stefanetti said.

Horsburgh Island was chosen as the next translocation site due to its size and similar lack of predators.

Hosburgh Island is much larger than the previous translocation sites. (Supplied: Parks Australia)

Fifty times as large as either Pulu Blan or Pulu Blan Madar, Hosburgh Island has the potential to host an even larger population of the species, thereby safeguarding its future.

Species milestone

Ms Stefanettis said she was hopeful the translocation, led by Parks Australia and Taronga Conservation Society Australia, would be successful.

"[We] have the potential to have hundreds of thousands of skinks living on Horsburgh," she said.

"To go from extinct in the wild to then have a really successful population flourishing in the wild, that is huge.

"It's a huge milestone for not only the species, but for our national park to achieve as well."

Mr Tieran said it was unlikely blue-tailed skinks would be able to be released back onto Christmas Island in the near future.

"For the time being, we have no viable control options for the wolf snake, [so] returning them to the wild on Christmas Island isn't an option," he said.

"It's certainly something that we're trying to progress towards, [but] snakes are notoriously difficult to control."

World.title: Breaking: Magnitude-7.8 earthquake strikes off coast of Indonesia
World.content:
A powerful earthquake has struck off the coast of Indonesia in the Flores region, triggering an early tsunami warning by the country's geophysics agency.

The magnitude-7.8 quake, as reported by Geoscience Australia, was followed by several aftershocks.

No immediate casualties or damage were reported.

The earthquake was recorded at a depth of 35 kilometres just before 5am, local time, the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) said.

Its epicentre was 68km north-north-west of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province.

Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), issued an early tsunami warning for some regions in the country. and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks.

The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores island.

Residents along affected coastlines were advised to move to higher ground as officials closely monitored coastal tide gauges for any changes.

Separately, Australia's tsunami warning centre said the undersea earthquake would have "no tsunami threat to the Australian mainland, islands or territories".

Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the "Ring of Fire," an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Date set for opening of $195m Powerhouse Parramatta
World.content:
The $915 million Powerhouse Parramatta will open its doors to the public on November 7, becoming Western Sydney's first state cultural institution.

The New South Wales government in May announced that construction of the museum had been completed four years after work began.

Seven expansive zones are part of the museum, including an 18-metre-high space of more than 2,200 square metres, which will feature Task Eternal, the largest exhibition about space exploration in Australia.

Inside the new Powerhouse Parramatta. (ABC News: Digby Werthmuller)

NSW Arts Minister John Graham said the opening marked the most significant cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House.

"It's a big moment for arts and culture in the west of Sydney," he said.

"The good news is it's also free, so for people under a bit of cost-of-living pressure, they'll be able to come in and see this incredible building, this great cultural institution for free.

"There's no easy way to build new cultural institutions, just as the building of the Opera House was controversial. As it proceeded, when the doors swung open, no-one was in doubt that this was an incredible addition to our city.

"I think the reaction from the public will be the same as they see this incredible building on the banks of the river right in the heart of Parramatta."

The first five exhibitions will showcase more than 3,000 objects, with more than 1,600 from the Powerhouse's own collection, with others sourced from collections around the world.

The first exhibition, Task Eternal, will include the historic Qantas Avro 504k aircraft.

The second major exhibition, announced today, The Mall, examines the history, evolution and cultural significance of the shopping mall.

Lisa Havilah says the museum is "built for the future". (ABC News: Helena Burke)

Powerhouse CEO Lisa Havilah said she was "thrilled" to announce the opening date.

"Powerhouse Parramatta is a museum built for the future, where local knowledge meets global perspectives," she said.

"We are thrilled to be opening our doors this November with five world-class exhibitions and a program that is as bold and diverse as the communities it serves."

World.title: Artefacts from across the globe returned to southern WA
World.content:
Cultural artefacts from Western Australia's southern coast have been returned home after spending hundreds of years in museums across the world.

They are on display in the Kalyagul: Connections to Menang Country exhibition at the Museum of the Great Southern, aiming to share knowledge with residents and visitors.

The exhibition is on display at the Museum of the Great Southern in Albany. (Supplied: Deakin University/Astrid Volzke)

The Menang word kalyagul means always, ever, continuing and is interwoven through the exhibition and the broader project it is part of, Entangled Knowledges: Kaartdijin, Science and History in the Robert Neill Collection, which is combining the knowledge of Menang elders, historians and scientists.

Closer look

In the 1840s, while he was a commissariat officer in Albany, Robert Neill painted watercolour drawings of fish found locally, building on his connections with the Menang people who shared their kaartdijin (knowledge).

Team members visit Albany. (Supplied: Deakin University/Astrid Volzke)

The items were sent back to the United Kingdom.

Deakin University history professor Tiffany Shellam said after noticing fish scales were attached to the drawings held at the London Natural History Museum they asked curators at the National Museum of Scotland if there were any fish in their collections.

"When I arrived there they had about 27 boxes of fish on the tables for us to have a look through, and it was just mind blowing," she said.

"What's so exciting about those fish skins is that they have on every fish they've got a label which has the Menang name, very much in bold kind of writing which really kind of dominates the label and what knowledge was contained on that label is really from the Menang people who caught the fish."

Shona Coyne is a senior curator and manager of repatriation and community engagement at the National Museum of Australia. (ABC Great Southern: John Dobson)

Acknowledgement of knowledge

Menang woman Shona Coyne, who is the lead curator of the exhibition, said it was a joy to see that happening.

"These kind of cases are quite rare," she said.

"Colonisers and other visitors to our place would often come here, extract the knowledge, claim it as their own, and send it off to museums and universities around the world.

"Whereas this occasion, Robert Neill actually acknowledged us and acknowledged our elders and wrote down the names of the people who speared the fishes as well, so it's been a wonderful archive for us to explore."

Larry Blight and Cameron Gravestock make gidji, or spears. (Supplied: Deakin University/Astrid Volzke)

Menang man Larry Blight was part of the team that travelled to the UK to see the collections.

"We were breaking down and deciphering ancient Menang language with our knowledge as well and filling in some blank spots for the curators, but not just the fish there were also plants," he said.

"We were telling them the ones that we knew, we were giving them their local Indigenous names and the usages as well, whether it's a medicine or a bush food and also our relationship with the animals as well."

A workshop was held in Albany with participants making traditional emu feather ornaments. (Supplied: Deakin University/Astrid Volzke)

The research located further artefacts in museums in Australia and abroad.

They included plant samples collected by Menang women Lucy Webb and Lucy Eades sent to the National Herbarium of Victoria in the late 19th century.

An exhibit on loan from the National Herbarium of Victoria. (Supplied: Deakin University/Astrid Volzke)

Herbarium collections manager Alison Vaughan said five specimens were attributed to Lucy Webb.

"One, it doesn't have Mrs Eades written on the label, but in an accompanying letter recognises that the specimen was collected by Mrs Eades," she said.

"It was the first and remains the only definitive evidence that we have of Aboriginal people collecting in the 19th century and contributing to the collection, although we know that there will be many more, especially through exploring expeditions and through other sort of colonial settler relationships."

A fish specimen from the Albany area being recorded. (Supplied: Deakin University/Astrid Volzke)

Part of the project was remaking the cultural material, which included emu feathered ornaments and fishing spears.

Ms Coyne said it was a powerful experience to recreate the plant collection made by one of her ancestors, returning to the site where it was made and adding her own sample to the herbarium's collection.

As part of the research, scientists and Menang traditional owners collected fish samples from the Albany area, with some joining the collections of Robert Neill in the National Museum of Scotland.

World.title: Ex-minister stands by staffer's stat dec over claims of inconsistencies
World.content:
Former Tasmanian minister Jane Howlett says she stands by a statutory declaration she tabled in parliament on behalf of a former staffer, despite claims over inconsistencies.

Ms Howlett appeared at a parliamentary hearing into caretaker conventions on Friday, during which she was questioned over her office's knowledge of messaging that breached election guidelines.

During last year's election campaign, government business Tasracing sent out messaging to its members speaking favourably of the Liberal party's TasInsure policy.

Emails obtained by the ABC under right to information provisions show her former chief of staff Luke Gaetani had been made aware of the message before it was sent out.

Jane Howlett says she does not recall what she told Tasracing about the Liberals' signature election policy, TasInsure. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

In response, Ms Howlett — who was racing minister — tabled a statutory declaration from Mr Gaetani in which he said he was not aware of Tasracing's intention to issue any public communications about TasInsure.

But at a hearing in June, Tasracing's communications consultant Nic Turner provided further emails that had been sent to Mr Gaetani titled "message to industry".

On Friday, Ms Howlett was questioned about the accuracy of the statutory declaration.

Dean Winter, Labor: "You also believe the stat dec is still accurate, is that correct?" Jane Howlett: "I'm not going to comment on that. It's Mr Gaetani's stat dec, he stands by that, Mr Winter." Dean Winter: "If you're not going to correct the record, I guess I have to assume you also stand by the stat dec because if you didn't, you'd have to withdraw it." Jane Howlett: "I will need to seek some advice on that, Mr Winter."

She later told the hearing that "there is no evidence that it's false".

The hearing earlier heard evidence from Tasracing chief executive officer Andrew Jenkins that he heard details of the TasInsure policy from Ms Howlett over the phone.

Ms Howlett said she did not recall the conversation.

Facebook post still up, despite assurances

At the time, Tasracing published a statement on its website speaking positively of the TasInsure policy, which Ms Howlett then shared on her Facebook page.

She earlier said she was unaware of the post until it was brought to her attention in parliament in December.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff asked the head of the state service to investigate multiple claims regarding election guideline breaches. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Howlett told the hearing the post had been deleted; however it was still there on Friday.

Ms Howlett: "I removed the post and corrected the record as soon as I was able to." Mr Winter: "The post and the comment are still there today." Ms Howlett: "I thought I'd removed them … I would have to through and have a look." Mr Winter: "I just did, it's still there."

Head of Tasmania's state service, Kathrine Morgan-Wicks, found the Tasracing messaging breached election guidelines and recommended staff receive training.

Investigation into staffer campaign claims

Ms Morgan-Wicks is now investigating a second matter regarding election guidelines.

Last month, former staffer Sharee Minnikin-Smith told the hearing that she was asked to carry out election campaigning for Ms Howlett in 2024, despite being employed as a taxpayer-funded advisor for another Liberal MP.

She said her work was "100 per cent for Jane Howlett" during office hours.

Sharee Minnikin-Smith was employed as a ministerial staffer, but claims she was instead made to work on Jane Howlett's election campaign. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Staffers are not allowed to undertake party political activities as part of their jobs, according to the Integrity Commission.

Ms Howlett told the hearing that Ms Morgan-Wicks is investigating this evidence; the government has disputed Ms Minnikin-Smith's claims.

Ms Howlett was questioned about whether taxpayer resources were used to aid her 2024 campaign in Lyons, as alleged by Ms Minnikin-Smith under parliamentary privilege.

Ms Howlett said all work was voluntary, as a secretary of a Liberal Party branch.

Ms Howlett: "Ms Minnikin-Smith was a member of the party and believer of our great party, and she did volunteer work." Mr Winter: "Did she use public resources to support your campaign … to your knowledge?" Ms Howlett: "I don't know if she used public resources or not, I was out campaigning every day, seven days a week, seven nights. The campaign was managed by the party."

Ms Minnikin-Smith also claimed she was told to use her parliamentary email address to send an email to Tasman Peninsula constituents the day before the election titled "A strong plan for the Tasman region".

Ms Howlett read out a text message from Ms Minnikin-Smith from the following day which read: "I have done Tasman and it has gone from my parliament email, how do I change it?"

"That indicates she made an error, like many people do," Ms Howlett told the hearing.

World.title: Hopes 'mini guts' will help researchers treat inflammatory bowel disease
World.content:
Ronan Somers looks like any other 12-year-old boy, but he has been battling a hidden illness.

At times, his ulcerative colitis has stopped him from doing the things he loves.

"I couldn't do a lot of stuff because I felt very tired," he said.

"It just made my stomach hurt and cramp and when I tried to do exercise it would hurt, and I'd go to the toilet six times a day, and that was really hard for me."

Ulcerative colitis is one of the two major types of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the other being Crohn's disease.

It is marked by inflammation and ulceration in the large intestine, causing at times painful and debilitating gastrointestinal symptoms.

There is no cure, but it can be managed with medication.

Ronan Somers says at times, IBD has stopped him from being able to do things a 12-year-old typically would. (ABC News: Steve Martin)

Ronan has missed one in five days at school this year due to illness and medical appointments.

The road to diagnosis and then finding the right treatment has been long and difficult.

"It was a disease we'd never heard of before, so it was a new journey to us," Ronan's mother Jasmin Alarcon said.

She said it took 904 days after diagnosis for doctors to finally pinpoint the treatment that would work for him.

"He went on a lot of medication that didn't work, so it was a bit of a of trial-and-error stage," she said.

Researchers create 'mini guts'

Ronan's long journey to remission — a state of having symptoms under control — is a common trajectory that scientists at Monash University are hoping to turn around.

For the first time, using human samples, they have developed tiny 3D models of individual paediatric IBD patients' intestinal lining, stored separately to and alongside its accompanying bacteria.

The organoids, nicknamed "mini guts", are a game-changing research tool.

"The benefit is it allows us to study the disease in living tissue in the lab so we don't have to go to the patient, but it also allows us to develop and test new therapies," lead researcher Helen Abud said.

Professor Helen Abud says the "mini guts" are a game-changer for researchers. (ABC News: Nathan O'Brien)

Researchers have also been able to create technology to inject that same gut bacteria back into the patients' organoid models, something that gives paediatric gastroenterologist Associate Professor Edward Giles optimism.

"[We can] really try to understand in a very detailed way the interaction between the bacteria and the lining of the bowel to see if we can understand what's driving inflammation and also understand potential new targets for treatment," Dr Giles said.

3D models help researchers study the disease in living tissue in the lab, allowing them to develop and test new therapies. (Supplied: Monash University)

The hope is that the advancement will enable research that leads to more precise and tailored treatments for patients.

"We're starting to have great ability to understand some of the complexity in this disease because, unfortunately, it is complex and very individual," Dr Giles, who co-authored the research paper, said.

"We do have good treatments, but there is a huge onus on patients to go through this process, and we aren't very good at targeting the right treatment to the right patient at the beginning of their journey."

Edward Giles co-authored the research paper. (ABC News: Nathan O'Brien)

The team has created a "living bio bank" of several different organoids, based on several different patients.

"The overall goal is to find the best treatment for each individual patient so we need to have a replica of a whole diversity of individual patients," Professor Abud said.

"And this patient population is from our local paediatric Australian patients, so it's going to be relevant to patients that are being treated here."

IBD prevalence growing

Australian National University School of Medicine and Psychology Emeritus Professor Paul Pavli described the research as "exciting".

"It is a very important study. It's meticulous work, it's painstaking and it's going to provide very valuable insight into the cause of some of these diseases," he said.

"This is early days yet, but the point is they're beginning to tease out how normal bacteria and how the bacteria that are obtained from Crohn's and colitis patients cause abnormalities in both normal mini guts and mini guts derived from Crohn's and colitis patients."

Dr Pavli, who also works as a consultant in gastroenterology at Canberra Hospital, said it would enable medical professionals and researchers to understand the basic mechanisms of how the bacteria and the lining of the gut cause inflammation, and could lead to personalised medical care.

"This is leading towards personalised medicine where you can actually identify the things that go wrong that cause inflammatory bowel diseases in such patients," Dr Pavli said.

"It's not something that's going to develop in the next two or three years or even five years. It's going to take some time to develop the techniques to be able to provide any sort of personalised medicine."

IBD is estimated to affect about 180,000 Australians, and for reasons experts are not yet able to explain, that number is on the rise.

By about 2030, the number of sufferers will amount to 1 per cent of the population.

The statistics are alarming for advocates such as Leanne Raven, the chief executive at Crohn's and Colitis Australia.

Leanne Raven says IBD has the least investment in research of all chronic conditions. (ABC News: Steve Martin)

"In Australia, the prevalence and the incidence is just compounding," Ms Raven said.

"We are worried because there are so many barriers to people getting diagnosed and then getting into remission.

" For about half of the people who are diagnosed, it can take five years to get them into remission after diagnosis. "

She said a recent study by her organisation found of all chronic conditions, IBD had the lowest investment in research.

"Being able to use technology to play around and test different things and see what response you get is fantastic, really innovative work," she said.

"Research is our hope for the future."

It is something Dr Pavli agreed with, but he said the field did not receive much funding.

"Crohn's and colitis are not sexy diseases," he said.

"They're not the sorts of conditions people have heard about because … it's not dinner party conversation, so from that point of view there's not a great deal of public awareness about them.

"These conditions are quite serious conditions affecting young people significantly and anything that provides some insight into what goes wrong is going to lead to better treatments."

World.title: Kumanjayi Little Baby to be remembered at funeral service  today
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Hundreds of members of the Alice Springs community are expected to turn out to mourn Kumanjayi Little Baby at a funeral service today.

The five-year-old — referred to since her death as Kumanjayi Little Baby for cultural reasons — was found deceased south of Alice Springs on April 30, after hundreds of volunteers spent days scouring the scrub for any sign of her.

Tributes to Kumanjayi Little Baby outside the house that she was taken from in April. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Jefferson Lewis, 47, has since been charged with her murder.

Since her death, Kumanjayi Little Baby's family has been in cultural grieving, known as sorry business.

Her grandfather Robin Japanangka Granites has today invited the community to come together for her funeral and encouraged those attending to wear pink, her favourite colour.

Speaking to the ABC last week, Mr Granites said it had been a difficult time for the family, but they were rallying together for the funeral.

He also thanked community members for their support as they had searched, and then grieved, together.

Kumanjayi Little Baby's family have invited the whole Alice Springs community to join them in mourning at today's funeral. (Supplied: NT Police)

The funeral begins at 10am ACST at the Alice Springs Garden Cemetery and is expected to draw a large crowd.

Alice Springs Mayor Asta Hill said she expected the funeral would be a healing experience for the community.

"It's going to be a really difficult day, of course, but there is also a lot of beauty and generosity in our community spirit, which I think is really highlighted in the way that day's been planned," she said.

World.title: Driver trapped in crashed car after alleged Melbourne carjacking
World.content:
A driver who crashed an allegedly stolen car on a Melbourne freeway had to be cut from the wreckage before being taken to hospital under police guard.

Victoria Police said the vehicle crashed on Eastlink early this morning.

The male driver, a 19-year-old from Pakenham, suffered serious injuries and two passengers, 21 and 18 from Clayton and Silvan, were also taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Police said the white Porsche was stolen from an address in Bentleigh about 9:20pm yesterday.

A group of males, including one allegedly armed with a machete, confronted the owner of the vehicle as they arrived home and demanded the keys to the car.

The owner, a 44-year-old woman, suffered a minor injury as the alleged offenders drove off in the car.

The driver of a van hit by the allegedly stolen car suffered non-life-threatening injuries. (ABC News)

The Porsche was spotted by police being driven in a dangerous manner and at speed across Melbourne's western and southern suburbs after the alleged carjacking.

Police pursued the vehicle after spotting it travelling inbound on Eastlink in Melbourne's east about 2:10am.

Victoria Police said the car was driven with its headlights off and performed a u-turn and started driving the wrong way into oncoming traffic.

Police called off their pursuit and the Porsche collided with a van shortly afterwards.

The driver of the van, 51, suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

Police said their investigation into the incident was ongoing and anyone with information or dash cam footage has been urged to contact CrimeStoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Tobacconist charged over black market empire, weeks after his bloody kidnapping
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Tobacconist charged over black market empire, weeks after his bloody kidnapping Perry Duffin August 15, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When tactical police raided a house in the north-west Sydney suburb of Dural they found Bilal Bou-Melhem bloodied, bound and held captive for a half-million dollar ransom. Two weeks later, police were again dispatched to track down the Mount Pritchard tobacconist. This time, it would end with him in handcuffs and facing illegal tobacco, criminal group and weapons charges. Bilal Bou-Melhem was arrested in March over allegedly running a black market tobacco empire from his family’s Mount Pritchard shop. NSW Police According to police documents released by the NSW Supreme Court during a bail hearing this week, Bou-Melham is no ordinary tobacconist. The 54-year-old has a lengthy criminal history, which includes eight years in prison for trying to acquire heroin imported in car parts in 2008. The documents allege Bou-Melham had not just returned to a life of crime since his release from jail in 2014, but was directing a black market smokes empire, had collected replica weapons, and was swearing vengeance against the people who put him back behind bars.



It was in February this year when four masked men swooped on Bou-Melhem outside his tobacco shop, and were caught on camera bundling him into a waiting car. A $500,000 ransom demand was sent to Bou-Melhem’s son warning the tobacconist would “rest in piss” if it wasn’t paid. A 16-year-old boy is among seven arrested over the plot. Police at the Mount Pritchard tobacconist during a raid earlier this year. NSW Police In March, the police returned to the tobacconist to serve the 53-year-old with a firearms’ prohibition notice. Searches of the tobacconist’s premises allegedly uncovered almost 250 kilograms of illegal tobacco, about 800,000 cigarettes, including in hidden compartments, the court documents revealed. That was on top of $54,000 in cash seized in February, the suspected proceeds from the black-market smokes. At Bou-Melhem’s home they allegedly found four replica pistols, including a Derringer, an air gun and shotgun shells.



Prison phone call recordings to Bou-Melhem’s son, disclosed in the court documents, allege the tobacconist tried to keep his business operating between complaints about boredom in prison, and his diet of bread, noodles and tea. Loading He allegedly discussed organising shipments of tobacco and the collection of debts and worried he was being taped, so pushed for in-person discussions. “They can see me, but they can’t listen to me,” Bou-Melhem allegedly said. He even considered smuggling smokes into the prisons for thousands of dollars, the police documents allege.



But his entrepreneurial spirit turned to rage and vengeance toward the people he suspected of informing or working against him, police allege. Bilal Bou-Melhem being led away in handcuffs in March. NSW Police “I’m looking for the dogs that did this to me and if I catch them, I’m going to kill them,” Bou-Melhem allegedly told his son in a March call. “Tell me his name, so I can send a message, so they can bash him/kill him,” he added, learning one suspected foe was in another prison. “They are the cause of everything. I’m going to make them pay every cent.”



Other people in Bou-Melhem’s world would have to be “disciplined”, or “taught a lesson”, the tobacconist allegedly said in phone calls. Some he named, others not. “Me going to jail is on him. My loss is on him. Everything is on him. Watch what I’m going to do to him,” he allegedly sprayed down the phone. Mahmoud Bou-Melhem was arrested in May as part of the investigation. NSW Police The tobacconist also allegedly directed threats against the police who seized his cash, police documents further claim. “I’m going to f--- him when I get out,” he allegedly said.



Bou-Melhem’s son, 28-year-old Mahmoud, was charged by Strike Force Barbalin with similar alleged tobacco and proceeds of crime offences in May. Ultimately, Bou-Melhem failed in his bid for release this week. His lawyer argued for house arrest, but the judge was unconvinced the community would be safe and he was refused bail. World.title: Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals
World.content:
CultureMoviesMIFF Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals Nell Geraets August 15, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If this year has made anything clear, it’s that we love “nuisance” animals. When Neil, the elephant seal, visited Seven Mile Beach near Hobart, thousands of people flocked to see him, including interstate travellers. When Jimothy, an abnormally round raccoon, was spotted zipping around the suburban streets of Seattle, he became an unofficial mascot for the local baseball team. And when the filmmakers of A24’s documentary Nuisance Bear arrived in Manitoba, they found themselves filming alongside legions of tourists, all desperately hoping to capture footage of the region’s migrating polar bears. Nuisance Bear documents the complicated coexistence between humans and migrating polar bears. But as adorable, funny or downright strange as it may be to see these wild animals encroaching on “human” spaces, Canadian filmmakers Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden discovered there’s something more insidious going on beneath the surface. “The more famous an animal gets, the more likely it’s going to die because there are just too many people harassing it,” says Weisman, co-directer of Nuisance Bear. “It will become too comfortable with humans, and then it will cross that line. It’s always the animal that loses.”



He encountered this harsh reality when filming Nuisance Bear, a 10-year project that won the Grand Jury Prize for US Documentary at Sundance, and is now screening at the Melbourne International Film Festival. Shot in Churchill, Manitoba – the “polar bear capital of the world” – and the nearby Inuit community of Arviat, the film explores the uneasy coexistence between humans and migrating polar bears, as climate change delays the seasonal freezing of Hudson Bay. Loading Just like Neil and Jimothy, the Manitoba polar bears attract major attention as they meander through populated towns. However, the documentary demonstrates how general wildlife appreciation can transform into spectacle, putting both ourselves and the animals at risk. It goes beyond our actions – even our perception of wildlife is flawed. When picturing polar bears, most envision the pristine arctic, areas untouched by humans. But Weisman says this is a colonial idea used to push Indigenous people off the land. “Before colonisation, there were nomadic people moving all around. There were always people interacting with animals everywhere, and so it’s a newer idea that there’s this separation between ourselves and the wilderness.”



Related Article MIFF Striking hakas and alien appendages: Inside the new wave of New Zealand horror It’s largely because of this constructed distinction that we’re so fascinated with “nuisance” animals. They appear mysterious and “other”, Osio Vanden says, and therefore something people want to immortalise on camera. This, however, can transform into harassment or habituate animals to human spaces. “On one hand, I love seeing [Jimothy] emerge from the woods and show that not all raccoons look the same,” Osio Vanden says. “Witnessing animals’ survival abilities is very inspiring. But all these things are a double-edged sword.” Take Neil the seal, who, according to the Department of Natural Resources and Environment, racked up a damage bill of $45,674 thanks to his bollard-smashing and traffic-cone crunching antics. Meanwhile, some US wildlife officials have expressed concern over Jimothy fans desperately seeking selfies with the raccoon (who is believed to have a disorder called short spine syndrome) since this could disrupt his natural behaviours.



Neil, the seal, has become an Aussie icon. But could his fame do more harm than good? Rebecca Morris, Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania Jimothy the raccoon went viral online because of his abnormally round body and long legs, which some believe to be the result of a disorder called short spine syndrome. Kiana Hall/Instagram The irony, Weisman says, is that these “pest” animals are actually more like us than we realise. The ingenuity required to survive alongside humans and thwart our efforts to drive them away rivals only our own. We may not look like a 1000-kilogram seal, and we may not love rubbish as much as Jimothy, but Weisman believes they still trigger deep reflection about how we live on the land and take up space. So, who is the real nuisance? It’s certainly not the animals, Osio Vanden says. “The bear in our film is constantly being pestered by crackers and cars when it’s just trying to go along its migration path. I imagine for most animals trying to navigate a human world, it’s super complex … We’re always thinking about how these things affect us, but how do we affect them? We’re a huge problem for ourselves and for all the living things we share this planet with.”



Related Article MIFF Young people are struggling like never before. These films ask why Nuisance Bear doesn’t point a finger at anyone in particular. While the Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities differ in their approach – the former generally support sustainable polar bear hunting while the latter tend to capture and relocate – the documentary doesn’t “pick a side”, other than, perhaps, the bear’s. Ultimately, Weisman hopes audiences never look at “nuisance” animals the same way. “When engaging with wildlife, they’re not just a spectacle. They look back at us. They’re affected by our behaviour. They’re sensitive – much more sensitive than humans are. We like to think that animals are not as intelligent as us because it justifies our cruelty. I just hope that people will look at ‘nuisance’ animals in a more nuanced and deep way.” Nuisance Bear will screen as part of MIFF on August 15 and 17. World.title: The NRL would be mad not to plant a flag in Crusaders country
World.content:
SportRugby UnionNew Zealand rugby Opinion The NRL would be mad not to plant a flag in Crusaders country Paul Cully Rugby columnist August 15, 2026 — 9:30am

August 15, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians hold many misconceptions about New Zealand and the interaction between rugby union and rugby league, bringing their own prejudices to the table as they try to characterise the NRL’s rise across the Tasman with the same “code war” terms that define the Australian landscape. But New Zealand sports fans are polymaths, happy to toggle between the Warriors and the All Blacks or Super Rugby teams, which is why Sky Sport enjoys such “dual screen” usage across the ditch, with punters happy to watch one game on their linear channel while using the broadcaster’s digital platform to watch the other code. Christchurch Stadium hosted the Warriors v Cowboys match in June. Getty Images Compare that to Australia. One of the cultural surprises I experienced when moving to Australia in the early 2000s was to discover that it wasn’t a rugby country, but a rugby league country ready to experience exponential growth once the sport’s governance was sorted out. Acquaintances with deep rugby league allegiances outnumbered rugby lovers by 10-1, and of that rugby league cohort many weren’t just ambivalent about the 15-man code – they actively wanted to see it fail.



But when the move to New Zealand was made more than a decade ago – long before the Wahs phenomenon – it was clear rugby league had a foothold: you could measure it by the sheer amount of NRL footy shorts sported by a younger demographic. The Warriors perform the haka before last weekend’s NRL clash against Penrith. Getty Images It is not uncommon for New Zealanders to love rugby and also have a preferred NRL side, which they follow with affection. So, if the NRL expands and puts a second team in New Zealand’s South Island, it will not necessarily be the death of rugby but an accurate reflection of a country that is sports-mad and produces an apparently endless supply of collision-sports athletes. Let’s get real about the NRL player depth fears. I could go through every one of the 14 New Zealand provinces in their National Provincial Competition and pick two players not contracted by Super Rugby teams who would be good enough to play in the NRL tomorrow.



And that’s even before the NRL goes deeper into the First XV rugby system. The NRL, in fact, would be mad not to plant a flag in Christchurch, the heart of Crusaders country, because the South Island is ready to host a side in terms of talent, stadium and supporter interest. Furthermore, the operator of Forsyth Barr Stadium in Dunedin would be keen to host up to four games a season, according to sources not authorised to comment publicly due to confidentially reasons. A second Kiwi team would only fail if the NRL asks too much of local government. New Zealand does not have the apparently limitless ability of Australian state governments to spend taxpayer money on sports teams. If the NRL asks for too much, it invites political risk because voters’ tolerance for the government largesse that has become de rigeur in Australia is much lower.



What will it mean for rugby? There will probably be a few stages. The first will be a bit of natural anxiety, the second will be the ditching of any complacency that still remains about rugby’s position in the pecking order (and that is a good thing), and the third will be the acceptance or even celebration that Christchurch can support two codes. Another perspective NRL 2026 Track record of New Zealand NRL bid team boss raises questions You will find that the Crusaders and the potential second New Zealand team would have the capacity and willingness to co-exist in a way that would be alien in Australia. You could even see someone such as All Blacks and Crusaders icon Richie Mo’unga, whose brothers played rugby league, expressing a desire to finish his career in the 13-man code in his home city of Christchurch. There will be other compelling bids for the 20th NRL licence, particularly from Ipswich, on the outskirts of Brisbane.



If cash is the deciding factor, south-east Queensland will probably win. But if the NRL is serious about making their code the sport of the Pacific, the South Island of New Zealand is the obvious choice – especially as the Warriors have become so well embedded that a second team would be more of a rival than a threat. Rugby would have to deal with it. In fact, it could be the catalyst to look anew upon Super Rugby and ask if serious changes are required in the face of a newcomer. World.title: McIntosh is the world record holder in this event. She failed to make the final
World.content:
SportSwimmingSwimming McIntosh is the world record holder in this event. She failed to make the final Tom Decent August 15, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irvine: The hopes of Australia’s Lani Pallister securing victory in the women’s 400m freestyle at the Pan Pacific Championships have received a major boost after a disastrous heat swim from Summer McIntosh saw the world record holder miss the final. In the biggest shock of the four-day meet in Irvine, two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, the Canadian superstar could manage only the ninth-fastest time overall. Summer McIntosh of Canada looks on. Getty Images McIntosh finished third in her heat behind Pallister (4:05.22) in a time of 4:08.56, leaving her 0.2 seconds behind the eighth-fastest qualifier in China’s Fan Yaqi. McIntosh was trying to conserve energy for Friday night’s final (midday Saturday AEST) but appeared shocked at missing the final of an event where she won a silver medal behind Ariarne Titmus at the 2024 Olympics. McIntosh’s time was 14 seconds slower than her world record.



The 19-year-old did not stop to speak to media after her race but addressed her swim on Instagram. “I take full responsibility for my misjudgment in this morning’s heats,” McIntosh wrote. She will race in the ‘B’ final but cannot win a medal. Women’s 400m freestyle – heats Katie Ledecky (USA) — 4:03.48 Erika Fairweather (NZL) — 4:04.50 Kennedi Dobson (USA) — 4:05.10 Lani Pallister (AUS) — 4:05.22 Maria Fernanda Costa (BRA) — 4:06.63 Moesha Johnson (AUS) — 4:07.75 Ichika Kajimoto (JPN) — 4:07.92 Yaqi Fan (CHN) — 4:08.36 Summer McIntosh (CAN) — 4:08.56 Jillian Cox (USA) — 4:09.14 Pallister, who has a personal best of 3:58.87 and won gold in the event at the recent Commonwealth Games, will square off against US great Katie Ledecky, who was the fastest qualifier in 4:03.48.



Related Article Swimming ‘One of the most infuriating things ever’: Cooper’s lane rope drama as Harris wins 100m gold Ledecky and Pallister have posted similar times this year, with both breaking the four-minute barrier, but the American will probably start as a slight favourite. Pallister produced a shock victory over McIntosh in the women’s 200m freestyle on night one, prompting questions about the Canadian’s form after illness forced her to withdraw from races at her trials. McIntosh bounced back to win the 400m individual medley on day two – another event in which she holds the world record – ahead of Australia’s Jenna Forrester, but said afterwards she was unhappy with her performance. Pallister is more of an 800m and 1500m specialist but said she was eager to test herself in the 400m.



“I had a pretty cruisy last 300 metres,” Pallister said after her heat. “My 400 [freestyle] is just sitting in this weird little space at the moment. I want so much more for that event.” Meanwhile, Australian Sam Short is a big gold medal chance in the men’s 400m freestyle after qualifying fastest for the final in a time of 3:44.34. “It’s going to be a hot race and way quicker than this morning,” Short said. “This will be a harder win than my 800. I have been flying in the 400 but [China’s] Zhang Zhanshuo is a better competitor than Bobby Finke at the moment.”

World.title: Parramatta Powerhouse opening date revealed
World.content:
NationalNSWArts Parramatta Powerhouse opening date revealed Jessica McSweeney August 15, 2026 — 9:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Powerhouse Parramatta will officially open to the public on Saturday, November 7 in what the government is celebrating as the most significant cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House. Most of the exhibitions held at the new museum will be free, with the opening program of five exhibitions including a celebration of the world’s aviation and space history and a major exhibition chronicling the evolution of shopping centres. The doors to the $915 million Powerhouse Museum along the Parramatta River will open to the public on November 7. Steven Siewert With a construction price tag of $915 million, plus pre-opening expenses including a documentary on its opening costing around $1.7 million, the building on the banks of the Parramatta River is one of the most significant new museum projects in the world. The opening comes more than a decade after plans for the western Sydney museum were announced in 2015. “When it opens this November, Powerhouse Parramatta will transform Parramatta, linking the centre with the riverfront,” NSW Arts Minister John Graham said.



“It will bring audiences from across Sydney, NSW, Australia and the world to explore its bold exhibitions and reshape what audiences think of a museum experience.” Related Article Art Fourteen heads stacked high: covers lift on global ‘welcome’ to Parramatta Powerhouse The first exhibition, Task Eternal, will trace humanity’s quest to defy gravity and take to the skies, exploring the history of international aviation. It will include a Qantas Avro 504k aircraft, a next-generation spacesuit and a rocket engine used for the Apollo space mission in the 1960s. The exhibition will occupy the largest gallery space in the new museum and will incorporate First Nations’ art and knowledge about the sky. The exhibition of more than 600 objects is a partnership with the British Museum and the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. Another exhibition, The Mall, will examine the “history, evolution and cultural significance” of shopping centres with Western Sydney at the centre. Blacktown was the site of a world-leading shopping centre design when a Westfield opened in 1959.



Westfield went on to export the shopping centre designs from Australia across the world. Final spit and polish on the Parramatta Powerhouse. Steven Siewert The two-storey exhibition will include more than 560 objects from the Powerhouse collection, plus more than 280 loans and personal stories from the local community. Highlights include items from the archive of Victor Gruen, the architect behind modern American shopping mall design, contributions from Australian brands like Mambo and Le Specs, and Steve Jobs’ signature Levis 501 jeans. “For years and years Parra Mall was the food court of choice for workers and locals alike and one of the few places to grab a quick lunch,” local MP Donna Davis said. “While Parra Mall has made way for the Metro I look forward to the Powerhouse Parramatta exhibition taking me back to the aromas and lunchtime shopping at the mall shopping at the mall in the 90s.”



Construction giant Lendlease completed construction on the Powerhouse in May, with work now focused on preparing exhibition and public spaces. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Almost 35 years after the Mabo decision, a daughter honours her father
World.content:
CultureArt & designExhibitions Almost 35 years after the Mabo decision, a daughter honours her father Linda Morris August 15, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a white-walled gallery at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Gail Mabo, the daughter of renowned land rights activist Eddie Koiki Mabo, sits in an ordinary office chair, knotting lengths of white macrame cord. Behind her lie bamboo frames for three navigational maps – one of three new commissions created to mark the MCA’s seven year international partnership with Tate Modern. Gail Mabo making Zenadth Kes, 2026, at the Museum of Contemporary Art. Steven Siewert “Back in history, we used to have maps that we would give to people travelling through the Torres Strait,” she explains. “They were small, handheld navigational maps you could hold out toward the east to align with boundary lines. “Shells represented inhabited islands. If you aligned the map to follow the bamboo line to the next shell, you knew there’d be people and water, a place where seafarers could stop.”



The currents of the Torres Strait, known as Zenadth Kes, were notoriously treacherous. Spanish navigator Luis Vaéz de Torres sailed his galleon, the San Pedro, through these waters in 1606. Later, English naval lieutenant James Cook steered HMB Endeavour past Possession Island on his return journey after raising the Union Jack at Botany Bay and collecting turtles for meat at Cooktown. Unlike Torres, Mabo notes, Cook “didn’t stop” on a voyage that would alter the course of First Nations history forever. Mabo uses red and blue thread to trace the passages of these European explorers in works that will go on public display for the first time this Saturday for the opening of Connections: MCA x Tate. The exhibition highlights the MCA’s commitment to celebrating the histories, diversity, creativity, and resourcefulness of First Peoples on a site of first contact at Circular Quay. Helen Ganalmirriwuy Garrawurra with dugout canoe and woven pandanus sail. Steven Siewert Mabo’s interpretive maps render ocean swells and intricate currents. Shells denote the 17 mapped islands of the Torres Strait, while knotted white threads and mother-of-pearl mark the booming pearling industry established in the late 18th century following the arrival of Japanese divers. Her grandfather was one of those pearl divers. When government authorities demanded he surrender his vessel in the late 1960s, he gave it a “Viking funeral”.



“Put a light to it,” Mabo says, “and sank it. “I’ve created smaller maps before, but this is the largest I’ve ever done,” she adds. “My little book scribbles are finally coming to life.” Connections features 15 of the 35 works jointly acquired by both institutions through a $2.75 million gift from the Qantas Foundation in 2015, which were featured at Tate Modern in 2021 for A Year in Art: Australia 1992 —a landmark exhibition that MCA Director Suzanne Cotter credits with elevating “the visibility of Australian artists on the world stage while building a shared collection of remarkable works that speak to the histories, experiences, and ideas shaping Australia.” The partnership also supported Richard Bell’s monumental Embassy installation in Tate’s Turbine Hall in 2023. Gail Mabo’s knotted shells. Steven Siewert



While Mabo learnt macrame from her mother, Bonita, these three maps – representing the western, central, and eastern straits – honour her father. Next year marks 35 years since the High Court handed down its landmark Mabo decision, overturning the legal fiction of terra nullius – the doctrine that Australia belonged to no one before 1788. Eddie Mabo passed away just months before the ruling was delivered. “I know in my heart he was with us that day,” she reflects. “I looked up at the sky, saw the clouds rolling away, and thought, ‘Yeah, he’s ready. Ready to dance.’” Expanding on the themes of cosmology, navigation, and migration, Yolngu artist Helen Ganalmirriwuy Garrawurra of East Arnhem Land has created a lip-lipa – a wooden dugout canoe fitted with a woven dhomola (sail) and painted with clan designs associated with the ancestral Djan’kawu sisters, creator beings of the Dreaming. The historic development of this nimble sail enabled long-distance sea travel across Arnhem Land waters, facilitating lucrative trade between Yolngu communities and Makassan (Indonesian) merchants. “My two daughters’ boys – my grandsons – helped me chop the tree to make the canoe,” Garrawurra says. “A big, tall tree in the bush.”

World.title: ‘It was a good lesson’: Claudia Karvan’s Logies fashion prep
World.content:
LifestyleFashionClaudia Karvan ‘It was a good lesson’: Claudia Karvan’s Logies fashion prep Courtney Thompson August 15, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thirty-five years ago, a 19-year-old Claudia Karvan was wandering through Sydney’s Paddington markets when she stumbled upon the stall for a fledgling Australian label, started by two sisters who were only a few years older than she was. “They were just cool young sisters,” Karvan recalls. “The clothes had great structure, silhouettes and good colour palettes.” Those sisters were Nicky and Simone Zimmermann. Their eponymous label, which started with that humble market stall, would come to be one of Australian fashion’s great success stories, taking them from Paddington to Paris with a company valued at over US$1 billion ($1.43 billion) in 2024. Karvan, meanwhile, has become one of the country’s most celebrated actors. Logie nominee Claudia Karvan tries on a Zimmermann dress for this year’s ceremony. Steven Siewert That personal resonance will be captured on Sunday, when the now-54-year-old will walk the Logies red carpet wearing Zimmermann’s Valiant maxi dress. The teal look made from silk satin chiffon debuted on their Fall 2026 runway during Paris Fashion Week in March.



“It’s sort of classic, but there’s a little bit of a bohemian flow to it, there’s a bit of drama, a bit of theatre to it,” says Karvan, who’s celebrating her 13th Logie nomination with the best supporting actress in a drama nod for her role in the SBS miniseries Homebodies. Related Article Logies There’s an elephant at the Logies host Robert Irwin will have to face. No, we’re not talking about an animal “It doesn’t have a train, so I don’t have to worry about people stepping on it all night, and I definitely don’t have to worry about any wardrobe malfunctions.” The actor says she’s learnt to keep things stylish yet secure at big events after a photographer captured a wardrobe mishap at the 2010 Logies – “it was a shame but a good lesson” – and often forgoes a stylist in favour of sourcing looks herself. “I love using stylists sometimes, but they can get into your head and slightly hijack how you might want to present yourself,” she says.



Her chosen gown was one of 10 or 15 Karvan considered ahead of the awards night, though after countless red carpets, she knows what she likes – and what she doesn’t. Karvan laughs as she recalls one option she tried on: “It was literally half a dress. A full arm, shoulder, half a back and an entire leg is out of this dress. Like, where’d the dress go?” Over the years, Karvan’s style has eschewed the typical Logie attendee’s fondness for sparkle, with a preference for vintage finds or local designers like Anna Cordell and Romance Was Born. Claudia Karvan wearing a red vintage dress from The Diva’s Closet at the 2004 TV Week Logie Awards. Getty Images “She’s exciting because she always does something different,” says fashion stylist Donny Gallela, who calls her decision to wear Zimmermann this year “a match made in heaven”.



“She’s not scared to stand out, have some fun. She’s a real creative soul and loves supporting Aussie designers.” Karvan says this year’s awards hold a special significance due to the indie Homebodies getting recognised, and her close friend Deborah Mailman being inducted in the Logies Hall of Fame. “The whole night will be about her and just celebrating her,” Karvan says. “I’m so excited.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter.
