World.title: Tobacconist charged over black market empire, weeks after his bloody kidnapping
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Tobacconist charged over black market empire, weeks after his bloody kidnapping Perry Duffin August 15, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When tactical police raided a house in the north-west Sydney suburb of Dural they found Bilal Bou-Melhem bloodied, bound and held captive for a half-million dollar ransom. Two weeks later, police were again dispatched to track down the Mount Pritchard tobacconist. This time, it would end with him in handcuffs and facing illegal tobacco, criminal group and weapons charges. Bilal Bou-Melhem was arrested in March over allegedly running a black market tobacco empire from his family’s Mount Pritchard shop. NSW Police According to police documents released by the NSW Supreme Court during a bail hearing this week, Bou-Melham is no ordinary tobacconist. The 54-year-old has a lengthy criminal history, which includes eight years in prison for trying to acquire heroin imported in car parts in 2008. The documents allege Bou-Melham had not just returned to a life of crime since his release from jail in 2014, but was directing a black market smokes empire, had collected replica weapons, and was swearing vengeance against the people who put him back behind bars.



It was in February this year when four masked men swooped on Bou-Melhem outside his tobacco shop, and were caught on camera bundling him into a waiting car. A $500,000 ransom demand was sent to Bou-Melhem’s son warning the tobacconist would “rest in piss” if it wasn’t paid. A 16-year-old boy is among seven arrested over the plot. Police at the Mount Pritchard tobacconist during a raid earlier this year. NSW Police In March, the police returned to the tobacconist to serve the 53-year-old with a firearms’ prohibition notice. Searches of the tobacconist’s premises allegedly uncovered almost 250 kilograms of illegal tobacco, about 800,000 cigarettes, including in hidden compartments, the court documents revealed. That was on top of $54,000 in cash seized in February, the suspected proceeds from the black-market smokes. At Bou-Melhem’s home they allegedly found four replica pistols, including a Derringer, an air gun and shotgun shells.



Prison phone call recordings to Bou-Melhem’s son, disclosed in the court documents, allege the tobacconist tried to keep his business operating between complaints about boredom in prison, and his diet of bread, noodles and tea. Loading He allegedly discussed organising shipments of tobacco and the collection of debts and worried he was being taped, so pushed for in-person discussions. “They can see me, but they can’t listen to me,” Bou-Melhem allegedly said. He even considered smuggling smokes into the prisons for thousands of dollars, the police documents allege.



But his entrepreneurial spirit turned to rage and vengeance toward the people he suspected of informing or working against him, police allege. Bilal Bou-Melhem being led away in handcuffs in March. NSW Police “I’m looking for the dogs that did this to me and if I catch them, I’m going to kill them,” Bou-Melhem allegedly told his son in a March call. “Tell me his name, so I can send a message, so they can bash him/kill him,” he added, learning one suspected foe was in another prison. “They are the cause of everything. I’m going to make them pay every cent.”



Other people in Bou-Melhem’s world would have to be “disciplined”, or “taught a lesson”, the tobacconist allegedly said in phone calls. Some he named, others not. “Me going to jail is on him. My loss is on him. Everything is on him. Watch what I’m going to do to him,” he allegedly sprayed down the phone. Mahmoud Bou-Melhem was arrested in May as part of the investigation. NSW Police The tobacconist also allegedly directed threats against the police who seized his cash, police documents further claim. “I’m going to f--- him when I get out,” he allegedly said.



Bou-Melhem’s son, 28-year-old Mahmoud, was charged by Strike Force Barbalin with similar alleged tobacco and proceeds of crime offences in May. Ultimately, Bou-Melhem failed in his bid for release this week. His lawyer argued for house arrest, but the judge was unconvinced the community would be safe and he was refused bail. World.title: Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals
World.content:
CultureMoviesMIFF Love watching Neil the seal? This doco unearths the truth about ‘nuisance’ animals Nell Geraets August 15, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If this year has made anything clear, it’s that we love “nuisance” animals. When Neil, the elephant seal, visited Seven Mile Beach near Hobart, thousands of people flocked to see him, including interstate travellers. When Jimothy, an abnormally round raccoon, was spotted zipping around the suburban streets of Seattle, he became an unofficial mascot for the local baseball team. And when the filmmakers of A24’s documentary Nuisance Bear arrived in Manitoba, they found themselves filming alongside legions of tourists, all desperately hoping to capture footage of the region’s migrating polar bears. Nuisance Bear documents the complicated coexistence between humans and migrating polar bears. But as adorable, funny or downright strange as it may be to see these wild animals encroaching on “human” spaces, Canadian filmmakers Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden discovered there’s something more insidious going on beneath the surface. “The more famous an animal gets, the more likely it’s going to die because there are just too many people harassing it,” says Weisman, co-directer of Nuisance Bear. “It will become too comfortable with humans, and then it will cross that line. It’s always the animal that loses.”



He encountered this harsh reality when filming Nuisance Bear, a 10-year project that won the Grand Jury Prize for US Documentary at Sundance, and is now screening at the Melbourne International Film Festival. Shot in Churchill, Manitoba – the “polar bear capital of the world” – and the nearby Inuit community of Arviat, the film explores the uneasy coexistence between humans and migrating polar bears, as climate change delays the seasonal freezing of Hudson Bay. Loading Just like Neil and Jimothy, the Manitoba polar bears attract major attention as they meander through populated towns. However, the documentary demonstrates how general wildlife appreciation can transform into spectacle, putting both ourselves and the animals at risk. It goes beyond our actions – even our perception of wildlife is flawed. When picturing polar bears, most envision the pristine arctic, areas untouched by humans. But Weisman says this is a colonial idea used to push Indigenous people off the land. “Before colonisation, there were nomadic people moving all around. There were always people interacting with animals everywhere, and so it’s a newer idea that there’s this separation between ourselves and the wilderness.”



Related Article MIFF Striking hakas and alien appendages: Inside the new wave of New Zealand horror It’s largely because of this constructed distinction that we’re so fascinated with “nuisance” animals. They appear mysterious and “other”, Osio Vanden says, and therefore something people want to immortalise on camera. This, however, can transform into harassment or habituate animals to human spaces. “On one hand, I love seeing [Jimothy] emerge from the woods and show that not all raccoons look the same,” Osio Vanden says. “Witnessing animals’ survival abilities is very inspiring. But all these things are a double-edged sword.” Take Neil the seal, who, according to the Department of Natural Resources and Environment, racked up a damage bill of $45,674 thanks to his bollard-smashing and traffic-cone crunching antics. Meanwhile, some US wildlife officials have expressed concern over Jimothy fans desperately seeking selfies with the raccoon (who is believed to have a disorder called short spine syndrome) since this could disrupt his natural behaviours.



Neil, the seal, has become an Aussie icon. But could his fame do more harm than good? Rebecca Morris, Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania Jimothy the raccoon went viral online because of his abnormally round body and long legs, which some believe to be the result of a disorder called short spine syndrome. Kiana Hall/Instagram The irony, Weisman says, is that these “pest” animals are actually more like us than we realise. The ingenuity required to survive alongside humans and thwart our efforts to drive them away rivals only our own. We may not look like a 1000-kilogram seal, and we may not love rubbish as much as Jimothy, but Weisman believes they still trigger deep reflection about how we live on the land and take up space. So, who is the real nuisance? It’s certainly not the animals, Osio Vanden says. “The bear in our film is constantly being pestered by crackers and cars when it’s just trying to go along its migration path. I imagine for most animals trying to navigate a human world, it’s super complex … We’re always thinking about how these things affect us, but how do we affect them? We’re a huge problem for ourselves and for all the living things we share this planet with.”



Related Article MIFF Young people are struggling like never before. These films ask why Nuisance Bear doesn’t point a finger at anyone in particular. While the Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities differ in their approach – the former generally support sustainable polar bear hunting while the latter tend to capture and relocate – the documentary doesn’t “pick a side”, other than, perhaps, the bear’s. Ultimately, Weisman hopes audiences never look at “nuisance” animals the same way. “When engaging with wildlife, they’re not just a spectacle. They look back at us. They’re affected by our behaviour. They’re sensitive – much more sensitive than humans are. We like to think that animals are not as intelligent as us because it justifies our cruelty. I just hope that people will look at ‘nuisance’ animals in a more nuanced and deep way.” Nuisance Bear will screen as part of MIFF on August 15 and 17. World.title: The NRL would be mad not to plant a flag in Crusaders country
World.content:
SportRugby UnionNew Zealand rugby Opinion The NRL would be mad not to plant a flag in Crusaders country Paul Cully Rugby columnist August 15, 2026 — 9:30am

August 15, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians hold many misconceptions about New Zealand and the interaction between rugby union and rugby league, bringing their own prejudices to the table as they try to characterise the NRL’s rise across the Tasman with the same “code war” terms that define the Australian landscape. But New Zealand sports fans are polymaths, happy to toggle between the Warriors and the All Blacks or Super Rugby teams, which is why Sky Sport enjoys such “dual screen” usage across the ditch, with punters happy to watch one game on their linear channel while using the broadcaster’s digital platform to watch the other code. Christchurch Stadium hosted the Warriors v Cowboys match in June. Getty Images Compare that to Australia. One of the cultural surprises I experienced when moving to Australia in the early 2000s was to discover that it wasn’t a rugby country, but a rugby league country ready to experience exponential growth once the sport’s governance was sorted out. Acquaintances with deep rugby league allegiances outnumbered rugby lovers by 10-1, and of that rugby league cohort many weren’t just ambivalent about the 15-man code – they actively wanted to see it fail.



But when the move to New Zealand was made more than a decade ago – long before the Wahs phenomenon – it was clear rugby league had a foothold: you could measure it by the sheer amount of NRL footy shorts sported by a younger demographic. The Warriors perform the haka before last weekend’s NRL clash against Penrith. Getty Images It is not uncommon for New Zealanders to love rugby and also have a preferred NRL side, which they follow with affection. So, if the NRL expands and puts a second team in New Zealand’s South Island, it will not necessarily be the death of rugby but an accurate reflection of a country that is sports-mad and produces an apparently endless supply of collision-sports athletes. Let’s get real about the NRL player depth fears. I could go through every one of the 14 New Zealand provinces in their National Provincial Competition and pick two players not contracted by Super Rugby teams who would be good enough to play in the NRL tomorrow.



And that’s even before the NRL goes deeper into the First XV rugby system. The NRL, in fact, would be mad not to plant a flag in Christchurch, the heart of Crusaders country, because the South Island is ready to host a side in terms of talent, stadium and supporter interest. Furthermore, the operator of Forsyth Barr Stadium in Dunedin would be keen to host up to four games a season, according to sources not authorised to comment publicly due to confidentially reasons. A second Kiwi team would only fail if the NRL asks too much of local government. New Zealand does not have the apparently limitless ability of Australian state governments to spend taxpayer money on sports teams. If the NRL asks for too much, it invites political risk because voters’ tolerance for the government largesse that has become de rigeur in Australia is much lower.



What will it mean for rugby? There will probably be a few stages. The first will be a bit of natural anxiety, the second will be the ditching of any complacency that still remains about rugby’s position in the pecking order (and that is a good thing), and the third will be the acceptance or even celebration that Christchurch can support two codes. Another perspective NRL 2026 Track record of New Zealand NRL bid team boss raises questions You will find that the Crusaders and the potential second New Zealand team would have the capacity and willingness to co-exist in a way that would be alien in Australia. You could even see someone such as All Blacks and Crusaders icon Richie Mo’unga, whose brothers played rugby league, expressing a desire to finish his career in the 13-man code in his home city of Christchurch. There will be other compelling bids for the 20th NRL licence, particularly from Ipswich, on the outskirts of Brisbane.



If cash is the deciding factor, south-east Queensland will probably win. But if the NRL is serious about making their code the sport of the Pacific, the South Island of New Zealand is the obvious choice – especially as the Warriors have become so well embedded that a second team would be more of a rival than a threat. Rugby would have to deal with it. In fact, it could be the catalyst to look anew upon Super Rugby and ask if serious changes are required in the face of a newcomer. World.title: McIntosh is the world record holder in this event. She failed to make the final
World.content:
SportSwimmingSwimming McIntosh is the world record holder in this event. She failed to make the final Tom Decent August 15, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irvine: The hopes of Australia’s Lani Pallister securing victory in the women’s 400m freestyle at the Pan Pacific Championships have received a major boost after a disastrous heat swim from Summer McIntosh saw the world record holder miss the final. In the biggest shock of the four-day meet in Irvine, two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, the Canadian superstar could manage only the ninth-fastest time overall. Summer McIntosh of Canada looks on. Getty Images McIntosh finished third in her heat behind Pallister (4:05.22) in a time of 4:08.56, leaving her 0.2 seconds behind the eighth-fastest qualifier in China’s Fan Yaqi. McIntosh was trying to conserve energy for Friday night’s final (midday Saturday AEST) but appeared shocked at missing the final of an event where she won a silver medal behind Ariarne Titmus at the 2024 Olympics. McIntosh’s time was 14 seconds slower than her world record.



The 19-year-old did not stop to speak to media after her race but addressed her swim on Instagram. “I take full responsibility for my misjudgment in this morning’s heats,” McIntosh wrote. She will race in the ‘B’ final but cannot win a medal. Women’s 400m freestyle – heats Katie Ledecky (USA) — 4:03.48 Erika Fairweather (NZL) — 4:04.50 Kennedi Dobson (USA) — 4:05.10 Lani Pallister (AUS) — 4:05.22 Maria Fernanda Costa (BRA) — 4:06.63 Moesha Johnson (AUS) — 4:07.75 Ichika Kajimoto (JPN) — 4:07.92 Yaqi Fan (CHN) — 4:08.36 Summer McIntosh (CAN) — 4:08.56 Jillian Cox (USA) — 4:09.14 Pallister, who has a personal best of 3:58.87 and won gold in the event at the recent Commonwealth Games, will square off against US great Katie Ledecky, who was the fastest qualifier in 4:03.48.



Related Article Swimming ‘One of the most infuriating things ever’: Cooper’s lane rope drama as Harris wins 100m gold Ledecky and Pallister have posted similar times this year, with both breaking the four-minute barrier, but the American will probably start as a slight favourite. Pallister produced a shock victory over McIntosh in the women’s 200m freestyle on night one, prompting questions about the Canadian’s form after illness forced her to withdraw from races at her trials. McIntosh bounced back to win the 400m individual medley on day two – another event in which she holds the world record – ahead of Australia’s Jenna Forrester, but said afterwards she was unhappy with her performance. Pallister is more of an 800m and 1500m specialist but said she was eager to test herself in the 400m.



“I had a pretty cruisy last 300 metres,” Pallister said after her heat. “My 400 [freestyle] is just sitting in this weird little space at the moment. I want so much more for that event.” Meanwhile, Australian Sam Short is a big gold medal chance in the men’s 400m freestyle after qualifying fastest for the final in a time of 3:44.34. “It’s going to be a hot race and way quicker than this morning,” Short said. “This will be a harder win than my 800. I have been flying in the 400 but [China’s] Zhang Zhanshuo is a better competitor than Bobby Finke at the moment.”

World.title: Parramatta Powerhouse opening date revealed
World.content:
NationalNSWArts Parramatta Powerhouse opening date revealed Jessica McSweeney August 15, 2026 — 9:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Powerhouse Parramatta will officially open to the public on Saturday, November 7 in what the government is celebrating as the most significant cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House. Most of the exhibitions held at the new museum will be free, with the opening program of five exhibitions including a celebration of the world’s aviation and space history and a major exhibition chronicling the evolution of shopping centres. The doors to the $915 million Powerhouse Museum along the Parramatta River will open to the public on November 7. Steven Siewert With a construction price tag of $915 million, plus pre-opening expenses including a documentary on its opening costing around $1.7 million, the building on the banks of the Parramatta River is one of the most significant new museum projects in the world. The opening comes more than a decade after plans for the western Sydney museum were announced in 2015. “When it opens this November, Powerhouse Parramatta will transform Parramatta, linking the centre with the riverfront,” NSW Arts Minister John Graham said.



“It will bring audiences from across Sydney, NSW, Australia and the world to explore its bold exhibitions and reshape what audiences think of a museum experience.” Related Article Art Fourteen heads stacked high: covers lift on global ‘welcome’ to Parramatta Powerhouse The first exhibition, Task Eternal, will trace humanity’s quest to defy gravity and take to the skies, exploring the history of international aviation. It will include a Qantas Avro 504k aircraft, a next-generation spacesuit and a rocket engine used for the Apollo space mission in the 1960s. The exhibition will occupy the largest gallery space in the new museum and will incorporate First Nations’ art and knowledge about the sky. The exhibition of more than 600 objects is a partnership with the British Museum and the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. Another exhibition, The Mall, will examine the “history, evolution and cultural significance” of shopping centres with Western Sydney at the centre. Blacktown was the site of a world-leading shopping centre design when a Westfield opened in 1959.



Westfield went on to export the shopping centre designs from Australia across the world. Final spit and polish on the Parramatta Powerhouse. Steven Siewert The two-storey exhibition will include more than 560 objects from the Powerhouse collection, plus more than 280 loans and personal stories from the local community. Highlights include items from the archive of Victor Gruen, the architect behind modern American shopping mall design, contributions from Australian brands like Mambo and Le Specs, and Steve Jobs’ signature Levis 501 jeans. “For years and years Parra Mall was the food court of choice for workers and locals alike and one of the few places to grab a quick lunch,” local MP Donna Davis said. “While Parra Mall has made way for the Metro I look forward to the Powerhouse Parramatta exhibition taking me back to the aromas and lunchtime shopping at the mall shopping at the mall in the 90s.”



Construction giant Lendlease completed construction on the Powerhouse in May, with work now focused on preparing exhibition and public spaces. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Almost 35 years after the Mabo decision, a daughter honours her father
World.content:
CultureArt & designExhibitions Almost 35 years after the Mabo decision, a daughter honours her father Linda Morris August 15, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In a white-walled gallery at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Gail Mabo, the daughter of renowned land rights activist Eddie Koiki Mabo, sits in an ordinary office chair, knotting lengths of white macrame cord. Behind her lie bamboo frames for three navigational maps – one of three new commissions created to mark the MCA’s seven year international partnership with Tate Modern. Gail Mabo making Zenadth Kes, 2026, at the Museum of Contemporary Art. Steven Siewert “Back in history, we used to have maps that we would give to people travelling through the Torres Strait,” she explains. “They were small, handheld navigational maps you could hold out toward the east to align with boundary lines. “Shells represented inhabited islands. If you aligned the map to follow the bamboo line to the next shell, you knew there’d be people and water, a place where seafarers could stop.”



The currents of the Torres Strait, known as Zenadth Kes, were notoriously treacherous. Spanish navigator Luis Vaéz de Torres sailed his galleon, the San Pedro, through these waters in 1606. Later, English naval lieutenant James Cook steered HMB Endeavour past Possession Island on his return journey after raising the Union Jack at Botany Bay and collecting turtles for meat at Cooktown. Unlike Torres, Mabo notes, Cook “didn’t stop” on a voyage that would alter the course of First Nations history forever. Mabo uses red and blue thread to trace the passages of these European explorers in works that will go on public display for the first time this Saturday for the opening of Connections: MCA x Tate. The exhibition highlights the MCA’s commitment to celebrating the histories, diversity, creativity, and resourcefulness of First Peoples on a site of first contact at Circular Quay. Helen Ganalmirriwuy Garrawurra with dugout canoe and woven pandanus sail. Steven Siewert Mabo’s interpretive maps render ocean swells and intricate currents. Shells denote the 17 mapped islands of the Torres Strait, while knotted white threads and mother-of-pearl mark the booming pearling industry established in the late 18th century following the arrival of Japanese divers. Her grandfather was one of those pearl divers. When government authorities demanded he surrender his vessel in the late 1960s, he gave it a “Viking funeral”.



“Put a light to it,” Mabo says, “and sank it. “I’ve created smaller maps before, but this is the largest I’ve ever done,” she adds. “My little book scribbles are finally coming to life.” Connections features 15 of the 35 works jointly acquired by both institutions through a $2.75 million gift from the Qantas Foundation in 2015, which were featured at Tate Modern in 2021 for A Year in Art: Australia 1992 —a landmark exhibition that MCA Director Suzanne Cotter credits with elevating “the visibility of Australian artists on the world stage while building a shared collection of remarkable works that speak to the histories, experiences, and ideas shaping Australia.” The partnership also supported Richard Bell’s monumental Embassy installation in Tate’s Turbine Hall in 2023. Gail Mabo’s knotted shells. Steven Siewert



While Mabo learnt macrame from her mother, Bonita, these three maps – representing the western, central, and eastern straits – honour her father. Next year marks 35 years since the High Court handed down its landmark Mabo decision, overturning the legal fiction of terra nullius – the doctrine that Australia belonged to no one before 1788. Eddie Mabo passed away just months before the ruling was delivered. “I know in my heart he was with us that day,” she reflects. “I looked up at the sky, saw the clouds rolling away, and thought, ‘Yeah, he’s ready. Ready to dance.’” Expanding on the themes of cosmology, navigation, and migration, Yolngu artist Helen Ganalmirriwuy Garrawurra of East Arnhem Land has created a lip-lipa – a wooden dugout canoe fitted with a woven dhomola (sail) and painted with clan designs associated with the ancestral Djan’kawu sisters, creator beings of the Dreaming. The historic development of this nimble sail enabled long-distance sea travel across Arnhem Land waters, facilitating lucrative trade between Yolngu communities and Makassan (Indonesian) merchants. “My two daughters’ boys – my grandsons – helped me chop the tree to make the canoe,” Garrawurra says. “A big, tall tree in the bush.”

World.title: ‘It was a good lesson’: Claudia Karvan’s Logies fashion prep
World.content:
LifestyleFashionClaudia Karvan ‘It was a good lesson’: Claudia Karvan’s Logies fashion prep Courtney Thompson August 15, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thirty-five years ago, a 19-year-old Claudia Karvan was wandering through Sydney’s Paddington markets when she stumbled upon the stall for a fledgling Australian label, started by two sisters who were only a few years older than she was. “They were just cool young sisters,” Karvan recalls. “The clothes had great structure, silhouettes and good colour palettes.” Those sisters were Nicky and Simone Zimmermann. Their eponymous label, which started with that humble market stall, would come to be one of Australian fashion’s great success stories, taking them from Paddington to Paris with a company valued at over US$1 billion ($1.43 billion) in 2024. Karvan, meanwhile, has become one of the country’s most celebrated actors. Logie nominee Claudia Karvan tries on a Zimmermann dress for this year’s ceremony. Steven Siewert That personal resonance will be captured on Sunday, when the now-54-year-old will walk the Logies red carpet wearing Zimmermann’s Valiant maxi dress. The teal look made from silk satin chiffon debuted on their Fall 2026 runway during Paris Fashion Week in March.



“It’s sort of classic, but there’s a little bit of a bohemian flow to it, there’s a bit of drama, a bit of theatre to it,” says Karvan, who’s celebrating her 13th Logie nomination with the best supporting actress in a drama nod for her role in the SBS miniseries Homebodies. Related Article Logies There’s an elephant at the Logies host Robert Irwin will have to face. No, we’re not talking about an animal “It doesn’t have a train, so I don’t have to worry about people stepping on it all night, and I definitely don’t have to worry about any wardrobe malfunctions.” The actor says she’s learnt to keep things stylish yet secure at big events after a photographer captured a wardrobe mishap at the 2010 Logies – “it was a shame but a good lesson” – and often forgoes a stylist in favour of sourcing looks herself. “I love using stylists sometimes, but they can get into your head and slightly hijack how you might want to present yourself,” she says.



Her chosen gown was one of 10 or 15 Karvan considered ahead of the awards night, though after countless red carpets, she knows what she likes – and what she doesn’t. Karvan laughs as she recalls one option she tried on: “It was literally half a dress. A full arm, shoulder, half a back and an entire leg is out of this dress. Like, where’d the dress go?” Over the years, Karvan’s style has eschewed the typical Logie attendee’s fondness for sparkle, with a preference for vintage finds or local designers like Anna Cordell and Romance Was Born. Claudia Karvan wearing a red vintage dress from The Diva’s Closet at the 2004 TV Week Logie Awards. Getty Images “She’s exciting because she always does something different,” says fashion stylist Donny Gallela, who calls her decision to wear Zimmermann this year “a match made in heaven”.



“She’s not scared to stand out, have some fun. She’s a real creative soul and loves supporting Aussie designers.” Karvan says this year’s awards hold a special significance due to the indie Homebodies getting recognised, and her close friend Deborah Mailman being inducted in the Logies Hall of Fame. “The whole night will be about her and just celebrating her,” Karvan says. “I’m so excited.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: Probe into fatal dog attack continues
World.content:
The local MP said he was distressed to hear that a young child had died after a dog attack in the Christchurch suburb of Aranui.

Police found the child in a critical condition after being called to a house on Basingstoke Street just before 5pm on Friday. They later died at the scene.

MP for the Christchurch East electorate, Reuben Davidson, said it was a real tragedy for their family, as well as for the wider community.

Police investigators have left the scene.

The dog, which lived at the house, was removed by Animal Control and police were speaking with the residents and providing support.

"Upon arrival, emergency services located a young child in a critical condition," Senior Sergeant Dan Overend said.

"Despite the immediate efforts of first responders, and a member of the household, the child sadly died at the scene."

Basingstoke Street, Christchurch, 15 August. Tim Brown / RNZ

Overend said the dog involved was known to the occupants of the address and lived at the property.

"Occupants of the address are assisting police with enquiries."

St John said two ambulances, two rapid response units and one operations manager attended.

World.title: Pacific reach out to NZ for information on bird flu
World.content:
Pacific governments have asked New Zealand for advice on handling the H5 avian influenza, or bird flu, according to the Ministry of Primary and Industries.

An adviser on seabirds in New Zealand said Pacific countries and territories should prepare for H5 bird flu.

The avian influenza has now been detected in both Australia and New Zealand.

The Australian government reports 205 confirmed events of H5 bird flu in wild birds. The risk to human health remains low.

In New Zealand, the native bird found to be infected with the deadly H5 bird flu in Wairarapa was actually the country's first case of the virus, not the second, RNZ revealed.

The co-chairperson of the Northern New Zealand Seabird Trust, Karen Baird, has worked as a threatened migratory species adviser for the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme - SPREP.

She said it's difficult to predict when H5 bird flu will arrive in Pacific island countries.

"But obviously now it's in Australia and New Zealand, the chances of it actually getting to the Pacific are much greater. Some of the seabirds that have brought the virus to New Zealand and Australia, do range up to into the Pacific to some extent."

Baird said the biggest threat for the Pacific is its wildlife, especially in islands where some species are endemic and already under pressure.

"Those small populations of endemic species that are highly threatened ...if they got into those populations there is a potential for them to potentially wipe out some species which would be horrific.

So, yes, the potential impact for the Pacific is significant."

MPI shares information with Pacific

The Ministry of Primary and Industries chief veterinary officer has confirmed information has been shared with six Pacific countries, following questions from RNZ Pacific.

Dr Mary van Andel said MPI, in coordination with MFAT and regional partners, has received requests for information and advice relating to preparedness, surveillance, testing arrangements, wildlife management, and outbreak response.

"New Zealand has proactively shared highly pathogenic avian influenza readiness information from its readiness activities with six Pacific partner countries as part of its broader support for animal health preparedness which is funded by MFAT."

MPI said the information is being used to strengthen national planning and preparedness activities.

New Zealand has worked with regional organisations and partners to strengthen preparedness across the Pacific. This has included supporting regional training on HPAI in wildlife, developing and delivering simulation exercises in Fiji, and working with the Pacific Community (SPC) on wildlife-focused HPAI training and preparedness workshops in counties.

Pacific governments are actively monitoring the global and regional avian influenza situation, including developments in New Zealand and Australia, as part of their ongoing biosecurity and animal health preparedness activities.

Last month, the Cook Islands Ministry of Agriculture said it is taking a precautionary approach by increasing public awareness.

World.title: Strong earthquake strikes off coast of Indonesia
World.content:
A powerful earthquake has struck off the coast of Indonesia, followed by several aftershocks, the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre says, triggering an early tsunami warning by the country's geophysics agency.

The EMSC recorded a quake of magnitude 7.7 around 4.58am local time at a depth of 35 km, followed by at least three aftershocks.

USGS reports four quakes ranging from 5.5 to 6.1 in magnitude within 45 minutes after the first earthquake.

Indonesia's geophysics agency BMKG issued an early tsunami warning for some regions in the country.

A series of earthquakes off the coast of Indonesia. Screenshot / USGS

Separately, Australia's tsunami warning centre said the undersea earthquake will have "no tsunami threat to the Australian mainland, islands or territories".

World.title: 'For my wellbeing': Lulu Sun takes break from tennis
World.content:
Lulu Sun says she wants to enjoy some life outside the court, so is taking a break from top-flight tennis to escape its "relentless" demands.

In a social media post, Sun said the physical and mental requirements of life on the world tour had affected her wellbeing.

The 25-year-old, who reached the Wimbledon quarter-finals in 2024 has struggled with injuries and mixed form this year.

"I wanted to take a bit of your time to share something personal with you," she wrote on Instagram.

"In professional tennis, as in life, there is constant pressure to perfect oneself. The physical and mental demands of a competition schedule are relentless and can impact your life in more ways than one.

"With that in mind, I have decided to take some time away from competition to give myself a little space for my wellbeing and to enjoy life beyond the tennis court. It will give me the opportunity to step away from the demands of competition, reset and prepare for what's ahead."

Lulu Sun. Photosport

Sun turned professional in 2022 and switched allegiance from Switzerland to her native New Zealand two years ago, before going on her headline-grabbing Wimbledon run, where she became the first New Zealand singles player since 1983 to reach the final eight of the Grand Slam tournament.

Her world ranking has slipped from a high of 39th to 119th.

She missed January's ASB Classic in Auckland before a first-round elimination at the Australian Open, her only appearance in the main draw at a grand slam tournament this year.

It's unclear how long her break will last.

"I find it hard to express how deeply appreciative I am to all my team members, friends, family and fans for all their continuous belief in me," Sun wrote.

World.title: Hato Hone St John braced for another spike in ambulance callouts
World.content:
Some figures in this story have been updated

St John is bracing for another spike in 111 calls this weekend as record-breaking demand for ambulances continues across the motu.

Citing extreme pressure from seasonal illness, St John declared a major incident response last Sunday and activated its Emergency Operations Centre for the first time since Covid-19 emerged.

St John said its major incident declaration would remain in place this weekend as it continued to manage sustained pressure across the ambulance service.

Ambulance operations director Doug Gallagher said the past week had continued to be very busy, with Thursday's volume of calls one of the five highest on record.

St John was managing the situation closely and ensuring it was fully staffed, he said.

"On Thursday 13 August, 2404 calls came into ambulance through 111, with demand continuing at the record-breaking levels experienced over recent weeks. We expect ambulance workload to remain high this weekend," Gallagher said.

Record ambulance calls pushing already stretched system Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

"Despite the demand into ambulance [on Thursday], on average Hato Hone St John call handlers answered 94.3 percent of 111 calls within 15 seconds, and 8.3 percent of calls were managed through our Hear and Advise pathway, where patients received health advice without the need for an ambulance response. "

Saturday, 8 August was St John's busiest day on record, receiving 2562 calls through 111, a 34 percent increase from a typical day.

"Maintaining the major incident response gives us a clear national structure for monitoring demand, ambulance availability and patient-safety risks, co-ordinating decisions and resources, and taking further action as conditions change. It also supports close coordination with Health New Zealand and hospital partners," Gallagher said.

Emergency ambulance help remained available, and people should call 111 immediately when someone is seriously ill or injured, or there is an immediate threat to life, he said.

St John declares a major incident response last Sunday. RNZ/Jessica Hopkins

"For non-emergency health concerns, people are encouraged to seek advice early and check which services are available locally.

"These options may include an online GP, a pharmacist, an urgent care clinic or a free call to Healthline on 0800 611 116. This is available 24/7 and there is a callback option available if you would like Healthline to call you. Visit healthy.org.nz to find out more.

World.title: Pacific Music Awards thriving on stage, struggling behind the scenes
World.content:
The Pacific Music Awards marked its 22nd year this week celebrating Pasifika excellence in music, however organisers say the event is struggling financially.

A fixture on the New Zealand Pasifika calendar for over two decades, the awards is usually held at Manukau's Due Drop Events centre attracting a large audience with the event simultaneously livestreamed.

On the night, RnB crooner Sam V who took home the best Pacific Soul/RnB award for the fifth year running, criticised the government's level of arts funding in his award's speech.

"Mr Paul (Goldsmith) from National, you mentioned that our government is investing in the arts, I mean it's good lip service but if that's the case then the PMAs struggling don't exist," he said.

"A quick search on Google, I think you'll find that our government spends billions on our defence force - a defence force that protects us from tall poppy syndrome maybe... I'm pretty sure if we can put billions in our defence force then we can keep celebrating Pacific excellence."

The Pacific Music Awards 2026 Held at the Due Drops event Centre in Manukau ,Auckland 12 August 2026. Images Copyright Stijl 2026 Mandatory Credit Stijl / Emma Beavis Emma Beavis

However, Goldsmith, who attended the awards, said he "disagrees with those characterisations".

In a statement sent to RNZ Pacific, the minister said that the government is serious about getting the country's finances back in order.

"The Ministry and Crown entities have delivered a two per cent baseline saving, along with everyone else in this year's budget, because as a country we are still running substantial deficits."

Goldsmith reaffirmed the government's commitment to the arts in a speech at the awards, and further clarified in his statement that $1.7 billion is invested in the sector for over four years.

Yet for the Pacific Music Awards Trust, the reality of running the event is becoming precarious, pushing them to what the awards trustee Petrina Togi-Sa'ena describes "as trying to survive and keep the event alive".

In a Facebook post from mid-July, Togi-Sa'ena wrote the Trust was seeking public donations starting from $10.

"It's always humbling having to ask our community for support, when we know it's already challenging times for our people."

Paul Goldsmith at last nights PMAs Tagata Pasifika

Funding at a glance

The Pacific Music Awards receives funding through multiple government-supported agencies including Creative New Zealand, NZ on Air, New Zealand Music Commission and Pacific Media Network.

While most of the agencies have not publicly disclosed how much they have given to the awards, NZ on Air contributed up to $33,000 in the last financial year compared with up to $24,000 in 2024.

Other media reports state that Auckland Council also allocated $35,000.

Togi-Sa'ena told RNZ Pacific that existing funds have mostly gone towards the event's production and stage, trimming back spending on travel for awards finalists and winners and catering for guests.

Signature Choir. Stijl / Charl Louw

She said the trust secured several new sponsors last year, but added that there's been a reduction in government funding and other sources including gaming trusts are unable to provide more financial support.

Despite funding from various agencies, Togi-Sa'ena said the awards run on a year-to-year basis making it difficult to plan long-term. Creative New Zealand is the only major sponsor providing a three-year agreement.

"We're always in an annual cycle, so subject to each year it's working out what is the state of play each year, and then we're set in these specific timelines with funders and agencies as well," she said.

"We don't have the ability to grow, we don't have the ability for all those costs that we would love to have."

Public appeal generates support

The financial squeeze from the past three years led to a public fundraising appeal in July - Togi-Sa'ena said it was a hard call but the response has been encouraging.

"Donations have been coming in, it's created a bit more awareness, a couple of potential sponsors have reached out. Others have provided some additional support."

Togi-Sa'ena said they will be reviewing the awards format and are looking at alternative methods to raise revenue including ticket sales, community support and corporate funds.

She said that despite the uncertainty with funding, there is still a strong push from the Pasifika community to keep the event going.

World.title: Fast-track process begins for Wellington's second Mt Victoria Tunnel project
World.content:
The fast-track process has begun for a multibillion-dollar project that would radically change inner-city Wellington - but critics say it's on the "fast-track to nowhere".

On Friday, the fast-track application for the SH1 Wellington Improvements project - which envisions the construction of the second Mt Victoria and Terrace Tunnels - was officially lodged.

NZTA said it was a "significant milestone" for the project and would allow officials to protect the route.

But while $185 million has been approved for design, consents and early works, funding for major construction of the plans had not been provided, and there was no start date for building to begin.

In a Wellington City Council meeting earlier this month, councillors opposed to the plan labelled it a "ghost road" and a "ghost project", but the minister in charge insisted the government was committed to delivering it.

Wellington's Terrace Tunnel at the northbound entrance. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

What's ultimately on the cards?

An additional Mount Victoria tunnel was a National Party campaign promise, with improvements in the area discussed for years.

NZTA has previously said the total costs to design, purchase land and construct the project would cost between $2.9b and $3.8b.

It would significantly change central city roads, including adding a second Mt Victoria and Terrace Tunnel, and the roads around the Basin Reserve would be re-designed so traffic would move in both directions.

Changes would also be made in Te Aro, with three lanes on Vivian Street and Karo Drive, as well as a widening of Ruahine Street and Wellington Road in Kilbirnie en route to the airport.

Approximately 3.2 hectares of Town Belt would be taken for the project, Wellington City Council officials said in a recent agenda, while hundreds of privately-owned and commercial properties will either be purchased by NZTA or will be right next to it.

NZTA has previously said it had identified 176 properties it might need to buy, and another 146 properties where it might need to buy below-ground land, for the construction of the two tunnels.

So far, $33m has been spent on contractors and consultants.

An image showing NZTA's proposed Mt Victoria tunnel. NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi

'Ghost road' or 'gift horse'?

Debate reignited over the controversial project in a council meeting earlier this month, as councillors discussed a list of priorities officials would take to the fast-track panel.

Council officials will highlight key concerns with the project, advocating that less Town Belt land is taken, that people still have the ability to walk safely around the Basin Reserve, that there's adequate walking and cycling space through the Mount Victoria Tunnel, and that disruption from building the tunnels and roads is considered.

The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) said while timelines varied, on average it took 117 working days for a decision to be made on a fast-track application.

The panel will decide whether to approve the project, approve it with conditions, or decline it within a timeframe.

Motukairangi/Eastern Ward councillor Jonny Osborne questioned why the project was going through the fast-track process at all.

"I would note the project has no funding attached or start date. So you really have to ask yourself why are they fast-tracking it? It's fast-tracked to nowhere.

"But anyway, that's for them to decide, we at council must continue this charade."

Osborne is among a number of Green Party-backed councillors who are [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/580659/green-mps-councillors-launch-campaign-against-second-mt-victoria-tunnel-in-wellington opposed to the project, saying it "utterly ignores" the reality of climate change by increasing the number of cars on the road, including around Hataitai and Kilbirnie.

"I just want to make it clear that we as a council expect that any of the risks that arise from changes to travel patterns that may happen if this ghost project does happen are mitigated ... especially around schools and other community facilities that are frequently used by schools or other at-risk communities," Osborne said.

An artist's impression of the Mt Victoria tunnel seen from Hataitai. Supplied / NZTA Waka Kotahi

Pukehīnau/Lambton Ward and fellow Green party councillor Geordie Rogers, who described the project as a "ghost road", backed an amendment Osborne put forward which sought to use the fast-track process as a route towards pedestrianisation of Cuba Street.

He said the project would increase traffic on roads such as Taranaki Street, Ghuznee Street and Abel Smith Street.

The measure ultimately failed, with Wellington Mayor Andrew Little saying it was a "waste of time" to use the fast-track process for a separate debate on pedestrianising Cuba Street.

"Our role as council is to mitigate the worst aspects of that project."

Not all councillors agree on the issue. Independent Pukehīnau Lambton ward councillor Nicola Young has said she wants the project to go ahead, but doubted whether it would happen for years - or even decades.

The late Tony Randle, who had represented the Takapū/Northern Ward, voiced his support for it, saying it would ease long-standing bottlenecks in the city.

This was crucial if the city wanted to grow, he had said.

"I hope this project is not a charade...this is a project the Government has come and offered us, and don't look a gift-horse in the mouth.

"This will make Wellington better because we are struggling with congestion."

Inside Mount Victoria Tunnel. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Minister insists project will go ahead

In a statement, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said it wasn't true the Mt Victoria Tunnel project was on a "fast-track to nowhere", or was a "ghost road".

"The project is in the major project pipeline and we are committed to delivering it.

"The SH1 Wellington Improvements project will unlock economic growth, improve productivity, and give Wellingtonians a safer, faster and more reliable connection between the region, the CBD, the hospital and the airport."

A spokesperson for the EPA said the panel can approve a project without government funding attached, so long as it meets statutory criteria of having significant regional and national benefits.

The panel will meet with several invited parties, she said, which change depending on the project.

NZTA's project sponsor, Robyn Elston, said the application is now being reviewed by the team at the EPA.

When it has been accepted as complete it would be made public on NZTA's website, Elston said.

World.title: Aucklanders get first look inside new Karanga-a-Hape Station
World.content:
Thousands of Aucklanders are expected to get their first look inside the City Rail Link's (CRL) Karanga-a-Hape Station Saturday, as the city counts down to the opening of the $5.5 billion project.

The station is the second of three new or redeveloped stations to be opened to the public as part of a series of free "First Look" events ahead of the CRL opening to passengers on 13 September.

Karanga-a-Hape Station, in the heart of the city, features New Zealand's longest escalator, taking passengers 33 metres underground beneath Pitt Street.

Its design also includes a ceiling shaped like three Kauri snail shells, reflecting the Kauri forests that once covered the Karangahape ridgeline.

The Karanga-a-Hape Station design includes a ceiling shaped like three Kauri snail shells. Supplied: CRL

The station's opening comes after a decade of construction on the country's largest transport infrastructure project.

The CRL includes twin 3.45km rail tunnels beneath Auckland's city centre, two new underground stations at Karanga-a-Hape and Te Waihorotiu, and the redevelopment of Maungawhau Station.

When it opens on 13 September, trains will run directly through the city centre for the first time, rather than stopping at Waitematā Station.

Three 'Atua panels' designed by artist Reuben Kirkwood form the threshold element at the Karanga-a-Hape Station entrance. Supplied: CRL

Auckland Transport says the new link is expected to double the number of Aucklanders who live within a 30-minute train journey of the city centre.

At peak times, trains will run through the city centre every five minutes, while services elsewhere on the network are expected to run at an average of about 10min intervals.

Off-peak services will run every 15min throughout the day, including weekends, compared with every 20min currently.

The Karanga-a-Hape underground station will house the longest escalator in New Zealand, at 40 metres long Supplied: CRL

The station's opening date was formally announced last week by Transport Minister Chris Bishop and Auckland mayor Wayne Brown.

Bishop said the opening would mark a turning point for Auckland after a project that had been discussed for about a century and had caused years of disruption for businesses and communities during construction.

The CRL has cost $5.5b and taken about 10 years to build.

The public will have another chance to explore the new network next Saturday, when Te Waihorotiu Station will be opened for a final First Look event on 22 August.

World.title: Bezos consortium enters 'definitive agreement' to buy Liverpool stake
World.content:
A consortium containing Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is buying a minority stake in Premier League club Liverpool, the English soccer giant says.

Club owner Fenway Sports Group (FSG) said in a statement it entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale to 1892 Holdings.

The investor group is led by Amit Bhatia, who is married to a daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, and has taken a stake of more than 30 per cent in the 20-time English champion. The deal reportedly values Liverpool at around $US6 billion ($8.4 billion).

Boston-based FSG paid $US400 million to take over Liverpool in 2010 and also owns the Boston Red Sox. FSG said in July that it had been approached by the Bhatia-led consortium regarding a "strategic minority investment" in the club.

Eduardo Saverin is part of the investment group with Jeff Bezos. (Getty Images: Sam Barnes/Sportsfile)

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said in the statement.

It marks the first foray into soccer by Bezos, who, according to Forbes, is the fourth-richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US280 billion. He founded Amazon in 1994 and has been executive chairman since 2021.

Saverin is a Brazilian businessman worth about $US36 billion, according to Forbes.

Bhatia, a British-Indian entrepreneur, was the co-owner of second-tier English team Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before stepping down recently.

Amit Bhatia during his time as the chairman of Queens Park Rangers. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

"We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come," Bhatia said in the statement.

Under the leadership of FSG and its principal owner John Henry, Liverpool ended a 30-year wait to be English champion in 2020 and added another Premier League title last year. That tied Manchester United on 20 English top-flight league championships.

The club was European champion for a sixth time — a record for an English team — in 2019.

The Premier League is one of the biggest competitions in sports, with its teams now largely owned by oil-rich Gulf states or private equity.

Liverpool sack manager Arne Slot after underwhelming season The Dutchman won the Premier League title in his first season, but failed to live up to expectations the following year as Liverpool finished fifth.

Liverpool now has three of the richest people in the world as minority owners.

That does not mean, however, that the club can simply start spending recklessly in the transfer market on new players.

That is because the Premier League has financial rules in place to protect the competitive balance of the competition and ensure the financial sustainability of clubs.

In broad terms, a club's on-pitch spending is related to 85 per cent of its "football-related revenue and net profit/loss from player sales," the Premier League says.

Instead, the difference will come in how Liverpool — already one of the top teams in world soccer — is marketed more around the world under Bezos and Saverin, especially.

The deal is likely to bring more commercial revenue into the club, thereby improving its profits.

World.title: Hockeyroos and Kookaburras tackle World Cup with fresh perspectives
World.content:
Kookaburras midfielder Liam Henderson has the attitude of a winner.

It is a confidence that comes with being part of a team used to sustained excellence, backed by a growing reputation as one of hockey's global rising stars.

And in his second year on the national team, the 22-year-old is ready to deliver at the World Cup which begins this weekend.

"We think we can win it. And if other teams don't think we can, we'll just prove them wrong," he told ABC Sport from the team's base in Belgium.

Liam Henderson (right) is heading to his first World Cup. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world, and won the last of their three World Cup titles in 2014.

Recent FIH Pro League victories over the top two ranked teams, Belgium and Netherlands, mean Henderson's confidence is justified.

"Everyone brings their natural game. We're a force to be reckoned with," he said.

"The last two games we played against the two world's best, we had two wins and two losses. We can beat them. And if it's our day, anything can happen."

The Kookaburras have won the World Cup three times. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

The team's last major tournament was the Paris 2024 Olympics, which ended in an uncharacteristic quarter-final exit.

There has been significant change since then with a new coach, Mark Hager, and the retirements of some of their longest serving players including Eddie Ockenden, Aran Zalewski, and Andrew Charter.

But a hallmark of the Kookaburras throughout their history has been a constant ability to regenerate and maintain their position amongst the world's top teams.

"As a hockey community, we're always watching our national teams. And when you watch them, something you aspire to do is just be in that team," Henderson said.

The Kookaburras are ranked fourth in the world. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"And once you're there, I think every chance you get, you just want to work as hard as possible.

"I think another piece of that is the group that we have at the moment are all so close.

"We're such good mates, all of us, and such a welcoming team that you just want to play for each other. It's something you really want to be a part of."

Hockeyroos to rise up

The men's tournament will be played in Wavre, just outside of Brussels, played concurrently with the women's event in Amstelveen, Netherlands.

That is where the Hockeyroos are based, led by the most experienced player in the team, co-captain Kaitlin Nobbs, heading to her third World Cup.

She is part of one of the sport's most illustrious dynasties, with both parents having represented Australia, alongside her grandmother, aunty, and uncle — the Kookaburras coach.

Kaitlin Nobbs is playing at her third World Cup. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"Coming into this one it marks the 40th anniversary from when my mum went to a World Cup as well representing the Hockeyroos," Nobbs told ABC Sport.

"So looking at the past and reflecting and seeing where we've come from, where the Hockeyroos have come from until now, it means the world to be able to go out and represent the team and captain them."

Her dad, Michael Nobbs, died earlier this year, and has provided her with extra motivation to excel.

"I think he would be so chuffed that I'm playing and enjoying the game and trying to take the most out of it that I can," she said.

"He loved hockey more than anyone and loved watching me play. So I'm sure he'll be watching and following along from wherever he is."

The Hockeyroos are ranked eighth in the world, and after winning the last of their three Olympic golds in 2000, have not managed to reach those heights again, although bronze at the 2022 World Cup was a highlight.

Katrina Powell took over as coach just before the Tokyo Olympics in the wake of systemic cultural issues in the women's program, and after stepping down last year, she was replaced by former South Africa men's international Rhett Halkett.

The Hockeyroos have had a period of change over the past two years. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"I think we are more than capable of playing in the finals for a medal," Nobbs said.

"Rhett comes from a bit of a European background, so we've changed up how we've played in the past year.

"This year in itself has been enough stress for the next four years or the last four years because we've had to play Pro League, qualify for this World Cup, change our structure, change our way of play.

The Hockeyroos celebrate a penalty shootout win over the Netherlands, to secure a spot in next year's FIH Pro League. (Supplied: Hockey Australia)

"So it has been a crazy journey, but I think all of those things give you experience and evidence leading into big tournaments like this that you can lean on."

Growing the game

The interest in hockey is at a different level in Europe, particularly in Belgium and the Netherlands, and it is something Henderson is embracing.

"Just walking around the streets, you're seeing billboards, you're seeing [players] on bus stops," Henderson said.

"I think the general population know more about the game."

Henderson has also started to make a name for himself in India, another hockey hotbed, after fetching the highest price at the Hockey India League auction last year — around $71,500.

While not in the same ballpark as the IPL, it is a lucrative league for Australians, who usually juggle studying or work alongside playing.

"I was actually in the gym with a few of my teammates when [the auction] was going down," Henderson said.

"It was more just shock. I'd only played 11 international games at that stage. And I think just showed potentially what people think I can do.

"The team obviously were very successful, we won a tournament. It was such a valuable experience for me. You can't put a price tag on that."

Henderson and Nobbs also play in Australia's domestic league, Hockey One, and hope to see its continued growth.

"It's finally a competition that gets talked about, I think, internationally and really good players from abroad wanting to come over and be part of that competition," Nobbs said.

"We obviously compete with a lot of sports in Australia, cricket, soccer, netball, everything.

"So to have a product like that growing and something exciting that young kids can come and watch is definitely a good thing."

World.title: What went wrong for the Suns this year and how 2027 can be much better
World.content:
Sometimes an essay is needed to describe what has happened on the footy field. Sometimes a book will only start to scratch the surface.

But sometimes a single word will do it best. As the Gold Coast Suns filtered off a frigid Manuka Oval after beating GWS, one word seemed to sum up the mood in a nutshell: Finally.

For the first time since May 15, the Suns had entered the winner's circle. At the time of their last win, the Suns sat fourth on the ladder, with many believing they were poised for a real shot at a deep finals run.

But as the weeks drew shorter and the nights colder, their hopes faded.

By the start of July, the hopes of a top-four finish had effectively vanished. Two weeks later, their finals hopes were on life support. By the end of the month, even the wildcard spots were taken off the table.

Damien Hardwick summed up the year via the slightly misheard words of one of the big four of American thrash metal.

"There's a great line by Metallica that I'm going to butcher, where 'sometimes you can see the light at the end of the tunnel, but it's a freight train coming the other way'. That's how it's felt this year. That's the reality of it," he said.

Despite the season being lost, both Hardwick and his playing staff were overjoyed with the win.

"It's been … it's been a while. The boys were really hungry for a win today and I thought we brought the spirit and it was great to sing that song again," Suns star Matt Rowell told ABC Sport after the win over GWS.

For one week, everything worked as it should for the side many thought to be a premiership contender. The win wasn't just one in isolation, it also practically ended the season for their Expansion Cup rivals the Giants.

For both sides, the hope is that a small slice of pain in 2026 will set them up for success in 2027. But to do so, there has to be an understanding of what exactly went wrong.

Hardwick's hard year with Gold Coast

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks, there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after mentoring by a few others.

Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted, and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.

It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after a few others have mentored them.

Few coaches have been more highly credentialed in recent years than Hardwick. Beyond the three flags the Tigers won under his guidance, his impact across the league is clear.

While Hardwick served an apprenticeship under a more kick-mark style operator in Alistair Clarkson, his own method differed to that of former co-worker Chris Fagan. Instead, the influence of Hardwick is best seen through the defensive-first-yet-free-flowing styles exhibited by Collingwood and GWS under former Hardwick assistants Craig McRae and Adam Kingsley.

Hardwick's teams have an idiosyncratic stylistic footprint. Under his reign at Richmond, the Tigers overhauled teams with chaos, not control. The side often lost the marking battle but played surge football, running on adrenaline and enthusiasm. Instead of a side built on winning and scoring from clearances, their drive came from scoring on the intercept.

McRae and Kingsley, alongside West Coast's Andrew McQualter, have regularly influenced proceedings in September. The Hardwick school sits as a counterbalance to the way that sides such as Brisbane pick through defences by controlling the ball.

Despite being so influential to how football is played in 2026, Hardwick is quick to note that this may not have been his finest year.

"I feel I haven't had my best year as a coach with regard to bending a little bit of my system of how we want to play," he said. "So those realisations are very, very important. And these are the things that actually your greatest growth comes from."

In the wake of teams inspired by the control-heavy game styles influenced by Alistair Clarkson's Hawthorn sides, Tigerball was risky, dangerous and exciting.

All good coaches evolve over time. And all good "brands" are strategised against and countered. Football is not a solved game with a perfect way to play.

The developing Suns Hardwick inherited were quite different from the Tigers he left. Instead of building from a rock-solid counterattacking defensive unit, they led with the contested, stoppage game the premiership Tigers largely eschewed.

In 2025, Hardwick bent to accommodate both strands, leaning on rising stars Anderson, Rowell, Miller and Humphries to dominate in the middle and using Noble, Rioli and Jeffrey to provide drive on the counterattack.

There were clear parts of the game plan that held strong across both seasons. Gold Coast continued to lean on handball more than most and played into chaotic situations.

But the other part of the balance, that of the stoppage game, fell away.

Last year, the Suns finished +3.3 in clearance differential and third in the league for scoring differential from stoppages.

This year — with a group in flux with early season injuries to Matt Rowell and the incorporation of Christian Petracca — the Suns sit last for clearance differential and fourth-worst for stoppage scoring differential.

Notably, the win in Canberra came in one of the hardest, most contested games of the season. The game was cold, wet and physical and played largely at ground level. The sides combined for just 96 marks all day — about half of the average game this year.

"We love the wet weather footy, as you can tell, and I think it really suited us today," midfielder Bodhi Uwland told ABC Sport post-game.

ABC AFL Daily podcast Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron are joined by a rotating cast of AFL legends, including some of the sharpest minds in the game, to pull apart the biggest stories in Aussie Rules.

"We like being a contested team, that surge mentality, like getting the ball forward. And I think we really showed that today and we're able to really adapt to the conditions."

The Suns played for territory first and results later in Canberra. Despite dominating hitouts and clearances, the Giants still scored more from stoppage. But the high defensive wall that the Suns were able to establish helped the Suns re-enter the winner's circle.

Reigning Brownlow Medallist Rowell led the way for the Suns with one of the finest games imaginable in tough conditions. Despite the number of accolades he has already accumulated in his short career, the game may have been one of his best yet.

"That's one of the best performances I've seen from Rowell, to be honest, like, especially from behind the ball. Seeing him u-turning out of stoppage, shrugging tackles and just getting it forward … and he did it so consistently throughout the game. It was an amazing performance." Uwland said.

It wasn't just his teammates who were effusive about his effort.

"Yeah, he's a difference maker. It's a pleasure to have a guy like that in our footy club who, you see, the way the game plays today." Hardwick added.

"You know, it's 40-odd possessions, 22 contested, I think 18 tackles and 12 clearances as well. It's just one of those games you go, 'Wow'.

"You know, they're video game numbers, but he revels in those conditions. You know, that's the way he plays the game and it's such a pleasure to watch those players that give absolutely everything."

Rowell's preseason Origin injury threw the Suns' midfield balance off at the start of the season and left the side looking for what was their best look through the middle as the season developed. The Suns are blessed with highly capable players at the contest, with more bodies than opportunities most weeks.

The game in Canberra was a hint of what it could look like when it worked for the Suns.

Despite reports in the media of a loss of connection in recent weeks, at least in wake of the win the connection between coach and group seemed to be growing and evolving through the adversity.

"We haven't had the year we've wanted, but I think he's been really impressed by the way we've kept our spirit as a group," Rowell said.

"Even though we can't make finals, we've still got a lot of pride as a group. I think that really showed today. Yeah, Dimma's (Hardwick's) connection with the group is growing each game."

Suns keen to rise in 2027

In the wake of the Canberra game, attention for both sides turned, at least a little, to next season. The balance between running out a season where a premiership is an impossible task and preparing for the next one is a tough balance to strike for all teams.

"Yeah (2027 starts now). We have spoken about that. You look at Sydney — a great example from last year. You know, they had a disappointing year, much like we have this year, and they sort of went to work on some things. Look where they are now." Hardwick said after the game.

"That was our challenge. We spoke to the players about it. Noah and his leaders have just been absolutely leading the charge in that space."

Given how few competitive games there are each year, not a single one needs to be wasted. A flag is always the goal for each of the league's 18 clubs, even if it's not this year's.

Having shown the quality to win a final last year, Gold Coast's prospects of recovery look reasonably bright. Roughly half of the teams in the 18-team era to win a final then dip to double-digit ladder placings returned to finals the following year.

Most of the rest took two years to get back, with Melbourne and Collingwood grabbing the 2021 and 2023 flags. Most encouragingly, only three times since 2012 has a finals-winning team immediately crashed down the ladder and failed to recover at all.

These gap years have almost become routine as footy becomes ever more even and competitive. Almost every year since 2020, at least one side has found itself dipping and another recovering from such a dip.

The one slight pause for both the Suns and Giants is the relatively low placement of all four of the Hardwick-styled teams in 2026. Of the four, only McRae's Pies will play finals, entering via the wildcard round. As always, the question will be whether that style of play is conducive to winning football in 2026 and beyond, or whether the next evolution is upon us already.

Still, the Gold Coast list might be the most talented in the league. If they can get the strategic balance right, and a little luck to fall their way, the sky is the limit for this Suns group.

World.title: Freo locks up minor premiership after downing Crows in thriller
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Caleb Serong played a starring role as Fremantle snared just the second minor premiership in the club's history with a 24-point win over Adelaide in Perth.

Scores were level early in the final quarter of Friday night's blockbuster following Crows forward Riley Thilthorpe's second goal of the night.

But buoyed by a thundering 55,010-strong crowd, Fremantle did what it has done all season — blowing its rival off the park with a devastating burst.

Michael Frederick started the run when he nailed a tough set shot after being tackled high.

Jye Amiss (centre) kicked 5.1 in the win while Josh Treacy (right) took six contested marks. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Although Josh Treacy, Luke Jackson and Andrew Brayshaw missed their shots after that, Amiss bobbed up for his fifth goal of the night by snapping from the goalsquare.

And when Isaiah Dudley dodged and weaved his way through three Crows players before unleashing a successful snap, the margin was 22 points and it was game over.

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox rubbed it in by roughing up an opponent and then pointing to the scoreboard after kicking a goal in the dying minutes of the 16.16 (112) to 13.10 (88) win.

The triumph boosted Fremantle's record to 19-3, securing the club a second minor premiership to go with their 2013 efforts.

It also meant Fremantle will end the home-and-away season with a perfect 12-0 record at Perth Stadium.

Adelaide (14-8) now faces a huge battle to snare a top-four berth, with the loss even leaving them vulnerable to slipping into the dreaded wildcard spots from seventh to 10th.

Amiss finished with 5.1 in a powerful display, Josh Treacy was huge with six contested marks but a wayward 1.4, Dudley kicked three goals, while Serong was influential with 29 disposals, 12 clearances, 536m gained and two goals.

Crows playmaker Izak Rankine racked up a monster 14 disposals in the opening term on the way to 39 possessions, 10 clearances, 717m gained and one goal.

Adelaide star Izak Rankine finished the match with a game-high 39 disposals. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Adelaide had an interesting lead-in to the match, with players forced to evacuate their hotel just hours before bounce down due to a fire alarm going off in their hotel.

Amiss missed an early set shot sitter from 15m out as Adelaide skipped out to a two-goal lead.

But Amiss soon made amends, nailing three other set shots for the term — from 50m, 40m and 35m — to give Fremantle a 13-point edge by quarter time.

Fremantle led by just five points at half-time, and the third quarter was a rollercoaster ride featuring four lead changes and five occasions when the scores were even.

Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce suffered a huge scare when his heavily-strapped left knee hyper-extend during a collision, leaving him hobbled for the next couple of minutes.

The action was fierce and fast, but it was Fremantle who produced more of the memorable moments.

Treacy hurt himself while completing a team-lifting tackle on Max Michalanney.

The Fremantle powerhouse dusted himself off after a few deep breaths and kicked a goal moments later.

Serong nailed a goal from just inside the centre square following a dazzling series of handballs from the Dockers.

And when Brayshaw dribbled one through with the outside of his right boot, Fremantle turned for home with a seven-point edge.

The Dockers kicked five goals to three in a powerful final term to wrap up top spot on the ladder with one round to spare.

AAP
